evt-funerary-customs: Aerial view of the Tunnug 1 burial mound in the Uyuk Valley, Tuva — one of the earliest large Scythian royal kurgans, currently under excavation.
evt-scythian-animal-style: A gold panther plaque from the Krasnodar region (late 7th century BC), its curled body and stylized musculature a textbook example of Scythian animal-style metalwork.
evt-scythian-mirror: Two Iron Age Scythian bronze mirrors — plain circular discs with a central handle loop, the standard form found across kurgan burials from Ukraine to Siberia.
evt-scythian-triad: The great gold pectoral from Tovsta Mohyla (4th century BC) unites all three poles of the Scythian triad in a single object: animal-style art, elite goldsmithing, and the ritual adornment of a warrior-king.
evt-anacharsis: A portrait engraving of Anacharsis derived from an ancient gem — the Scythian prince who traveled to Greece around 590 BC and was later counted among the Seven Sages.
evt-olbia-colony: Excavated ruins of Olbia (Greek Olbia Pontica) on the Black Sea shore in modern Ukraine — the main Greek trading post through which Scythian grain, furs, and slaves flowed south to the Aegean.
evt-amber-route: The European Amber Road, tracing the prehistoric trade network that carried Baltic amber south through Poland and central Europe to the Mediterranean world.
evt-greek-black-sea-trade: Bronze arrowhead proto-money from the Greek Black Sea region — cast in the shape of Scythian arrow tips, these served as small-denomination currency in the coastal trading ports where Greeks and Scythians exchanged goods.
evt-darius-invasion: A map of Darius I's 513 BCE campaign route north of the Black Sea into Scythian territory, tracing the Persian army's fruitless chase across the steppe as the Scythians refused to fight.
evt-herodotus-scythians: Marble bust of Herodotus, the Greek historian who dedicated Book IV of his Histories to a detailed account of Scythian lands, customs, and origin myths (Metropolitan Museum of Art).
evt-panticapaeum-trade: Ruins of ancient Panticapaeum (modern Kerch, Crimea), the Greek colony that became the commercial hub linking Scythian grain and slaves to the Mediterranean world.
evt-kul-oba-kurgan: Gold vase from the Kul-Oba kurgan (Crimea, second half of the 4th century BC), its relief frieze depicting Scythian warriors in characteristic dress — one of the finest pieces recovered from a royal burial mound.
evt-solokha-kurgan: The Solokha gold comb (c. 430–390 BC), recovered from the Solokha kurgan near the Dnieper River, its sculpted handle showing three Scythian warriors in a fierce cavalry clash — a masterpiece of steppe goldsmithing.
evt-scyles: Coins attributed to the Scythian king Scyles, whose embrace of Greek rites at Olbia so enraged his subjects that they deposed and executed him — the only material evidence of his reign.
evt-scythian-archers-athens: Red-figure plate by the Athenian potter Epiktetos (c. 520–500 BC) depicting a Scythian archer in spotted tunic and pointed cap, carrying his characteristic bow and gorytus — Greek evidence of the foreign bowmen who policed Athens.
evt-scale-armor: A modern reconstruction of a Scythian mounted warrior, showing the overlapping iron scale armor (lorica squamata-style) that gave steppe fighters both flexibility and protection in close combat.
evt-tabiti-goddess: A 4th-century BC Scythian gold plaque from Ivanovskaya stanitsa depicting the snake-legged Great Goddess, the divine figure scholars identify with Tabiti, supreme deity of the Scythian pantheon.
evt-sword-cult: A Scythian sword with an elaborately worked gold scabbard from Velyka Bilozerka, 4th century BC — the kind of weapon that served as a living altar to Ares, thrust blade-first into a great earthen platform during the annual sword cult ceremony.
evt-scythian-shamanism: A Pazyryk felt hanging (5th–4th century BC) showing a horseman approaching an enthroned figure beside a sacred ritual tree — one of the richest surviving images of Scythian-world ceremonial and shamanic practice.
evt-enarees: Detail of the gold Karagodeuashkh headdress (4th century BC) showing ritual figures in ceremonial dress, from a kurgan burial that may be linked to the enarees — the gender-transgressive Scythian shamans described by Herodotus.
evt-scythian-women-warriors: A Greek red-figure vase painting (Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich) showing an Amazon warrior in the patterned leggings and tunic characteristic of Scythian dress — the Greek visual shorthand for the steppe women fighters whose burial archaeology has since confirmed were real.
evt-tomyris: Peter Paul Rubens, "The Head of Cyrus Brought to Queen Tomyris" (c. 1622–23): the Massagetae queen fulfills her vow to give the Persian king his fill of blood after he killed her son — one of antiquity's most memorable acts of vengeance.
evt-pazyryk-burials: The Pazyryk burial mounds rise from the Altai highland steppe in Siberia, where the region's deep freeze preserved tombs and their contents for over two thousand years.
evt-scythian-tattoos: A scholarly reconstruction of the tattoos found on the Pazyryk 2 mummy, showing the elaborate animal-style designs — griffins, deer, and predatory cats — that covered his arms, torso, and legs.
evt-zopyrion-disaster: Ancient bronze helmet and sword hilt from the Moldovan steppe, the region where Zopyrion's Macedonian army was annihilated by Scythian forces around 331 BCE.
evt-sarmatian-displacement: Sarmatian cataphracts in full scale-armor, carved on Trajan's Column — the heavily armored cavalry tradition that let the Sarmatians overwhelm and displace the Scythians from the Pontic steppe.
evt-scythian-neapolis: Aerial view of Scythian Neapolis (near modern Simferopol, Crimea), the last refuge city of the Crimean Scythians, showing the surviving stone tower and excavated foundations.
evt-skilurus: The mausoleum at Scythian Neapolis where King Skiluros was buried, a rare surviving stone structure from the late Scythian kingdom in Crimea.
evt-palakus: Stone relief portrait of King Palakus, son of Skiluros, who led the Crimean Scythians in their prolonged struggle against the expanding Pontic Kingdom.
evt-strabo-late-scythians: Portrait engraving of the Greek geographer Strabo, whose Geography recorded the remnant Scythians of Crimea and the steppe as a diminished people overwhelmed by Sarmatians and Romans.
evt-ovid-exile: Eugène Delacroix, Ovid Among the Scythians (1859) — the exiled Roman poet depicted reclining in the steppe, tended by nomads, a romantic rendering of his miserable years on the Black Sea frontier.
evt-chertomlyk-kurgan: The silver amphora from the Chertomlyk kurgan, a 4th-century BCE Scythian royal burial near the Dnieper River, decorated with scenes of horse taming that blend Greek craftsmanship with Scythian subject matter.
evt-alexandropol-kurgan: The Alexandropol kurgan as it appeared before excavation in 1852–1856, one of the largest Scythian royal burial mounds on the Ukrainian steppe, yielding weapons, horse gear, and Greek-made vessels.
evt-earliest-maya-settlements: A map of the Maya world spanning southern Mexico through Honduras, marking both the Classic-era cities and the older Preclassic sites where the civilization first took root.
evt-maya-earliest-pottery: A painted Maya ceramic cylinder vase from Sacul, decorated with a seated lord and glyphic text — early evidence of the sophisticated pottery tradition that emerged from the Preclassic Maya.
evt-nakbe-monumental: Stone steps climbing through the Petén jungle at Nakbe, one of the earliest Maya sites where monumental architecture appeared around 1000 BCE — centuries before the great Classic cities rose.
evt-el-mirador-rise: La Danta pyramid at El Mirador rises above the Petén canopy — at roughly 230 feet, one of the largest pyramids ever built, constructed during El Mirador's peak in the late Preclassic period.
evt-maya-sacbe-roads: A sacbe at Dzibilchaltún stretches arrow-straight through the Yucatán scrub, its raised white limestone causeway still linking plazas across the site as it did during the height of the Classic period.
evt-maya-script-origins: A grid of carved Maya hieroglyphs from Palenque — the same intricate glyph-block system that first appears in inscriptions around 300 BCE and would go on to record everything from royal lineages to star tables.
evt-san-bartolo-murals: A fragment of the San Bartolo murals — painted around 100 BCE and discovered in 2001, these vivid scenes of Maya gods and creation mythology are the oldest known narrative paintings in the Maya world.
evt-maya-long-count: The east face of Quiriguá Stela C, whose Long Count inscription records one of the earliest written Maya calendar dates — a monument to the civilization's obsessive, precise tracking of time.
evt-tikal-founded: Tikal's Great Plaza, with Temple I rising at right and the North Acropolis at left — the city that grew from a modest Preclassic settlement around 900 BCE into the most powerful kingdom of the Classic Maya world.
evt-cacao-as-currency: A Classic Maya codex scene shows a seated lord presiding over a cacao vessel — the beans in the bowl doubled as currency and ritual offering throughout the Maya world.
evt-maya-zero: A page from the Dresden Codex showing the Maya vigesimal numeral system in action — the shell-shaped zero glyphs interspersed among bars and dots represent one of humanity's earliest independent inventions of the concept of nothing.
evt-maya-astronomy: A figure from the Madrid Codex sits in an observatory posture, representing the astronomer-priests who tracked Venus across the sky and built tables accurate to within a few minutes per century.
evt-jade-trade-network: Maya jade necklaces and pendants on display capture the deep-green stone that flowed from the Sierra de las Minas quarries across hundreds of miles of trade routes to elite courts throughout the lowlands.
evt-siyaj-kahk-conquest: Tikal Stela 31, carved around 445 CE, records Siyaj K'ahk's arrival from Teotihuacan and the new order he imposed on the city — the most detailed account of the conquest that reshaped the Classic Maya world.
evt-yax-nuun-ahiin: Stela 4 at Tikal depicts Yax Nuun Ahiin I, the Teotihuacan-backed ruler who took the throne after Siyaj K'ahk's conquest, wearing a mosaic headdress that blends Maya and central Mexican traditions.
evt-copan-dynasty-founded: A carved disc from Copán shows two rulers facing each other across a column of dynastic glyphs, commemorating the lineage that K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' founded around 426 CE and that would endure for sixteen generations.
evt-palenque-founded: The palace complex at Palenque, draped in jungle mist, stands at the heart of the city whose ruling dynasty traces its founding to the early Classic period — one of the most architecturally refined capitals in Maya history.
evt-calakmul-city: Calakmul's twin pyramids rise above the Yucatán jungle canopy — at its height, this city rivaled Tikal as the dominant power of the Classic Maya world.
evt-tikal-calakmul-rivalry: The overlapping spheres of influence of Calakmul (Kaan) and Tikal (Mutal) during the Classic period, showing the two superpowers whose proxy wars drew in cities across the lowlands.
evt-caracol-defeats-tikal: Caana (Sky Palace) at Caracol, Belize — the massive pyramid complex of the city that humiliated Tikal in 562 CE, setting off decades of Calakmul dominance.
evt-calakmul-peak: The jade funerary mask of Yuknoom Ch'een II, the Snake King who ruled Calakmul for nearly 50 years and built the most powerful political network the Classic Maya world ever saw.
evt-dos-pilas-wars: Carved stone panels from Dos Pilas, on display in Guatemala's National Museum, record the war captives and political legitimacy claimed by a city that began as Tikal's outpost and ended as Calakmul's weapon.
evt-tikal-defeats-calakmul: Scholarly drawing of Tikal Stela 30, recording Jasaw Chan K'awiil I's defeat of the Calakmul king in 695 CE — the moment Tikal broke the Snake Kingdom's century-long grip on the lowlands.
evt-jasaw-chan-kawiil: Temple I at Tikal, the funerary pyramid Jasaw Chan K'awiil I built for himself after his victory over Calakmul — a statement in stone that the city was back.
evt-pakal-reign: Pakal's jade funeral mask, assembled from hundreds of carved jade tiles, was placed over the ruler's face when he was entombed beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions around 683 CE.
evt-temple-inscriptions: The Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque rises nine terraces above the jungle floor, its staircase concealing the hidden shaft that leads down to Pakal's royal tomb.
evt-kan-bahlam-ii: Kan Bahlam II, Pakal's son and successor, is depicted in full royal regalia on Tablero XVII at Palenque, where he commissioned the magnificent Cross Group temples to cement his dynastic legitimacy.
evt-shield-jaguar-ii: Lintel 24 from Yaxchilán shows Shield Jaguar II holding a torch as Lady Xoc performs a bloodletting ritual below him, a scene that declared both his military power and his dynasty's spiritual authority.
evt-lady-xoc: Lintel 25 from Yaxchilán captures Lady K'abal Xook's vision ritual — blood drawn from her own tongue conjured the serpent from which an ancestor warrior emerges, making her act of sacrifice a dynastic founding moment.
evt-bird-jaguar-iv: Bird Jaguar IV is shown on Lintel 16 from Yaxchilán, now in the British Museum, grasping a captive by the hair in the classic gesture of Classic Maya royal victory.
evt-yaxchilan-dynasty: The ruins of Yaxchilán cling to a horseshoe bend of the Usumacinta River, its labyrinthine plazas and temples accessible only by boat — a natural fortress that its rulers exploited to dominate the river trade.
evt-18-rabbit-capture: Stela H at Copán portrays 18 Rabbit (Uaxaclajuun Ub'aah K'awiil) in extravagant costume as the Maize God — erected in 730 CE, just a decade before his capture and beheading by Quiriguá's ruler K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Yopaat.
evt-quirigua-stelae: Stela E at Quiriguá, erected around 771 CE, stands over 35 feet tall and is among the largest freestanding stone monuments in the ancient Maya world, its surface dense with the hieroglyphic record of K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Yopaat's reign.
evt-copan-altar-q: Altar Q at Copán, shown here in the site museum, depicts all sixteen rulers of the dynasty seated around its four sides, culminating in Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat receiving the scepter of power from the dynasty's founder K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' across 350 years of time.
evt-maya-ballgame-peak: The Great Ball Court at Chichén Itzá — the largest in Mesoamerica at 551 feet long — embodies the ballgame's role as both civic spectacle and cosmological reenactment of the Hero Twins' mythic contest against the lords of the underworld.
evt-maya-blue-pigment: Traces of Maya blue still cling to carved stone reliefs at Bonampak, the vivid turquoise pigment — made by binding indigo dye into palygorskite clay — remarkably stable after more than a thousand years.
evt-bonampak-murals: The murals of Bonampak, painted around 790 CE in Room 1, show a royal court ceremony in full color — musicians, dancers, and lords in elaborate costume — offering the most vivid surviving window into Classic Maya courtly life.
evt-lady-six-sky: A Maya queen stands triumphant over a bound captive on this stela from Naranjo, now in Guatemala's national museum — the type of war-trophy monument Lady Six Sky commissioned after leading Naranjo's military resurgence in the 680s CE.
evt-classic-maya-collapse: A population chart tracking the Maya southern lowlands shows the dramatic crash — densities that peaked near 110 people per square kilometer around 800 CE plummeted within a century as city after city went dark.
evt-puuc-architecture: The Sayil Palace showcases the hallmark Puuc style: a dense mosaic frieze of cut-stone masks and colonnettes crowning plain lower walls, the whole facade carved with a precision that set northern Yucatán apart from the southern lowland tradition.
evt-uxmal-rise: The elliptical Pyramid of the Magician at Uxmal — built in multiple stages from the 6th to 10th centuries — rises nearly 115 feet on a rounded footprint unique in the Maya world, and remains the most recognizable monument of the Puuc heartland.
evt-chichen-itza-rise: El Castillo (the Pyramid of Kukulcán) towers over the main plaza at Chichén Itzá, the northern city that rose to dominate the Yucatán Peninsula after the Classic collapse.
evt-el-castillo: The carved feathered-serpent head at the base of El Castillo's northern staircase — on the spring equinox, the shadow cast by the pyramid's terraces creates the illusion of the serpent descending to earth.
evt-sacred-cenote: The Sacred Cenote at Chichén Itzá — a natural limestone sinkhole roughly 200 feet across — was the site of ritual offerings including jade, gold, and human sacrifices cast into its dark waters.
evt-mayapan-league: The ruins of Mayapán, the walled city that served as the political capital of the League of Mayapán and dominated the northern Yucatán for over two centuries.
evt-maya-maritime-trade: The clifftop temples of Tulum overlook the Caribbean coast — this walled Postclassic port city was a key node in the Maya long-distance canoe trade network that hugged the shores of the Yucatán Peninsula.
evt-spanish-contact: Spanish conquest routes across the Yucatán Peninsula from the 1520s through the 1540s, tracing the decades-long campaign that ended Maya independence across the region.
evt-dresden-codex: Pages from the Dresden Codex — one of only four surviving pre-Columbian Maya books — showing the dense columns of glyphs and astronomical tables that made it the most mathematically sophisticated manuscript in the pre-Columbian Americas.
evt-popol-vuh-tradition: The Hero Twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque, the central figures of the Popol Vuh creation epic, depicted in the vivid Maya codex style that carried this oral tradition across centuries before it was ever written down.
evt-cordoba-expedition: Maya warriors drive off the Córdoba expedition at Champotón in 1517 — the first violent clash between Spanish explorers and the people of Yucatán.
evt-diego-de-landa: The Maya 'alphabet' recorded by Diego de Landa in his Relación de las Cosas de Yucatán — an imperfect but invaluable phonetic key that centuries later helped crack the Maya script.
evt-popol-vuh-written: The title page of Francisco Ximénez's early 18th-century transcription of the Popol Vuh — the first surviving written record of the K'iche' Maya creation epic.
evt-books-of-chilam-balam: Pages from the Book of Chilam Balam of Ixil, one of a series of Yucatec Maya manuscripts that preserved prophecy, history, and ritual knowledge through the colonial era.
evt-fall-of-tayasal: The Spanish military routes converging on Nojpetén (Tayasal) in 1697, the final conquest that ended the last independent Maya kingdom on the island in Lake Petén Itzá.
evt-silk-road-steppe: A relief map of the Silk Road across Eurasia, tracing the overland trade corridors that the Scythian and later steppe peoples controlled, connecting China, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean world.
evt-scythian-metallurgy: A gold deer plaque from the Kostromskoy kurgan in Kuban (7th century BC) — one of the defining images of Scythian goldsmithing, its curled recumbent body and branching antlers executed with extraordinary precision.
evt-philip-defeats-ateas: A gold stater of Philip II of Macedon bearing the head of Apollo — the king whose cavalry crushed the 90-year-old Scythian king Ateas at the Danube in 339 BC, killing him and seizing 20,000 horses.
evt-mithridatic-defeat: A map of the Pontic Kingdom at its height under Mithridates VI, showing the Black Sea territories where his general Diophantus campaigned against the Crimean Scythians and definitively broke their power.
evt-palakus-war: A gold stater of Mithridates VI Eupator of Pontus, minted at Pergamon — the king whose general Diophantus twice invaded Crimea, defeated Palakus, and ended Scythian independence on the steppe.
evt-gold-pectoral: Detail of the top register of the Tovsta Mohyla gold pectoral (4th century BC), showing two Scythian men stitching a fleece garment — a rare glimpse of everyday life woven into the most spectacular piece of Scythian goldwork ever found.
evt-kukulcan-cult: A carved stone panel from Chichén Itzá depicts the feathered serpent Kukulcán in low relief — the deity whose cult spread from central Mexico into Yucatán and gave the great pyramid El Castillo its name.
evt-chichen-itza-decline: El Caracol, the circular astronomical observatory at Chichén Itzá, still stands after a thousand years — by the time the Toltec-influenced city began to unravel in the 11th century, structures like this had made it the intellectual capital of the northern Maya world.
evt-mayapan-fall: Stucco warrior figures on a platform wall at Mayapán, carved during the city's final century — the same city where the Cocom-Xiu rivalry exploded into civil war and brought the League of Mayapán crashing down around 1441.
evt-bartatua: The Sam'al victory stele of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (671 BCE), now in the Pergamon Museum — the monument that commemorates the very alliance in which the Scythian king Bartatua bound himself to Assyria and gave his daughter to the empire.
evt-idanthyrsus: The Behistun relief carving of Skunkha, a Scythian king shown in the tall pointed cap of the Saka Tigrakhauda, standing captive before Darius I — the only surviving stone portrait of a Scythian royal from the era of the Darius invasion.
evt-aristeas: A marble acroterion from the Hermitage depicting an Arimaspos warrior gripping two griffins by the horns — the exact mythological confrontation that Aristeas of Proconnesus described in his lost poem Arimaspeia, written after his legendary journey to the far northern steppes.
evt-grain-export: Bronze coins of Borysthenes (Olbia), the Greek Black Sea port through which Scythian grain reached the Aegean world — the city's name on the reverse and the river-god portrait on the obverse mark it as the commercial gateway of the steppe.
evt-scythian-oral-tradition: A scholarly illustration of Scythian stone stele figures (kamennye baby), the carved memorial standing stones that the Scythians erected across the steppe to anchor the memory of their ancestors — the closest physical trace of a culture that kept its history entirely in spoken form.
evt-king-wu: A Ming-dynasty portrait of King Wu of Zhou, the warrior-king who overthrew the Shang and founded the Zhou dynasty.
evt-king-cheng: A traditional portrait of King Cheng of Zhou, who inherited the throne as a child and oversaw the consolidation of Zhou rule under the Duke of Zhou's regency.
evt-duke-zhou-regent: A traditional painted portrait of the Duke of Zhou, the regent-statesman who stabilized the young dynasty, codified its ritual system, and became Confucius's ideal of virtuous governance.
evt-rebellion-three-guards: A map of the Rebellion of the Three Guards, showing the movement of Zhou royal forces against the rebel princes and their Shang allies in the early years of the dynasty.
evt-fengjian-system: A map of the Western Zhou feudal states (1046–771 BCE), showing the network of noble fiefdoms — Jin, Qi, Lu, Chu, and others — that the Zhou kings granted to allies and relatives under the fengjian system.
evt-da-yu-ding: The Da Yu Ding, a massive early Western Zhou bronze ritual cauldron whose interior inscription records King Kang's grant of lands and people to a nobleman named Yu — one of the longest early Zhou bronze inscriptions known.
evt-mao-gong-ding: The Mao Gong Ding, a late Western Zhou bronze cauldron bearing the longest known bronze inscription in Chinese history — 497 characters recording a royal charge to the Duke of Mao.
evt-zhou-li-ritual: A complete set of bronze bianzhong (ritual bells) arranged on their original lacquered frames — the kind of ceremonial instrument at the heart of Zhou li, where music, sacrifice, and social hierarchy were all one unified practice.
evt-book-of-songs: A calligraphic page from the Shijing (Classic of Poetry) paired with a landscape illustration — the 305 poems of this anthology were the Zhou court's shared cultural vocabulary, memorized by every educated official for centuries.
evt-king-mu: An 18th-century illustration of King Mu's legendary journey by royal chariot — Zhou tradition credited him with traveling to the far western mountains aboard a team of eight divine horses, a journey that passed into Chinese myth.
evt-temple-heaven-precursor: The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests at the Temple of Heaven in Beijing — built in the Ming dynasty but heir to three thousand years of Chinese heaven-worship rites that the Zhou kings codified and made central to royal legitimacy.
evt-i-ching: A Song Dynasty printed edition of the I Ching, showing the hexagram commentary that Zhou scholars built atop the original divination lines — layers of interpretation that made this oracle text China's most enduring philosophical work.
evt-king-li-exile: Bronze inscription rubbing from the Duo You Ding, a Western Zhou ritual vessel commissioned during King Li's reign recording a military campaign — one of the few surviving documentary traces of his turbulent era.
evt-gonghe-regency: Traditional portrait of King Xuan of Zhou, who came to power after the fourteen-year Gonghe Regency ended in 828 BCE and briefly restored royal authority before the dynasty's final slide.
evt-sima-qian: Traditional portrait of Sima Qian, the Han-dynasty historian whose Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) is our primary source for the entire Zhou period, compiled around 91 BCE.
evt-king-you-beacon: Traditional illustration of Bao Si, the royal consort whose legendary indifference to the beacon fires lit to amuse her left King You's court with no allies when the Quanrong actually attacked in 771 BCE.
evt-fall-western-zhou: A Western Zhou bronze pan bearing a long dedicatory inscription — vessels like this were the dynasty's record-keeping medium, and their production ceased abruptly when the Quanrong sacked Hao in 771 BCE.
evt-luoyang-capital: Bronze bell excavated from the Wangcheng (Royal City) site at Luoyang, the very ground of the Eastern Zhou capital founded in 770 BCE after the court fled west and began the dynasty's long twilight.
evt-eastern-zhou: An Eastern Zhou bronze li (tripod cooking vessel) bearing the curvilinear interlace patterns that mark the dynasty's mature bronze style.
evt-spring-autumn-begins: A period map of the Spring and Autumn era (722–481 BCE) showing the competing states — Qi, Jin, Chu, Qin, and the rest — jostling for dominance across the Zhou world.
evt-duke-huan-qi: A traditional illustration of Duke Huan of Qi (齊桓公), the first of the Spring and Autumn hegemons, who unified the northern lords under Qi's banner.
evt-guan-zhong: A Han dynasty stone-relief rubbing depicting Duke Huan of Qi (center, labeled 桓公) with his indispensable chancellor Guan Zhong (right, labeled 管仲) at court.
evt-duke-wen-jin: A map of the Battle of Chengpu (632 BCE), Duke Wen of Jin's decisive victory over Chu that cemented Jin's status as hegemon of the Spring and Autumn period.
evt-king-zhuang-chu: A woodblock portrait of King Zhuang of Chu (楚莊王), the southern king who rattled his sabers at the Zhou heartland and asked pointedly about the weight of the Zhou royal cauldrons.
evt-partition-jin: Coins minted separately by Han, Wei, and Zhao after the three great families divided the state of Jin in 376 BCE — each new state stamping its own currency as proof of independence.
evt-confucius: A Tang-dynasty ink portrait of Confucius, the robed philosopher whose ideas about ritual, virtue, and righteous government would shape Chinese civilization for two thousand years.
evt-laozi: Zhang Lu's Ming-dynasty painting of Laozi riding an ox, depicting the legendary sage departing westward — the journey that, by tradition, produced the Dao De Jing.
evt-mozi: A traditional portrait of Mozi, the craftsman-philosopher who challenged Confucian hierarchy with a radical doctrine of impartial love and universal concern for all people.
evt-analects: A Tang-era manuscript of the Analects recovered from the Dunhuang cave library, preserving Confucius's teachings as recorded by his disciples after his death in 479 BCE.
evt-dao-de-jing: The Mawangdui silk manuscript of the Dao De Jing, dating to around 200 BCE — one of the oldest surviving copies of the text that became the foundation of Daoist thought.
evt-warring-states-begin: A map of the seven warring states at their peak around 260 BCE, with Qin dominating the west and six rivals still holding on across the north, east, and south.
evt-crossbow-invention: A Warring States–era lacquered crossbow, the precision trigger mechanism visible at the stock — the weapon that let a trained peasant kill a charging aristocratic charioteer at range.
evt-sun-tzu: Bamboo slips inscribed with the text of Sun Tzu's Art of War, the format in which this fifth-century BCE military treatise was first written and circulated.
evt-cavalry-king-wuling: A statue of King Wuling of Zhao in Congtai Park, Handan — the ruler who shocked his own court by ordering Zhao's army to abandon chariot warfare and fight in nomadic cavalry dress.
evt-su-qin-zhang-yi: A traditional portrait of the diplomat Su Qin, whose Vertical Alliance persuaded six rival states to band together against Qin — until his counterpart Zhang Yi talked them all back out of it.
evt-mencius: Traditional portrait of Mencius (Meng Ke), the Confucian philosopher who argued that human nature is fundamentally good and that just rulers must earn the loyalty of the people.
evt-zhuangzi: The Butterfly Dream — a Chinese ink painting depicting Zhuangzi asleep beneath a willow, butterflies drifting above, illustrating his famous parable about the boundary between dreaming and waking reality.
evt-xunzi: Traditional portrait of Xunzi, the Confucian thinker who broke with Mencius by arguing that human nature is inherently flawed and must be shaped through ritual, education, and law.
evt-han-feizi: A Qing dynasty edition of the Han Feizi text on display at the Hunan Museum, preserving the Legalist arguments that would become the governing philosophy of the Qin empire.
evt-shang-yang-reforms: A modern stone bust of Shang Yang, the reformer who dismantled Qin's old aristocratic order and replaced it with a merit-based military system that turned Qin into the era's most fearsome state.
evt-qu-yuan: Qu Yuan depicted in flowing robes with flowers in his hair, holding a staff — the classic iconographic portrait of the Chu statesman and poet whose exile produced some of the most celebrated verse in the Chinese tradition.
evt-li-sao: An illustrated woodblock-print page from the Li Sao, Qu Yuan's visionary lament of exile, showing the poem's text alongside figures from its mythological imagery.
evt-linzi-city: A museum scale model of ancient Linzi, the Qi capital and one of the largest cities of the Warring States era, with an estimated population of around 350,000 people crammed into its walled districts.
evt-dragon-boat-festival: A Qing dynasty circular painting inscribed with characters for 'dragon boat racing,' evoking the annual festival said to have originated when villagers raced their boats to recover the body of the drowned poet Qu Yuan.
evt-iron-age-china: A museum display of iron tools excavated from Warring States-era sites — blades, hooks, and agricultural implements that mark China's shift from bronze to iron technology.
evt-cast-iron-blast-furnace: A woodblock illustration from the Tiangong Kaiwu (1637) showing workers operating a Chinese blast furnace and fining hearth, depicting the iron-smelting technology pioneered during the Warring States period.
evt-ox-drawn-iron-plow: An iron sickle and V-shaped iron plow tip from the Han dynasty — the direct descendants of the ox-drawn iron plow technology that transformed Chinese agriculture during the Warring States period.
evt-coinage-spread: A bronze spade coin (bu) from the Warring States period, labeled in Chinese as a Warring States artifact — one of the standardized currency forms that spread commerce across the competing states.
evt-silk-road-precursors: A map showing the overland and maritime routes of the Silk Road, with the red northern overland paths through Central Asia tracing the corridors that Zhou-era traders first began to open.
evt-dujiangyan-irrigation: A panoramic view of the Dujiangyan irrigation system on the Min River in Sichuan, built by Li Bing around 256 BCE — still functioning today, it transformed the Chengdu plain into one of China's most productive agricultural regions.
evt-great-wall-precursors: The surviving rammed-earth city wall at Xinzheng, dating to the Eastern Zhou period (c. 770–230 BCE), showing the large-scale wall-building tradition that individual Warring States deployed before Qin unified and extended them into the Great Wall.
evt-battle-changping: A campaign map of the Battle of Changping (260 BCE), showing Qin's encirclement of the Zhao army in one of the deadliest engagements of the ancient world.
evt-bai-qi: A traditional portrait of Bai Qi (白起), the Qin general whose tactical genius at Changping ended with the execution of some 400,000 Zhao prisoners.
evt-end-zhou: Bronze inscriptions inside a late Western Zhou ritual ding — the dynasty's last kings left their record in metal, even as the world they had built slipped from their grasp.
evt-allahabad-pillar: The Allahabad Pillar standing in Prayagraj — originally an Ashokan column, Samudragupta had his conquest proclamation carved onto its already-ancient surface.
evt-iron-pillar: The Iron Pillar of Delhi, forged during Chandragupta II's reign around 400 CE, has stood rust-free for sixteen centuries — a testament to Gupta-era metallurgical skill that modern science still marvels at.
evt-prabhavatigupta-regency: The Padmapani Bodhisattva fresco at Ajanta, painted during the Vakataka period when Prabhavatigupta served as regent and channeled Gupta patronage into the caves her dynasty sponsored.
evt-kalidasa: A painted illustration of Kalidasa at work composing poetry, from a 19th-century edition — the great Sanskrit poet whose plays and lyric verse defined the Gupta golden age of literature.
evt-kalidasa-meghaduta: A Mughal-era miniature illustrating a scene from Kalidasa's Meghaduta (The Cloud Messenger), in which an exiled yaksha implores a passing monsoon cloud to carry his love-message home.
evt-mrcchakatika: Raja Ravi Varma's portrait of Vasanthasena, the courtesan at the heart of the Sanskrit play Mricchakatika (The Little Clay Cart), one of ancient India's most beloved stage dramas.
evt-vatsyayana: Manuscript leaves of Vatsyayana's Kama Sutra in Sanskrit Devanagari script, with a 13th-century commentary, purchased in Nepal in 1885 — the ancient text that systematized not just eros but all the arts of civilized living.
evt-panchatantra: An illustrated 18th-century manuscript page from the Panchatantra showing birds massed against the ocean — one of the fable collection's vivid animal tales that spread from Gupta-era India across the whole world.
evt-gupta-natyashastra-study: The Nataraja — Shiva as Lord of the Cosmic Dance — from the LACMA collection; Shiva is the patron deity of classical Indian performing arts, and the Natyashastra itself frames all dance, music, and drama as an act of divine creation in his image.
evt-aryabhata: A modern statue of Aryabhata outside a scientific institution in Bihar, honoring the fifth-century mathematician and astronomer whose Aryabhatiya transformed Indian science.
evt-aryabhata-pi: Sanskrit verses from the Aryabhatiya, the compact 499 CE treatise in which Aryabhata stated his remarkably accurate approximation of pi as approximately 3.1416.
evt-surya-siddhanta: The opening verse of the Surya Siddhanta in an 1847 Sanskrit edition, the foundational Hindu astronomical treatise that calculated the length of the solar year to within minutes of modern measurements.
evt-sushruta-samhita: Palm-leaf manuscript of the Sushruta Samhita at LACMA, the ancient surgical treatise describing hundreds of procedures — including rhinoplasty — that would not appear in European medicine for over a millennium.
evt-shikhara-temples: A shikhara tower at Khajuraho rises in the distinctive curvilinear spire style that Gupta-era architects pioneered, its surface alive with carved figures.
evt-udayagiri-caves: The colossal Varaha avatar panel at Udayagiri caves, carved under Chandragupta II, shows the boar-headed Vishnu rescuing the earth goddess from the cosmic ocean.
evt-dashavatara-temple: The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh, built around the early 6th century, is one of the finest surviving examples of early Gupta stone temple architecture.
evt-bhitargaon-temple: The Bhitargaon temple in Uttar Pradesh is the oldest surviving fired-brick Hindu temple with a towering shikhara, dating to the Gupta period around the 5th century.
evt-devi-mahatmya: A page from a Devi Mahatmya manuscript, the foundational Sanskrit text celebrating the goddess Durga's victory over the buffalo demon, composed during the Gupta period.
evt-vasubandhu-abhidharma: The Kofukuji statue of Vasubandhu, Asanga's younger brother and fellow Yogacara master, whose Abhidharmakosha became the definitive Buddhist philosophical encyclopedia.
evt-nalanda-university: The excavated ruins of Nalanda's main temple complex in Bihar, the university that grew from a Gupta-era monastic foundation into the ancient world's greatest center of Buddhist learning.
evt-faxian-visit: A statue of the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Faxian, who walked from China to India around 399 CE to collect sacred texts and returned with accounts of Gupta civilization at its height.
evt-kumaragupta-i: A gold coin of Kumaragupta I showing the king wrestling a lion, one of the most vivid surviving portraits of this long-reigning Gupta emperor.
evt-huna-invasions: A silver coin portrait of Khingila, the Alchon Hun king whose forces began pressing into the Gupta frontier in the mid-fifth century.
evt-bhitari-pillar: The Bhitari Pillar standing in situ — Skandagupta erected this stone column to proclaim his victories over the Pushyamitras and the Huna invaders.
evt-budhagupta: A gold coin of Budhagupta (477–487 CE), struck during the last period of meaningful Gupta central authority before the empire fragmented.
evt-mihirakula: A coin portrait of Mihirakula, the ferocious Huna ruler whose reign of destruction across northern India shocked contemporary observers.
evt-yashodharman-defeats-huns: An artist's reconstruction of the 528 CE battle in which Yashodharman's forces routed Mihirakula and the Hephthalite Huns, ending their grip on northern India.
evt-bhanugupta-goparaja: The Eran stone pillar inscription of Bhanugupta, the primary epigraphic record naming the warrior Goparaja and his wife's sati — one of the last Gupta imperial inscriptions.
evt-narasimhagupta-baladitya: Gold coins of Narasimhagupta Baladitya, the Gupta king credited by Xuanzang with defeating the Huna ruler Mihirakula and briefly stabilizing the empire in its final decades.
evt-successor-states: Silver coins of Isanavarman of the Maukhari dynasty (circa 535–553 CE), one of the regional successor kingdoms that carved up the Gupta heartland as central power dissolved.
evt-gupta-gold-coins: A Gupta gold dinar showing Chandragupta I and Queen Kumaradevi seated together — the dynasty's gold coinage was so fine it became the benchmark currency across South Asia.
evt-shakuntala: Raja Ravi Varma's oil painting of Shakuntala reclining in the forest with her companions and a deer — a scene drawn directly from Kalidasa's celebrated play Abhijnanasakuntalam.
evt-kalidasa-raghuvamsa: A 17th-century manuscript copy of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsa, the dynastic epic tracing the lineage of Rama, written here in Sanskrit verse in the Nepali script.
evt-kalidasa-kumarasambhava: Raja Ravi Varma's painting of Murugan (Kartikeya/Skanda), the six-faced war god whose miraculous birth is the very subject of Kalidasa's epic poem Kumarasambhava.
evt-kalidasa-vikramorvashiya: Raja Ravi Varma's 1896 painting of Urvashi the celestial apsara descending toward the mortal king Pururavas — the central lovers of Kalidasa's Sanskrit play Vikramorvashiya.
evt-vishakhadatta-mudrarakshasa: An artistic depiction of Chanakya (Kautilya), the brilliant minister whose political maneuvering in establishing the Mauryan empire is the dramatic subject of Vishakhadatta's Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa.
evt-decimal-place-value: The Bakhshali manuscript, a birch-bark mathematical text from ancient India that contains some of the earliest known examples of place-value decimal notation.
evt-varahamihira-person: A 1399 CE Kathmandu copy of Varahamihira's Brihajjataka, one of the polymath's major works on astrology, copied in Nepalaksara script on palm leaf.
evt-concept-of-zero: A detail of the Bakhshali manuscript with a red arrow indicating one of the earliest known written zeros — a dot placeholder that would eventually become the circular symbol the world uses today.
evt-huna-second-wave: A coin portrait of Toramana, the Hephthalite ruler who led the second, more devastating wave of Huna invasions deep into the Gupta heartland.
evt-aryabhata-person: An artistic depiction of Aryabhata gazing at the heavens, reflecting his dual role as mathematician and astronomer at the court of the Gupta golden age.
evt-varahamihira: Palm-leaf folios of the Brihat Samhita, Varahamihira's encyclopedic sixth-century work ranging from astronomy and meteorology to architecture and gemology.
evt-asanga-yogacara: The celebrated portrait statue of Asanga at Kofukuji, Japan, captures the philosopher-monk who founded the Yogacara school of Buddhist thought in 4th-century India.
evt-faxian-record: An 1869 sketch map tracing Faxian's overland and maritime route through India and Central Asia, based on his Fogguo Ji — the earliest surviving Chinese eyewitness account of the Gupta empire.
evt-skandagupta-pushyamitras: A rubbing of the Bhitari Pillar inscription in which Skandagupta records his victory over the Pushyamitras before turning to face the Hunas.
evt-ujjain-second-capital: A silver coin of Chandragupta II issued from his western mint at Ujjain, where he established a second imperial capital after conquering the Satraps and gaining control of the lucrative western trade routes.
evt-chandragupta-i: A gold Gupta dynasty coin depicting Chandragupta I and his Lichchhavi queen Kumaradevi standing together, minted to celebrate their politically transformative marriage alliance.
evt-samudragupta: A gold coin of Samudragupta showing the emperor as a standing warrior figure, part of the extensive coin series he used to broadcast his conquests and royal legitimacy.
evt-samudragupta-allahabad-21-kings: 18th-century drawing of the Allahabad Pillar by Joseph Tiefenthaler — Samudragupta's victory inscription listing 21 defeated northern kings is carved into its polished sandstone shaft.
evt-ramayana-mahabharata-finalized: A popular bazaar print of the Bhagavad Gita's climactic scene — the philosophical centerpiece of the Mahabharata — which reached its final textual form during the Gupta era.
evt-vakataka-gupta-alliance: The Ajanta Caves carved into a horseshoe cliff in Maharashtra — the great artistic fruit of the Vakataka-Gupta alliance, funded through the political partnership sealed by Prabhavatigupta's marriage.
evt-bhartrihari-vakyapadiya: A Sanskrit manuscript illustration from the Wellcome Collection depicting a sage figure, representative of the philosophical Sanskrit scholarly tradition in which Bhartrihari's Vakyapadiya — a landmark treatise on the philosophy of language — was composed.
evt-skandagupta: Gold coins of Skandagupta (c. 455–480 CE), the warrior-emperor who held the Gupta realm together against the Huna onslaught.
evt-austronesian-expansion: Men of the Tao people of Orchid Island (Taiwan) launch a traditional painted canoe — a living thread back to the Austronesian seafarers who spread across Southeast Asia and the Pacific over thousands of years.
evt-funan-kingdom: A Funan-era sandstone Bodhisattva Lokeshvara from the Mekong Delta region — one of the earliest surviving sculptures showing how Indian religious art had already taken deep root in mainland Southeast Asia by the first centuries CE.
evt-monsoon-trade: Monsoon clouds build over the southern Indian coastline near Nagercoil — the same seasonal winds that ancient mariners learned to read to sail reliably between India, Southeast Asia, and China.
evt-han-china-trade: A Han Dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE) molded brick relief from the National Museum of China, showing the material culture of the empire whose merchants and envoys first extended China's commercial reach into maritime Southeast Asia.
evt-indianization: The brick remains of a Hindu-Buddhist temple at Bujang Valley, Malaysia — among the oldest archaeological evidence of Indianization on the Malay Peninsula, where Indian traders and priests transmitted Sanskrit learning, temple-building, and royal ideology centuries before Srivijaya rose.
evt-suvarnabhumi: A 7th-century Sanskrit stone inscription from Cambodia bearing the term "Suvarnabhumi" (the Land of Gold) — one of the earliest written records of the legendary name ancient Indian and Pali texts used for the golden peninsula of Southeast Asia.
evt-dapunta-hyang: A museum reconstruction of Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa, the warrior-king whose military expedition in 682 CE — recorded on the Kedukan Bukit inscription — marks the founding moment of the Srivijayan empire.
evt-yijing-arrival: A charcoal portrait of Yijing, the Chinese Buddhist monk whose 671 CE stopover in Srivijaya gave the world its first outside description of the kingdom.
evt-kedukan-bukit: The Kedukan Bukit stone, inscribed in 683 CE in Old Malay, is the oldest surviving document to name Srivijaya and record Dapunta Hyang's founding expedition.
evt-talang-tuwo: The Talang Tuwo stone (684 CE), displayed in Jakarta's National Museum, records Dapunta Hyang's dedication of a royal garden and reveals Srivijaya's deep Mahayana Buddhist piety.
evt-telaga-batu: The Telaga Batu oath stone, with its distinctive serpent-crowned arch and spout, was used to administer loyalty oaths that bound Srivijaya's far-flung officials and vassals to the crown.
evt-kota-kapur: The Kota Kapur pillar inscription on Bangka Island (686 CE) records Srivijaya's conquest of the island and issues a vivid curse against anyone who dares rebel against the kingdom.
evt-conquest-bangka: A Borobudur relief panel depicting a Srivijayan outrigger vessel under sail — the kind of warship that carried Dapunta Hyang's forces in his conquest of Bangka and Jambi.
evt-strait-malacca-control: The Strait of Malacca, highlighted in red, is the narrow channel between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula that Srivijaya dominated for centuries, taxing every ship that passed.
evt-tang-tribute: A Tang-dynasty copy of the celebrated Lanting Xu calligraphy scroll, an artifact of the courtly civilization whose emperors received Srivijayan tribute missions from the 670s onward.
evt-old-malay: A close-up of a Kerinci manuscript written in an early Malay script, illustrating the ancient writing tradition that Srivijaya spread as Old Malay became the region's language of commerce and authority.
evt-mahayana-center: A Maitreya Bodhisattva illumination from the Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita, a core Mahayana sutra studied at Srivijayan monasteries.
evt-sailendra-dynasty: A carved relief from Borobudur depicting a Sailendra royal court scene, the dynasty whose alliance with Srivijaya reshaped Buddhist power across the archipelago.
evt-borobudur: Monks circumambulate Borobudur at dawn, the great Sailendra-era stupa on Java that stands as the most enduring monument of Srivijaya's Buddhist world.
evt-muara-takus: The Muara Takus temple complex in Riau, Sumatra — a Srivijayan-era Buddhist stupa cluster that marked the empire's reach deep into the island interior.
evt-bronze-buddhas: The Jalong bronze Buddha Brahmin statue from Perak, Malaysia — a museum label confirms it was influenced by Srivijayan statuary of the 9th to 11th centuries.
evt-atisha-studies: A Tibetan thangka portrait of Atisha, the Bengali scholar who traveled to Srivijaya to study under its master teachers for twelve years before carrying that learning back to reform Buddhism in Tibet.
evt-bukit-seguntang: The ancient stone Buddha unearthed at Bukit Seguntang in Palembang, the sacred hill that served as Srivijaya's spiritual heart and the legendary origin of Malay kingship.
evt-arab-zabag: A map of the Abbasid Caliphate at its height (c. 850 AD) shows the Arab world whose geographers first wrote detailed accounts of the fabulously wealthy kingdom they called Zabag.
evt-spice-trade: The ancient maritime Silk Route carried spices from Southeast Asian islands through the Indian Ocean to Arabia, Persia, and on to the Mediterranean — with Srivijayan ports at the center of that flow.
evt-camphor-trade: Processed camphor cubes like these — harvested from the great forests of Borneo and Sumatra — were among the most prized aromatics in medieval trade, commanding extraordinary prices from China to the Arab world.
evt-balaputradeva: A museum reconstruction figure representing Balaputradeva, the Srivijayan king whose diplomatic endowments at Nalanda in India demonstrated his empire's wealth and its reach across the Indian Ocean world.
evt-nalanda-monastery: The ruins of Nalanda's great temple complex in Bihar, India — the Buddhist university where Balaputradeva of Srivijaya funded an entire monastery, securing his empire's place in the international Buddhist world.
evt-manjusri-vihara: The Pala Empire controlled Bengal, where Srivijaya's Balaputradeva received a grant of five villages from the Pala king to endow the Manjusri Vihara, cementing a Buddhist alliance between India and maritime Southeast Asia.
evt-belitung-shipwreck: Changsha ware bowls recovered from the Belitung shipwreck, now displayed in Singapore — the 9th-century wreck carried over 60,000 pieces of Chinese ceramics bound for West Asian markets via Srivijayan waters.
evt-kedah-port: The Candi Batu Pahat ruins in Kedah's Bujang Valley are among the oldest temple remains in Southeast Asia, evidence of the thriving Indianized port culture that made Kedah a key tributary node in Srivijaya's trade network.
evt-rajendra-chola: A sculptural portrait of Rajendra Chola I, whose military campaigns carried the Chola banner from the Ganges delta to the shores of Southeast Asia.
evt-chola-raid-1025: The Chola Empire at its height around 1030, showing trade routes stretching east to Srivijaya's ports — the very reach that made Rajendra's naval raid across the Bay of Bengal possible.
evt-bay-of-bengal-trade: The Bay of Bengal, the body of water at the center of the medieval trade triangle linking southern India, Srivijaya, and China — the highway that made the maritime empire possible.
evt-srivijaya-attacks-mataram: Candi Badut, one of the oldest surviving Hindu temples in East Java, dates to the Mataram Kingdom period — the Javanese polity that Srivijaya attacked and pushed back from the sea lanes in the late 8th century.
evt-jambi-capital-shift: A 17th-century French map of the Sunda islands shows Sumatra with Jambi and Palembang marked along the eastern coast, the region where Srivijaya's political center shifted as royal power drifted upriver from Palembang.
evt-kediri-singhasari-rise: A map of 12th- to early 13th-century Southeast Asia shows Kediri's territory on Java alongside Srivijaya's domains on Sumatra, capturing the moment when Javanese rivals began drawing merchants away from the old Srivijayan network.
evt-pamalayu-1275: The Amoghapasa statue sent by King Kertanagara of Singhasari to Sumatra in 1286, a diplomatic gift that symbolized Java's growing reach into what had been Srivijayan territory.
evt-islam-arrives-aceh: The Cakra Donya, a large bronze bell gifted to the Samudera Pasai Sultanate in northern Sumatra around 1409, stands as one of the oldest surviving artifacts from the region where Islam first took root in the archipelago.
evt-ibn-battuta-visits: A 19th-century engraving after Hippolyte Léon Benet depicts Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan scholar-traveler who stopped in Sumatra around 1345 and recorded a thriving Muslim sultanate where Srivijayan Buddhist power had once reigned.
evt-singhasari-1292-collapse: Candi Singosari, the 13th-century funerary temple in East Java built to honor the Singhasari kings, stands as the final monument of a dynasty that collapsed violently in 1292 when a rebellion killed the last king just as the Mongols arrived offshore.
evt-yuan-attack-java: A map of Kublai Khan's 1293 naval expedition traces the Yuan fleet's route from southern China down through the South China Sea to Java, the enormous Mongol force that Raden Wijaya lured into his trap and then turned against his enemies.
evt-majapahit-conquest-1377: A carved relief panel from Candi Penataran, a Majapahit-era East Java temple, showing figures from the Krishnayana cycle — stone testimony to the imperial power that swept across Palembang in 1377.
evt-majapahit-rise: The maja fruit photographed at Candi Brahu in Trowulan, the Majapahit heartland — the bitter fruit whose name, combined with pahit (bitter), gave the empire its identity.
evt-parameswara: A period portrait of Parameswara, the Srivijayan prince turned fugitive who founded Malacca around 1400 and set the stage for the Malay world's next great chapter.
evt-malacca-sultanate: A map of Indian Ocean trade routes centered on Melaka (Malacca), showing the extraordinary web of ports — from Kilwa to the Moluccas — that the Sultanate knitted together at its fifteenth-century peak.
evt-malay-language-survival: An original manuscript page of the Hukum Kanun Melaka, the fifteenth-century Malaccan legal code written in Jawi script — one of the great written monuments of the Old Malay tongue that Srivijaya carried across the archipelago.
evt-teo-early-settlement: An aerial view of Teotihuacan's valley floor looking north along the Avenue of the Dead, the natural basin that drew the city's first settlers around 100 BCE.
evt-teo-cuicuilco-eruption: The western face of Cuicuilco's circular stepped pyramid, one of the few structures to survive the lava flows from the Xitle volcano that buried the city around 50 CE and sent refugees north toward Teotihuacan.
evt-teo-urban-planning: The Avenue of the Dead stretches nearly 2.5 miles through Teotihuacan's carefully planned grid, its dead-straight axis deliberately offset from true north to align with astronomical events — a design choice baked in from the city's earliest planning phase.
evt-teo-pyramid-sun: The Pyramid of the Sun rises 216 feet above the valley floor — the third-largest pyramid in the ancient world — its massive stepped silhouette still dominating the Teotihuacan skyline two millennia after it was built.
evt-teo-pyramid-moon: The Pyramid of the Moon anchors the northern end of the Street of the Dead, its broad plaza and flanking platform shrines visible in this aerial view looking south along the city's ceremonial spine.
evt-teo-talud-tablero: A surviving talud-tablero wall at Teotihuacan shows the signature two-part profile — a sloping talud base topped by a vertical framed tablero panel — the architectural vocabulary the city exported across Mesoamerica.
evt-teo-lime-plaster: A green-bird procession mural at Teotihuacan's Temple of the Feathered Conch Shells shows the polychrome painting that lime-plaster stucco made possible — Teotihuacan's builders coated virtually every interior surface with this smooth, paint-ready material.
evt-teo-moon-plaza: The Pyramid of the Moon anchors the northern end of the Avenue of the Dead, flanked by the smaller altars of the Moon Plaza — the city's grandest ceremonial gathering space.
evt-teo-feathered-serpent: Carved feathered serpent heads and goggle-eyed storm god masks crowd the talud-tablero facade of the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, one of the most elaborately decorated structures in the pre-Columbian Americas.
evt-teo-feathered-serpent-deity: A Mixtec codex illustration of Quetzalcoatl as the feathered serpent alongside the wind deity Ehecatl — the same divine figure whose cult Teotihuacan projected across Mesoamerica through monumental temple art.
evt-teo-storm-god: Deities including Tlaloc, the goggle-eyed rain and storm god, appear in the Codex Borgia — an iconographic tradition rooted in the Teotihuacan murals that first spread the storm deity's image across Mesoamerica.
evt-teo-temple-burning: The stairway of the Temple of the Feathered Serpent bears rows of carved serpent and storm-god heads that were deliberately buried under the Adosada platform after the temple's apparent defacement around 300 CE.
evt-teo-thin-orange-pottery: An effigy jar in thin orange earthenware from Teotihuacan (250–650 AD), the city's signature export ware traded across Mesoamerica.
evt-teo-apartment-compounds: Low-walled residential platforms flanking Teotihuacan's Avenue of the Dead hint at the apartment compounds that housed the city's hundreds of thousands.
evt-teo-monte-alban-relations: The main plaza of Monte Albán, the Zapotec hilltop capital in Oaxaca whose rulers maintained a formal diplomatic presence at Teotihuacan.
evt-teo-ballgame: Performers re-enact the Mesoamerican ballgame, showing players using their hips to drive a heavy rubber ball toward the stone ring — a ritual sport played across the ancient city.
evt-teo-spearthrower-owl: Tikal Stela 31, erected around 445 CE, depicts Spearthrower Owl's imagery and celebrates the Teotihuacan-backed dynasty he founded at the Maya city.
evt-teo-yax-nuun-ahiin: Tikal Stela 4 portrays Yax Nuun Ahiin I, the Teotihuacan-connected lord installed at Tikal after the 378 CE entrada, wearing central Mexican warrior regalia alongside traditional Maya iconography.
evt-teo-kaminaljuyu: A stone sculptural head from Kaminaljuyú, the highland Guatemala city that came under heavy Teotihuacan cultural and political influence around 400 CE.
evt-teo-atlatl-warfare: An ornately carved Aztec atlatl (spear-thrower) on display at the Museo Nacional de Antropología, Mexico City — the weapon type that gave Teotihuacan's warriors a decisive range advantage across Mesoamerica.
evt-teo-great-goddess: The Great Goddess of Teotihuacan gazes frontally from a mural in the Tetitla apartment compound, her elaborate headdress and outstretched hands central to the city's dominant religious iconography.
evt-teo-tepantitla-murals: The Tepantitla murals depict a teeming paradise — the Tlalocan — where small human figures swim, play, and gather flowers beneath a mountain stream pouring from the Great Goddess above.
evt-teo-old-god-fire: A ceramic head of Huehueteotl, the Old God of Fire, shows his signature wrinkled face and toothless grin — one of the oldest continuously venerated deities across Mesoamerica.
evt-teo-tetitla-murals: A museum replica of Tetitla Mural 7 preserves the rich polychrome imagery that once covered the apartment compound's portico walls, layering ritual symbols in deep ochres and greens across every surface.
evt-teo-atetelco-murals: The Atetelco compound's walls are still covered in repeating red-on-white murals of coyotes and warriors arranged in diamond-grid patterns, showing the reach and standardization of Teotihuacan's official visual program.
evt-teo-epiclassic-aftermath: Xochicalco, one of the Epiclassic successor cities that rose to regional power after Teotihuacan's fall in the seventh century.
evt-teo-millon-mapping: A population model derived from René Millon's 1960s–70s mapping survey, showing Teotihuacan's dramatic rise and sharp collapse against archaeological data points.
evt-teo-unesco: The UNESCO World Heritage plaque installed at Teotihuacan in December 1987, designating the Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan as a site of outstanding universal cultural value.
evt-teo-sierra-navajas: The ventral face of a Mesoamerican-origin obsidian scraper sourced from Sierra de las Navajas — the same green obsidian quarried near Teotihuacan that traveled as far as the Spiro Mounds in Oklahoma, tracing the city's vast trade reach.
evt-teo-batres-excavation: Workers haul rubble by Decauville rail cart during Leopoldo Batres's controversial 1905–10 excavation of the Pyramid of the Sun — an operation that stripped the pyramid's outer layers and reshaped its profile for Mexico's 1910 centennial celebrations.
evt-tamil-merchants: A Tamil-script stone inscription from Northamalai, South India, recording the activities of the Ainurruvar — the Five Hundred, the powerful guild of Tamil merchants whose members traded as far as Srivijaya and left inscriptions across the Indian Ocean world.
evt-sangrama-vijayottungavarman: Gangaikonda Cholapuram, the great Shiva temple Rajendra Chola I built in Tamil Nadu to celebrate his 1025 naval victory — the raid that captured the Srivijayan king Sangrama Vijayottungavarman and shook the maritime empire to its core.
evt-perry-black-ships: A Japanese watercolor made in 1854 captures one of Perry's steam-powered warships flying the American flag — the "black ships" that Japan had never seen before.
evt-meiji-restoration: Emperor Meiji depicted in Western military dress in this oil portrait by Takahashi Yuichi — the young sovereign who became the symbol of Japan's transformation from feudal shogunate to modern imperial state.
evt-emperor-meiji: An early photograph of Emperor Meiji as a young man, seated in Western military uniform — a deliberate image of a ruler modernizing the monarchy alongside the nation.
evt-charter-oath: The Charter Oath of 1868, the five-article declaration in which Emperor Meiji pledged deliberative assemblies, open debate, and the pursuit of knowledge throughout the world — the founding statement of the new Japan.
evt-boshin-war: A nishiki-e woodblock print depicting the 1869 naval Battle of Hakodate, the final engagement of the Boshin War in which imperial forces crushed the last Tokugawa holdouts in Hokkaido.
evt-tokyo-capital: The Seimon Ishibashi stone bridge at the Imperial Palace in Tokyo, the site that became the heart of Japan's new capital when the emperor moved his seat from Kyoto in 1869.
evt-conscription: Japanese conscript soldiers march off to war, embodying the new national army that the 1873 Conscription Law forged from a population that had never before been asked to serve.
evt-land-tax-reform: A Meiji-era land certificate (地券) issued by the Imperial Japanese government to an Akita Prefecture landowner, the paper instrument that replaced feudal tenure with fixed private title under the 1873 Land Tax Reform.
evt-iwakura-mission: The five senior leaders of the Iwakura Mission pose for a portrait abroad in 1871-73; Iwakura Tomomi sits at center in court dress while Okubo, Kido, Ito, and Yamagata flank him in Western suits.
evt-okubo-toshimichi: Okubo Toshimichi photographed in 1872, the austere architect of Meiji centralization who dismantled feudal domains and built a modern bureaucratic state before his assassination in 1878.
evt-kido-takayoshi: Kido Takayoshi in Western dress, the Choshu statesman who co-authored the Charter Oath and championed constitutional governance until his death in 1877 cut short his reformist vision.
evt-seikanron: A ukiyo-e triptych by Suzuki Toshimoto depicts the 1873 Seikanron debate at the imperial court, the confrontation between Saigo Takamori's war faction and Okubo's caution that split the Meiji leadership.
evt-yokohama-railway: A preserved D51 steam locomotive of the type that became synonymous with Meiji Japan's railway ambitions, the technology that first connected Tokyo and Yokohama in 1872 and then stitched the nation together.
evt-yen-currency: A Japanese 500-yen coin bearing the paulownia crest and kanji inscription, the direct descendant of the unified decimal currency the Meiji government introduced in 1871 to replace the chaotic patchwork of feudal coinage.
evt-saigo-takamori: A painted portrait of Saigo Takamori, the towering Satsuma samurai whose personal code of honor made him both the engine of the Meiji Restoration and its most famous casualty.
evt-satsuma-rebellion: A contemporary nishiki-e woodblock triptych of the Battle of Tabaruzaka, one of the bloodiest engagements of the Satsuma Rebellion, where Saigo's sword-bearing samurai clashed with the Meiji government's rifle-armed conscript army.
evt-shiroyama: A woodblock battle scene depicting the final stand at Shiroyama in September 1877, where Saigo Takamori and a handful of surviving samurai made their last charge against thousands of imperial troops.
evt-yamagata-aritomo: Yamagata Aritomo in full military dress, the Choshu general who commanded imperial forces against the Satsuma Rebellion and went on to build the modern Japanese army almost entirely in his own image.
evt-tomioka-silk: Workers tend rows of silk-reeling machines inside Tomioka Silk Mill, Japan's first government-operated model factory and the flagship of the Meiji industrialization drive.
evt-zaibatsu: A colorized Meiji-era photograph of Tokyo's emerging business district captures the Western-style brick commercial blocks where zaibatsu conglomerates like Mitsubishi and Mitsui established their financial headquarters.
evt-mitsubishi: Iwasaki Yataro, the ambitious former samurai-turned-entrepreneur who founded Mitsubishi in 1870 and built it into Japan's most powerful shipping and industrial conglomerate.
evt-bank-of-japan: The Bank of Japan's neoclassical headquarters in Tokyo, completed in 1896, embodied the Meiji government's determination to build Western-caliber financial institutions from scratch.
evt-yawata-steel: Smoke pours from the chimneys of the Yahata Iron and Steel Works in the Taisho era, the state-built giant that anchored Japan's heavy industrial revolution and supplied steel for the nation's railways and warships.
evt-japanese-emigration: Hundreds of Japanese children crowd a school assembly hall in Davao, Philippines in the 1930s, a vivid snapshot of the tight-knit emigrant communities that Meiji-era migrants established across Southeast Asia and the Pacific.
evt-freedom-movement: The imperial rescript of 1881 announcing that a national assembly would be established by 1890 — the direct concession wrested from the government by Itagaki's Freedom and People's Rights Movement.
evt-itagaki-taisuke: Itagaki Taisuke, the former Tosa samurai who founded Japan's first political party and championed constitutional government against the Meiji oligarchs.
evt-ito-hirobumi: Ito Hirobumi, the architect of the Meiji Constitution who traveled to Europe to study Bismarck's Prussia and returned to design a system that kept ultimate power with the emperor — and the oligarchs around him.
evt-meiji-constitution: A painting of the drafting conference for Japan's first constitution, where Ito Hirobumi and a small circle of Meiji leaders hammered out the document in near-total secrecy before presenting it to the nation in 1889.
evt-diet-opens: The National Diet Building in Tokyo, the institutional home of Japan's parliament — the body whose creation in 1890 marked the culmination of a decade of popular agitation for representative government.
evt-compulsory-education: The Meiji government's Department of Education in Tokyo, the bureaucratic engine behind the 1872 order that put every Japanese child in a schoolroom within a generation.
evt-tokyo-imperial-university: The Yasuda Auditorium at the University of Tokyo, successor to the Tokyo Imperial University founded in 1877 as the apex of the Meiji state's new hierarchy of Western-style learning.
evt-mori-arinori: Mori Arinori, Japan's first modern Education Minister, who reorganized the entire school system around national loyalty before his assassination in 1889.
evt-kitasato: Kitasato Shibasaburo, the bacteriologist who co-discovered the tetanus bacillus and identified the plague pathogen, and whose work abroad put Meiji Japan on the map of modern medicine.
evt-fukuzawa-yukichi: Fukuzawa Yukichi in 1891, the era's most influential public intellectual, whose writings on Western civilization and independence shaped an entire generation of Meiji reformers.
evt-imperial-rescript: An official copy of the 1890 Imperial Rescript on Education, bearing the imperial chrysanthemum seal, distributed to schools across Japan where it was read aloud at every ceremony.
evt-haibutsu-kishaku: Displaced Buddha statues photographed outside Kofukuji Temple in 1906, a record of the damage inflicted during the haibutsu kishaku anti-Buddhist purge that swept the country in the early Meiji years.
evt-yasukuni-shrine: The main hall of Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo, founded in 1869 to enshrine those who died for the emperor and later central to State Shinto's cult of military sacrifice.
evt-kokutai-ideology: A Meiji-era painting invoking Japan's mythological founding, the kind of sacred imperial imagery that kokutai ideology wove into school textbooks and public ritual to define the nation's eternal essence.
evt-natsume-soseki: Natsume Soseki, Japan's preeminent Meiji novelist, whose fiction explored the psychological cost of rapid Westernization on people caught between two worlds.
evt-rokumeikan: The Rokumeikan reception hall in Tokyo, photographed in the Meiji era, where Japan's elite hosted Western-style banquets and balls to perform civilization for foreign diplomats.
evt-sino-japanese-war: Japanese forces storm the walls of Pyongyang in September 1894, routing the Chinese army in one of the decisive battles of the First Sino-Japanese War fought on Korean territory.
evt-treaty-shimonoseki: The signed text of the Treaty of Shimonoseki, April 17, 1895, sealed by Ito Hirobumi and Mutsu Munemitsu for Japan and Li Hongzhang for the Qing, ending the First Sino-Japanese War on terms that shocked the world.
evt-triple-intervention: The Convention of Retrocession of the Liaodong Peninsula, November 1895, the document by which Japan was forced under Russian, French, and German pressure to hand back the territory it had just won in war.
evt-anglo-japanese-alliance: The signed original of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, dated London, January 30, 1902, sealed by ambassador Hayashi and Foreign Secretary Lansdowne — the first alliance on equal terms between a European power and an Asian nation.
evt-russo-japanese-war: A Japanese woodblock print captures the ferocity of the 1904 Battle of Liaoyang during the Russo-Japanese War, the conflict fought largely over dominance of Korea and Manchuria.
evt-port-arthur: 203 Meter Hill, the snow-covered ridge above Port Arthur whose capture in December 1904 cost Japan tens of thousands of casualties but finally gave their artillery the overlook needed to destroy the Russian fleet below.
evt-battle-tsushima: Tōjō Shōtarō's 1905 painting of the Battle of Tsushima shows Russian battleships burning and sinking as Japanese shells raise waterspouts across the strait — the most complete naval annihilation in the age of steam.
evt-admiral-togo: Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō in full dress uniform with his fleet of decorations, the man who masterminded the T-crossing maneuver at Tsushima and became the first Asian naval commander to defeat a European great power at sea.
evt-treaty-portsmouth: The final page of the Treaty of Portsmouth, September 5, 1905, bearing the signatures and seals of Sergei Witte and Jutaro Komura, the document that ended the Russo-Japanese War and earned Theodore Roosevelt a Nobel Peace Prize for brokering it.
evt-treaty-revision: An 1898 French cartoon shows European powers and Japan carving up China like a pie — the visual shorthand for the unequal treaty system that Meiji Japan spent thirty years fighting to escape from.
evt-annex-korea: The 1910 Japan-Korea Annexation Treaty, bearing the imperial seals that formally ended Korean sovereignty and folded the peninsula into the Japanese empire.
evt-meiji-death: Emperor Meiji in a formal painted portrait from near the end of his reign, the medals and sash of empire draped across a man who had ruled Japan through its most vertiginous transformation.
evt-nogi-suicide: General Nogi Maresuke in full military dress — the war hero who followed his emperor in death, performing junshi on the day of Meiji's funeral and stunning a modernizing Japan with an act from another age.
evt-meiji-shrine: The main hall of Meiji Shrine in Tokyo, built to enshrine the emperor's spirit and completed in 1920 — a century on, still one of Japan's most-visited sacred sites.
evt-grave-circle-b: A reconstruction painting of Grave Circle B at Mycenae shows the circular stone enclosure with upright grave markers, built around 1650 BCE and home to the earliest known Mycenaean royal burials.
evt-shaft-graves: The excavated remains of Grave Circle A sit within the fortified citadel of Mycenae, where Schliemann unearthed six shaft graves packed with gold masks, weapons, and jewelry in 1876.
evt-mask-agamemnon: The so-called Mask of Agamemnon — a beaten gold funeral mask from Shaft Grave V at Mycenae, dating to around 1550 BCE — became the iconic face of the Bronze Age Greek world the moment Schliemann pulled it from the earth.
evt-perseus-legendary-founder: A Roman marble statue of Perseus holding the severed head of Medusa represents the legendary hero said to have founded Mycenae, a myth the Mycenaeans themselves likely embraced to explain their city's divine origins.
evt-schliemann-mycenae: Heinrich Schliemann, photographed in the 1870s, was the self-made German merchant whose obsession with Homer drove him to dig at Mycenae in 1876 and upend everything scholars thought they knew about early Greece.
evt-tholos-tombs: A cross-section diagram of a Mycenaean tholos tomb shows the corbelled beehive chamber and dromos entrance passage — the signature burial form of the palace age.
evt-treasury-atreus: The Treasury of Atreus at Mycenae, built around 1250 BC, is the largest and most perfectly preserved tholos tomb in Greece, its dromos still imposing after three thousand years.
evt-vapheio-cups: One of the two Vapheio gold cups, repoussé-worked with a bull-hunting scene, stands as one of the finest surviving examples of Mycenaean metalwork from around 1500 BC.
evt-orchomenos-treasury-minyas: The ruined tholos chamber of the Treasury of Minyas at Orchomenos once rivaled the Treasury of Atreus in scale, marking Orchomenos as a major Mycenaean power center in Boeotia.
evt-megaron-architecture: The foundations of the great megaron at Mycenae, with its central hearth base still visible, formed the throne room and ceremonial heart of the palace complex.
evt-cyclopean-walls: The north postern gate at Mycenae, built from multi-ton limestone boulders fitted without mortar, exemplifies the cyclopean construction that later Greeks attributed to the mythical giants.
evt-lion-gate: The Lion Gate of Mycenae, built around 1250 BC, is the oldest surviving monumental sculpture in Europe, its twin lions flanking a column above the massive stone lintel.
evt-pylos-palace: The tholos tomb mausoleum associated with the Palace of Nestor at Pylos, one of the best-preserved Bronze Age beehive tombs in the western Peloponnese.
evt-gla-fortress: An aerial view of the Mycenaean fortress of Gla shows the massive rocky promontory rising from the drained plain of the former Lake Kopais, enclosed by nearly 3 miles of cyclopean walls.
evt-kopais-drainage: A map showing the location of Lake Kopais in Boeotia, the vast marshy lake that Mycenaean engineers drained around 1300 BC through an ambitious network of dykes and tunnels.
evt-tiryns-citadel: The massive cyclopean walls of the citadel of Tiryns still stand to considerable height, their multi-ton boulders a testament to the engineering ambition of the Mycenaean palace builders.
evt-midea-citadel: Cyclopean ruins of the Mycenaean citadel of Midea crown a hilltop in the Argolid, its strategic position overlooking the plain making it one of the three great Bronze Age strongholds of the region.
evt-conquest-crete: A map of the Mycenaean world at its height (1400–1100 BCE), showing palaces, settlements, and the expansion of Mycenaean influence southward to Knossos on Crete.
evt-linear-b: A reconstructed Linear B clay tablet from Pylos, its syllabic signs recording palace accounts in the earliest written form of Greek.
evt-dionysus-linear-b: A Roman marble copy of a Hellenistic Dionysus, ivy-crowned and holding a wine cup — a god whose name turns up on Mycenaean Linear B tablets a full millennium before this statue was carved.
evt-mycenaean-pottery-exports: A Mycenaean stirrup vase from the 14th–13th century BC — the most exported vessel form in the Bronze Age Mediterranean, found from Egypt to Spain.
evt-miletus-settlement: Ruins of ancient Miletus on the Anatolian coast — a site where Mycenaean settlers established one of the Bronze Age Aegean's most important overseas communities.
evt-uluburun-wreck: Museum reconstruction of the Uluburun shipwreck at Bodrum, Turkey, showing the late Bronze Age merchant vessel's hull loaded with copper ingots, tin, and luxury goods from across the Mediterranean.
evt-cypriot-copper-trade: Oxhide copper ingots on display in Athens — the standard Bronze Age trading unit for Cypriot copper, shaped to resemble a spread animal hide for easy stacking and portage.
evt-trojan-war: A Roman-era fresco depicting Ajax dragging Cassandra from the Palladium during the sack of Troy — the violent climax of the ten-year war that the Greeks would never fully live down.
evt-agamemnon-legendary: Agamemnon seated with scepter, labeled in Greek on this 4th-century BC lekanis from Taranto — the king whose name the ancient world attached to the whole expedition against Troy.
evt-destruction-troy-vi: The surviving stone walls of Troy VIIa at Hisarlik in modern Turkey — the fortifications that archaeologists now believe burned around 1180 BC, giving the Trojan War legend its real-world anchor.
evt-boar-tusk-helmet: A complete Mycenaean boar's tusk helmet at the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, assembled from hundreds of sliced tusk plates stitched to a leather cap — exactly as Homer describes Odysseus wearing one in the Iliad.
evt-wanax-system: A ceramic fragment bearing the word WANAKTI ("for the wanax"), the Mycenaean title for the supreme palace king recorded in the Linear B administrative texts.
evt-pylos-ta-tablets: A Linear B tablet from Nestor's Palace at Pylos, its careful syllabic script itemizing the luxury goods — inlaid chairs, footstools, and precious vessels — assembled for a palace banquet.
evt-cult-center-mycenae: A wall painting fragment from Mycenae showing animal-headed figures in procession, recovered from the Cult Center where ritual activity clustered within the citadel walls.
evt-tiryns-cult-center: A 13th-century BC mural of a figure-eight shield from Tiryns, the kind of cult imagery that decorated the rooms of Tiryns's sanctuary quarter and connected martial power with religious ritual.
evt-eleusis-mystery: A votive plaque from Eleusis depicting the rites of the Eleusinian Mysteries, a cult whose roots in grain goddess worship stretch back to the Mycenaean Bronze Age.
evt-phi-psi-figurines: A phi-type figurine (left, with rounded body) and a psi-type figurine (right, with upraised arms) side by side — the mass-produced terracotta icons found by the thousands across Mycenaean Greece.
evt-dendra-panoply: The Dendra panoply on display — the world's oldest complete metal suit of armor, its stacked bronze plates recovered from a 15th-century BC chamber tomb near Midea in the Argolid.
