evt-mycenae-power-center: The approach to the Lion Gate at Mycenae, the monumental entrance that announced the citadel's dominance over the Argolid and the wider Mycenaean world.
evt-destruction-pylos: The painted bathtub from the Palace of Nestor at Pylos, one of the last artifacts left in place before the palace was torched around 1180 BCE.
evt-sea-peoples-mycenaean: A line drawing of the Medinet Habu relief at Ramses III's temple, depicting the naval battle against the Sea Peoples — one of the few primary-source records of the raiders who helped unravel the Bronze Age world.
evt-warrior-vase: The Warrior Vase from Mycenae (c. 1200 BCE), showing a file of spear-carrying soldiers marching off to battle — one of the last great works of Mycenaean painted pottery before the collapse.
evt-sub-mycenaean: An amphoriskos from Tiryns dated 1025–900 BC, its geometric banding and simplified forms marking the stripped-down pottery style that defines the Sub-Mycenaean transitional period.
evt-lefkandi-burial: The excavated foundation of the Toumba building at Lefkandi on Euboea, the tenth-century BC heroön where a cremated warrior and his horse were buried beneath a massive apsidal hall — one of the most striking burials of the Greek Dark Ages.
evt-ionian-migration: A map of the ancient regions of central Greece — Thessaly, Boeotia, Attica, and Achaea — showing the heartland from which Ionian refugees fled westward and across the Aegean after the Bronze Age collapse.
evt-homer-preserves: A Roman marble bust of Homer at the British Museum, the conventional image of the blind poet whose Iliad and Odyssey crystallized centuries of oral tradition about the Mycenaean world into enduring epic verse.
evt-samurai-stipends: A hand-colored 1873 Yokohama photograph by Suzuki Shinichi I captures a samurai in full armor and two swords — the class whose government stipends were abolished that same year, ending a warrior caste that had defined Japan for seven centuries.
evt-asuka-buddhism-arrives: The great bronze Buddha at Asuka-dera, cast in 609 CE — the oldest surviving large-scale Buddhist sculpture in Japan and a monument to the faith the Soga clan staked everything on.
evt-asuka-mononobe-nakatomi: Isonokami Jingu, the ancient shrine in Nara that served as the ancestral seat of the Mononobe clan and their cache of weapons and sacred regalia.
evt-asuka-soga-no-umako: A later painted portrait of Soga no Umako, the clan patriarch who outmaneuvered every rival to make Buddhism the religion of the Japanese court.
evt-asuka-battle-of-shigisen: A period illustration of Mononobe no Moriya, the anti-Buddhist general whose defeat at the Battle of Shigisen in 587 CE ended the old clan's power and opened Japan to the new faith.
evt-asuka-empress-suiko: A court painting of Empress Suiko, who reigned from 593 to 628 CE and became the first woman to hold the title of tennō — presiding over the golden age of Asuka Buddhism.
evt-asuka-shotoku-regency: A traditional painted portrait of Prince Shotoku seated at a writing desk, reflecting the studious regent who shaped early Japanese statecraft and Buddhism.
evt-asuka-ono-no-imoko: A traditional portrait painting of Ono no Imoko, the diplomat dispatched by Prince Shotoku to open direct relations with Sui China in 607 CE.
evt-asuka-horyu-ji-founded: The western precinct of Hōryū-ji, whose seventh-century wooden halls are among the oldest surviving timber structures on Earth.
evt-asuka-asuka-temples: The entrance gate of Asuka-dera, Japan's first full-scale Buddhist temple complex, founded by the Soga clan in 596 CE.
evt-asuka-tori-busshi: The Shakyamuni Triad at Hōryū-ji, the masterwork cast in bronze by Tori Busshi around 623 CE and the defining achievement of early Asuka-period sculpture.
evt-asuka-shotoku-death: A sculpted portrait of Prince Shotoku at Hōryū-ji's Shōryō-in, the memorial hall established after his death in 622 CE where his spirit is still venerated.
evt-asuka-tang-emerges: A Tang-dynasty copy of the celebrated Lanting Xu calligraphy scroll, emblematic of the cultural brilliance that made the new Tang empire the irresistible model for its neighbours.
evt-asuka-isshi-incident: A woodblock print depicting the assassination of Soga no Iruka on the palace floor in 645 — the pivotal coup that ended Soga dominance and opened the door to the Taika reforms.
evt-asuka-fujiwara-no-kamatari: A formal hanging-scroll portrait of Fujiwara no Kamatari flanked by his sons Fuhito and Jōe, from the Nara National Museum — the man whose alliance with Prince Naka no Ōe brought down the Soga and founded the dynasty that would run Japan for centuries.
evt-asuka-naniwa-capital: The excavated archaeological site of Naniwa Palace in modern Osaka, the short-lived capital established after the Taika coup before the court moved on to its later permanent homes.
evt-asuka-baekgang: A map of the 663 Battle of Baekgang showing the Japanese relief fleet converging on the mouth of the Geum River, where Tang and Silla forces destroyed it and ended Japan's bid to restore Baekje.
evt-asuka-water-castles: The surviving earthen rampart of Mizuki in Kyushu, built after the disaster at Baekgang as part of Japan's hasty coastal defense line against an anticipated Tang-Silla invasion that never came.
evt-asuka-emperor-tenji: A Utagawa Kuniyoshi woodblock portrait of Emperor Tenji (Tenchi), the prince who engineered the Isshi coup and then ruled as Japan's reforming emperor, shown here alongside his famous harvest poem.
evt-asuka-toraijin-baekje: Court figures in continental-style dress from the Takamatsuzuka tomb mural, reflecting the sophisticated Korean and Chinese cultural forms that Baekje refugees brought to Japan after 660.
evt-asuka-silla-unification: A map of Korea around 830 CE showing Unified Silla controlling the peninsula south of the Taedong River and the northern kingdom of Balhae above it — the geopolitical shape that emerged from Silla's victory over Baekje and Goguryeo.
evt-asuka-haku-ho-art: The elegant three-tiered East Pagoda of Yakushi-ji, one of the finest surviving examples of Hakuho-period Buddhist architecture, dating to the late 7th century.
evt-asuka-jinshin-war: Excavated foundation stones of the inner palace at Ōtsu-no-miya, Emperor Tenji's capital on Lake Biwa — the seat of power Prince Ōama marched to seize in the Jinshin War of 672.
evt-asuka-emperor-tenmu: Traditional portrait of Emperor Tenmu, the victorious prince who emerged from the Jinshin War to rule Japan and launch a sweeping centralisation of imperial power.
evt-asuka-yakushi-ji: The reconstructed West Golden Hall of Yakushi-ji, the grand temple complex Emperor Tenmu vowed to build for the recovery of Empress Jitō and completed by her successors in the Nara period.
evt-asuka-empress-jito: Portrait of Empress Jitō by Katsukawa Shunshō, depicting the formidable empress who completed Tenmu's centralisation programme, established Fujiwara-kyō, and held power through much of the 690s.
evt-asuka-fujiwara-kyo: A 1:1000 scale museum model of the Fujiwara-kyō palace complex, Japan's first fully grid-planned capital, built on Chinese Tang-dynasty principles and inaugurated by Empress Jitō in 694.
evt-nara-kakinomoto-hitomaro: Panel portrait of Kakinomoto no Hitomaro by Kanō Tan'yū, honouring Japan's greatest classical poet whose soaring elegies and court verse defined the style of the Man'yōshū anthology.
evt-asuka-taiho-code: A map of Japan's provinces as reorganized under the Taihō Code of 701, the comprehensive legal framework that restructured the country into a Chinese-style imperial state.
evt-asuka-fujiwara-no-fuhito: A traditional portrait of Fujiwara no Fuhito, the statesman who shaped the Nara state through the Taihō and Yōrō law codes and cemented Fujiwara dominance through strategic imperial marriages.
evt-nara-wado-kaichin: A Wadō Kaichin copper coin, Japan's first officially minted currency, issued in 708 CE and modeled on Tang Chinese coinage to support the new Nara capital economy.
evt-nara-empress-genmei: A traditional portrait of Empress Genmei, who moved the capital to Heijō-kyō in 710, commissioned the Kojiki, and oversaw Japan's first national coinage — one of the most consequential reigns of the Nara period.
evt-nara-heijo-kyo: The reconstructed Daigokuden (Great Audience Hall) of Heijō Palace, the ceremonial heart of Nara, Japan's first permanent imperial capital founded in 710 CE on a Chinese-grid plan.
evt-nara-kofuku-ji: Kōfuku-ji's East Golden Hall and five-story pagoda at Nara — the Fujiwara clan's great temple complex, relocated here when the capital moved in 710 and rebuilt as one of Nara's most powerful religious institutions.
evt-nara-kojiki: The sun goddess Amaterasu emerging from the heavenly cave, one of the most celebrated myths recorded in the Kojiki of 712 CE — Japan's earliest chronicle of divine origins and imperial legitimacy.
evt-nara-nihon-shoki: Pages from the Nihon Shoki (720 CE), Japan's second chronicle and first written in formal Chinese, recording the history of the imperial lineage from the age of the gods through the early seventh century.
evt-nara-emperor-shomu: A traditional Japanese painted portrait of Emperor Shōmu, the devout ruler who transformed Buddhism from a court religion into the spiritual backbone of the entire Japanese state.
evt-nara-fujiwara-four-deaths: The Great Hall of Tōdai-ji, built in the wake of the 735–737 smallpox epidemic that wiped out all four Fujiwara sons and convinced Emperor Shōmu that only a nationwide Buddhist campaign could protect Japan.
evt-nara-kokubunji-edict: The Yakushi Hall of Mutsu Kokubunji, one of the provincial temples ordered built across every province of Japan by Emperor Shōmu's 741 edict, turning Buddhism into an instrument of imperial administration.
evt-nara-todaiji: The Great Hall of Tōdai-ji — once the largest wooden building in the world — housing the colossal bronze Great Buddha that Emperor Shōmu poured his treasury, his labor force, and his faith into completing.
evt-nara-empress-komyo: Empress Kōmyō in prayer, painted by Shimomura Kanzan — she was arguably the most powerful Buddhist patron of the Nara period, founding hospitals and orphanages while pushing the court's religious ambitions alongside her husband Shōmu.
evt-nara-shoso-in: The Shōsō-in repository at Tōdai-ji, raised on log-cabin pillars that swell in humidity to seal the interior — a 1,300-year-old time capsule preserving Emperor Shōmu's personal treasures alongside Silk Road goods from as far as Persia.
evt-nara-gyoki: A bronze statue commemorating Gyōki, the wandering monk who defied government restrictions to build roads and irrigation works for ordinary people, eventually winning imperial recognition as Japan's first bodhisattva.
evt-nara-ganjin: The famous dry-lacquer portrait of Ganjin (Jianzhen) at Tōshōdai-ji, crafted by his disciples after his death — one of the oldest and most revered portrait sculptures in Japan, showing the blind monk serenely at rest after his sixth and final crossing attempt succeeded.
evt-nara-toshodai-ji: The Golden Hall (kondō) of Tōshōdai-ji, founded by Ganjin in 759 after his harrowing twelve-year journey to Japan — the temple he built to finally transmit proper Buddhist ordination rites to Japanese monks.
evt-nara-otomo-yakamochi: A Kanō school panel portrait of Ōtomo no Yakamochi, labeled Chūnagon Yakamochi, the poet-official who compiled and closed the Man'yōshū anthology.
evt-nara-empress-koken-shotoku: A court painting of Empress Kōken, who reigned twice — first as Kōken, then as Shōtoku — and whose relationship with the monk Dōkyō shook the Nara court to its foundations.
evt-nara-fujiwara-no-nakamaro: Map tracing Fujiwara no Nakamaro's desperate flight around Lake Biwa in 764, marking the road barriers, battles, and the final showdown at Arachi that ended his revolt.
evt-nara-hyakumanto-darani: Surviving hyakumantō darani scrolls — printed Buddhist charm texts that Empress Shōtoku ordered produced in one million copies, making them among the world's earliest examples of mass printing.
evt-nara-kibi-no-makibi: A portrait of Kibi no Makibi, the scholar who spent nearly two decades at the Tang court absorbing Chinese learning and returned to Japan to become one of the Nara era's most influential officials.
evt-nara-abe-no-nakamaro: Abe no Nakamaro gazing at the moon from a promontory in China, a scene inspired by his famous poem yearning for Japan — the scholar-diplomat who passed the Tang imperial exams but never made it home.
evt-nara-emperor-kammu: A traditional Japanese court painting of Emperor Kammu, the forceful 50th emperor who broke with Nara's Buddhist establishment and moved the capital twice in search of a fresh start.
evt-nara-nagaoka-kyo: A scale model of the Daigokuden (Great Hall of State) of Nagaoka Palace, the ill-fated capital Kammu built in 784 before abandoning it a decade later under a cloud of bad omens and political scandal.
evt-nara-prince-sawara: The Sudo Tenno shrine in Nara, dedicated to Prince Sawara, who was exiled after being implicated in an assassination and died en route — his angry ghost blamed for the disasters that plagued Nagaoka-kyo.
evt-nara-heian-capital: A detailed scale model of the Daidairi (Great Imperial Enclosure) of Heian-kyo, the grid-planned capital that Kammu established in 794 and that would remain Japan's imperial seat for over a thousand years.
evt-nara-emishi-campaigns: The reconstructed south gate of Taga Castle (Tagajo) in Miyagi Prefecture, one of the key frontier fortresses from which the imperial court launched its long military campaigns to subjugate the Emishi of the north.
evt-nara-manyoshu: Pages from the Genryaku-era Man'yōshū manuscript, one of the oldest surviving copies of Japan's greatest poetry anthology — 4,500 poems spanning a century of court and common voices, compiled around 759 CE.
evt-nara-dokyo-affair: A traditional scroll painting of the monk Dōkyō, the faith healer who rose from obscure Buddhist practice to become the closest confidant of Empress Shōtoku — and whose rumoured bid for the throne ended the era of regnant empresses.
evt-nara-tang-embassies: A painted scroll depicting a Japanese embassy ship crossing to Tang China, the perilous open-sea voyage that students, monks, and diplomats undertook generation after generation to carry Tang civilization back to Nara.
evt-lme-little-ice-age: A frost fair on the frozen Thames in 1684, one of the most dramatic effects of the Little Ice Age's centuries of biting winters.
evt-lme-great-famine: Medieval peasant laborers — the farming population that bore the catastrophic weight of the Great Famine of 1315–1317, when failed harvests killed millions across northern Europe.
evt-lme-dante-comedy: Domenico di Michelino's 1465 fresco shows Dante holding the Divine Comedy before the landscapes of Hell, Purgatory, and Florence — the poem that reshaped the Italian language and European literature.
evt-lme-petrarch-humanism: Francesco Petrarch, crowned with a laurel wreath, the 14th-century poet and scholar whose passionate rediscovery of classical antiquity laid the groundwork for the Renaissance.
evt-lme-avignon-papacy: The Palais des Papes in Avignon, the vast Gothic fortress-palace that served as the seat of seven popes from 1309 to 1377.
evt-lme-greenland-norse-end: The ruins of Hvalsey Church in southern Greenland, the last surviving structure of the Norse Eastern Settlement — the site of the final recorded Norse activity in Greenland in 1408.
evt-lme-black-death: An excavated plague mass grave at Martigues, France — one of countless emergency burial pits dug across Europe as the Black Death killed a third of the continent's population.
evt-lme-caffa-siege: The medieval towers of Caffa (modern Feodosia, Crimea), the Genoese trading port where Mongol forces reportedly catapulted plague-infected corpses over the walls in 1346, seeding the Black Death's westward journey.
evt-lme-jewish-pogroms-1349: A 14th-century illumination depicting the burning of Jews accused of poisoning wells — one of hundreds of pogroms that swept through German, Swiss, and French towns as panicked communities sought someone to blame for the plague.
evt-lme-boccaccio-decameron: A woodcut frontispiece from the 1492 printed edition of Boccaccio's Decameron, showing the ten young storytellers gathered in a garden — the framing device Boccaccio used to spin 100 tales while plague ravaged Florence.
evt-lme-edward-iii-claim: Edward III in full regalia as a Knight of the Garter, displaying the quartered arms of England and France that underpinned his claim to the French throne.
evt-lme-battle-poitiers: An illuminated manuscript scene from the Grandes Chroniques de France showing English archers routing the French cavalry at the Battle of Poitiers, 1356.
evt-lme-charles-v-france: Charles V 'the Wise,' King of France, in a contemporary illumination from the Bibliothèque nationale de France, wearing the fleur-de-lis mantle of French royalty.
evt-lme-henry-v: Henry V of England in a medieval miniature portrait, the warrior-king who led the English to Agincourt and very nearly made himself heir to the French crown.
evt-lme-battle-agincourt: An illuminated manuscript depiction of the Battle of Agincourt (1415), showing the two armies locked in the narrow field where Henry V's outnumbered force shattered the French nobility.
evt-lme-treaty-troyes: The original ratification document of the Treaty of Troyes (1420), bearing its lead seal, by which Henry V was recognised as heir to the French crown.
evt-lme-joan-of-arc-orleans: Jules Lenepveu's painting of Joan of Arc at the walls of Orléans, standard raised, leading the assault that broke the English siege in May 1429.
evt-lme-charles-vii-coronation: Joan of Arc stands with her white standard at the altar as Charles VII is crowned King of France at Reims Cathedral, July 1429.
evt-lme-joan-burned: The only surviving near-contemporary image of Joan of Arc, a miniature from 1429 showing her in full armour with sword and banner — painted the year of her greatest victories.
evt-lme-philip-the-good: Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, in a Flemish panel portrait wearing the collar of the Order of the Golden Fleece, which he founded and used to bind the greatest lords of Europe to his court.
evt-lme-battle-castillon: A 15th-century illuminated manuscript detail of the Battle of Castillon (1453), the last engagement of the Hundred Years War, where French artillery ended English rule in Aquitaine.
evt-lme-return-to-rome: A medieval illumination of Pope Gregory XI's coronation — the pope who ended the Avignon exile and returned the papacy to Rome in 1377.
evt-lme-western-schism: Disputing clerics in a 14th-century illumination from the Grandes Chroniques de France, capturing the fractious atmosphere of the Western Schism when rival popes competed for Christendom's loyalty.
evt-lme-council-constance: Václav Brožík's 19th-century painting of Jan Hus standing before the Council of Constance in 1415, which condemned him as a heretic before burning him at the stake.
evt-lme-sigismund-emperor: Albrecht Dürer's portrait of Emperor Sigismund of Luxembourg in full imperial regalia, the German king who convened the Council of Constance to end the Western Schism.
evt-lme-john-wycliffe: A portrait of John Wycliffe, the Oxford theologian whose insistence that scripture alone — not the pope — was the final authority made him the most dangerous intellectual in 14th-century England.
evt-lme-jan-hus: A 16th-century woodcut of Jan Hus of Prague, inscribed with the year of his burning at Constance — 1415 — and verse lines recording that he died rather than recant.
evt-lme-hussite-wars: An illuminated manuscript battle scene from the Hussite Wars, bearing the Hussite chalice banner and their rallying cry 'Veritas Vincit' — Truth Conquers — the slogan of a movement that held Catholic crusades at bay for fifteen years.
evt-lme-jacquerie: Knights suppress French peasant rebels in a medieval illuminated manuscript depicting the brutal crushing of the Jacquerie uprising of 1358.
evt-lme-ciompi-revolt: G. L. Gatteri's 19th-century painting captures the moment Florence's wool-workers — the ciompi — stormed the piazza and briefly seized control of the city in 1378.
evt-lme-john-ball: A c. 1470 illumination from Froissart's Chronicles shows the rebel priest John Ball on horseback addressing the massed army of Wat Tyler's rebels outside London.
evt-lme-peace-of-lodi: A contemporary map showing Italy's political divisions in 1454 after the Peace of Lodi established the peninsula's uneasy balance of power among Milan, Venice, Florence, the Papal States, and Naples.
evt-lme-medici-florence: Portrait of Piero de' Medici, son of Cosimo and father of Lorenzo, capturing the dynasty's refined civic image at the height of its Florentine influence.
evt-lme-brunelleschi-dome: Brunelleschi's dome crowning the Florence Cathedral, completed in 1436 — the largest masonry dome ever built and the engineering marvel that announced the Renaissance to the world.
evt-lme-donatello: Donatello's bronze Amor-Attys, a playful, psychologically alive figure that exemplifies his revolutionary break from Gothic stiffness toward naturalistic, classically inspired sculpture.
evt-lme-masaccio: Masaccio's Expulsion from the Garden of Eden in the Brancacci Chapel, Florence — painted around 1425, its raw emotional realism and use of light transformed European painting overnight.
evt-lme-van-eyck: Jan van Eyck's Portrait of a Man (1433), likely a self-portrait, showcasing his mastery of oil glazing — a technique that gave Flemish painting its unmatched luminosity and textural depth.
evt-lme-bosch: Hieronymus Bosch's Crucifixion of St. Julia triptych, a vivid example of his densely symbolic, otherworldly imagery that blended Christian devotion with a dark carnival of human folly.
evt-lme-gutenberg-press: A replica Gutenberg-style screw press at the International Printing Museum, showing the hand-operated mechanism that let a skilled printer produce hundreds of pages a day — an unimaginable speed in 1450.
evt-lme-gutenberg-bible: The Lenox Copy of the Gutenberg Bible at the New York Public Library, one of fewer than fifty complete copies surviving from the roughly 180 printed in Mainz around 1455.
evt-lme-printing-spreads: An incunable page from a 1470s printed edition of Valerius Maximus, showing the crisp movable-type columns and hand-rubricated initials typical of Europe's earliest printed books.
evt-lme-condottieri: Portrait of Bartolomeo Colleoni, the celebrated Venetian condottiere who commanded mercenary armies across northern Italy and left a fortune to the city that erected one of the Renaissance's greatest equestrian statues in his honor.
evt-lme-fall-constantinople: A 16th-century monastery fresco depicting the Ottoman siege of Constantinople, the moment in 1453 that ended the thousand-year Byzantine Empire.
evt-lme-wars-of-roses: A colored lithograph of the Battle of Barnet (1471), one of the bloodiest clashes in the dynastic struggle between the Houses of York and Lancaster for the English crown.
evt-lme-bosworth-field: Philip James de Loutherbourg's dramatic painting of the Battle of Bosworth Field (1485), where Henry Tudor defeated and killed Richard III, ending the Plantagenet dynasty.
evt-lme-ferdinand-isabella: Double portrait of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile, whose 1469 marriage unified Spain's two greatest kingdoms and launched an era of Catholic monarchy.
evt-lme-fall-granada: Francisco Pradilla's monumental painting of the Surrender of Granada (1492), as the last Moorish sultan Boabdil hands over the keys of the city to Ferdinand and Isabella.
evt-lme-jewish-expulsion-1492: The original Alhambra Decree of 1492, signed by Ferdinand and Isabella, ordering the expulsion of all Jews from the Spanish kingdoms within four months.
evt-lme-columbus-1492: Detail from Juan de la Cosa's 1500 world map showing Guanahani (San Salvador) and neighboring islands — the first European cartographic record of Columbus's landfall.
evt-lme-bartolomeu-dias: Stone relief of Bartolomeu Dias at South Africa House in London, commemorating the Portuguese navigator who in 1488 became the first European to round the Cape of Good Hope.
evt-lme-vasco-da-gama: A 16th-century Portuguese portrait believed to depict Vasco da Gama, the explorer who in 1498 completed the first sea voyage from Europe to India, opening the Age of Discovery's most lucrative trade route.
evt-lme-treaty-tordesillas: The original 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas document, by which Spain and Portugal divided the newly discovered world between themselves along a line drawn through the Atlantic.
evt-lme-prince-henry-navigator: Contemporary panel portrait of Prince Henry the Navigator, the Portuguese royal who funded and organized the systematic exploration of the African coast that made Portugal's maritime empire possible.
evt-lme-spanish-inquisition: A 19th-century engraving of an auto-da-fé, the public ceremony in which the Spanish Inquisition pronounced judgment and handed condemned heretics to secular authorities for punishment.
evt-lme-statute-of-laborers: Two peasant laborers thresh grain in an illumination from the Luttrell Psalter (c.1325–1335) — precisely the class of workers whose post-plague demands for higher wages prompted Edward III to freeze pay at pre-Black Death levels with the Statute of Labourers.
evt-lme-hundred-years-war: Froissart's Chronicles illumination of the Battle of Crécy (1346), showing English longbowmen and armored knights under the royal standard clashing with the French cavalry — the opening shock of a war that would consume both kingdoms for over a century.
evt-lme-calais-siege: A medieval illuminated manuscript depicting the Siege of Calais (1346–1347), where Edward III starved the port city into submission after Crécy, securing England its first permanent foothold on French soil.
evt-ming-hongwu-emperor: The official court portrait of the Hongwu Emperor, founder of the Ming dynasty, seated on the imperial throne in ceremonial robes bearing a golden dragon medallion.
evt-ming-founding: A Ming-dynasty iron spearhead, one of the military weapons that equipped the armies Zhu Yuanzhang led to overthrow Mongol rule and establish his new dynasty in 1368.
evt-ming-grand-secretariat-abolition: The Wenhua Hall complex within the imperial palace grounds, which housed the administrative offices that Hongwu abolished in 1380 to concentrate all executive power directly in his own hands.
evt-ming-lan-yu-purge: A modern statue of Lan Yu, the general whose spectacular victories against the Mongols made him too powerful in Hongwu's eyes, leading to his execution and the massacre of thousands in 1393.
evt-ming-hongwu-code: A portrait of the Hongwu Emperor in his later years, when the Da Ming Huidian legal code he commissioned standardized punishments and Confucian social obligations across the empire.
evt-ming-eunuch-system: A Tang-dynasty tomb mural depicting court eunuchs in ceremonial dress, illustrating the deep roots of the eunuch bureaucracy that Hongwu simultaneously restricted and institutionalized within Ming palace administration.
evt-ming-empress-ma: The official court portrait of Empress Ma, Hongwu's consort and the dynasty's founding empress, whose reputation for compassion and counsel made her one of the most celebrated women in Chinese imperial history.
evt-ming-tax-system: A map of the Ming empire at its early peak, showing the vast agricultural territories whose grain and silk taxes Hongwu reorganized into the Yellow Register system to fund his centralised state.
evt-ming-frontier-defense: A map of the Ming Great Wall tracing the Nine Frontier Garrison zones from Jiayuguan in the west to Shanhaiguan on the Bohai coast, the defensive cordon Hongwu established to contain the retreating Mongols.
evt-ming-yongle-emperor: A map of the Ming empire at its greatest reach under the Yongle Emperor, showing the expanded territory that his aggressive diplomacy and military campaigns carved out in the early fifteenth century.
evt-ming-jianwen-emperor: A portrait of the Jianwen Emperor, the young second ruler of the Ming whose brief reign ended in civil war when his uncle seized the throne and declared himself the Yongle Emperor.
evt-ming-jingnan-campaign: A formal court portrait of the Yongle Emperor (Ming Chengzu), the prince who launched the Jingnan civil war against his nephew and emerged victorious to become one of the most consequential rulers in Chinese history.
evt-ming-forbidden-city: The Forbidden City seen from Coal Hill at dawn, its sea of yellow-tiled rooftops stretching across the center of Beijing exactly as Yongle designed it — the symbolic and literal heart of the Ming empire.
evt-ming-yongle-encyclopedia: A surviving volume of the Yongle Encyclopedia (Yongle Dadian), opened to show its distinctive red-ruled columns and dense hand-copied text — a page from what was once the largest encyclopedia ever compiled.
evt-ming-grand-canal-rebuild: A convoy of cargo barges queuing along the Grand Canal in Jiangnan, illustrating the waterway's role as China's great north-south artery — first rebuilt under the Yongle Emperor to feed the new capital at Beijing.
evt-ming-temple-of-heaven: The Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests at the Temple of Heaven, the triple-tiered circular structure where the Ming emperor performed the annual rites asking Heaven for a bountiful harvest on behalf of all under his rule.
evt-ming-zheng-he-voyages: A period-style illustration of Chinese junk ships under sail, representing the massive multi-masted vessels that carried Zheng He's seven expeditions across the Indian Ocean.
evt-ming-zheng-he: A museum reconstruction of Admiral Zheng He in his court robes, with a painting of treasure ships visible in the background — the Muslim eunuch who commanded the greatest fleet the premodern world had ever seen.
evt-ming-treasure-ships: A full-scale replica of a Ming treasure ship at the Nanjing Treasure Boat Site museum, with a stone marker reading 'Zheng He Treasure Boat 1405–1433' — these behemoths were said to be five times the length of Columbus's Santa María.
evt-ming-tumu-crisis: A battle map of the Tumu Fortress Crisis (1449), showing the Oirat Mongol encirclement route and the Ming army's doomed march northwest of Beijing.
evt-ming-yu-qian: A portrait of Yu Qian by the Qing painter Gu Jianlong, depicting the Ming minister who organized Beijing's defense after the Tumu disaster and paid for it with his life.
evt-ming-great-wall: The Ming-era Great Wall snaking across the ridges at Jinshanling — the most ambitious stretch of the wall the Ming built to keep the northern steppe out.
evt-ming-zhengde-emperor: The formal seated portrait of the Zhengde Emperor (Ming Wuzong), the freewheeling young ruler whose disregard for court ritual kept his ministers in a permanent state of alarm.
evt-ming-altan-khan: A period Mongolian painting of Altan Khan enthroned, the Tümed chieftain whose cavalry reached Beijing's suburbs in 1550 and extorted favorable trade terms from the Ming.
evt-ming-wanli-emperor: The Wanli Emperor in imperial court dress — his 48-year reign was the longest of the Ming dynasty.
evt-ming-zhang-juzheng: Zhang Juzheng, the brilliant and domineering grand secretary who ran the empire on behalf of the young Wanli Emperor through the 1570s and 1580s.
evt-ming-silver-flow: The Manila-to-Acapulco return route (tornaviaje) discovered by Andrés de Urdaneta in 1565, the Pacific corridor that funneled New World silver into Ming China.
evt-ming-matteo-ricci: Matteo Ricci, the Italian Jesuit who spent nearly three decades in China, adopting Chinese dress and learning the language to win access to the imperial court.
evt-ming-jesuit-mission: Frontispiece of Athanasius Kircher's China Illustrata (1667), depicting Jesuits in Chinese robes flanking a map of China — a symbol of the order's remarkable cultural adaptation.
evt-ming-xu-guangqi: Matteo Ricci and Xu Guangqi (Paul) together in a period engraving — the two men collaborated on translating Euclid into Chinese and became the most celebrated partnership of the Jesuit mission.
evt-ming-three-kingdoms: A Ming Wanli-era woodblock-printed title page of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, showing the multiple editions competing in China's booming late-Ming book market.
evt-ming-water-margin: A page from a Ming woodblock edition of the Water Margin, combining a lively scene illustration with dense prose — the format that made the novel a bestseller across the empire.
evt-ming-journey-to-the-west: A colorfully painted cover page of a Journey to the West sequel, showing the pilgrim Xuanzang and his monstrous companions — the characters that captured the Ming popular imagination.
evt-ming-plum-in-golden-vase: A Ming woodblock illustration from the Jin Ping Mei depicting an affluent merchant household courtyard, the social world the novel anatomizes with pitiless precision.
evt-ming-wang-yangming: A traditional ink portrait of Wang Yangming, the philosopher-general whose doctrine that knowledge and action are one upended Neo-Confucian orthodoxy across East Asia.
evt-ming-printing-explosion: A diagram of a revolving Chinese movable-type typesetter from 1313, the technology that underpinned the Ming printing explosion and democratized access to novels, encyclopedias, and moral manuals.
evt-ming-blue-and-white-porcelain: A Ming Zhengde-period blue-and-white porcelain ablution basin inscribed with Arabic calligraphy, showing how Jingdezhen kilns customized their wares for global Muslim markets.
evt-ming-jingdezhen-kilns: A Ming polychrome wine jar from Jingdezhen painted with carp, lotus, and water weeds — a showpiece of the imperial kiln city that supplied the world's finest ceramics for three centuries.
evt-ming-wei-zhongxian: The Tomb of the Five Martyrs in Suzhou, erected to honor five scholars executed by Wei Zhongxian's faction in 1626 — one of the few surviving memorials to resistance against his reign of terror.
evt-ming-tianqi-emperor: Official court portrait of the Tianqi Emperor (r. 1620–1627), the carpenter-emperor who handed effective control of the Ming government to the eunuch Wei Zhongxian while absorbed in his woodworking.
evt-ming-nurhaci: Formal court portrait of Nurhaci, the Jurchen chieftain who unified the northeastern tribes under the Eight Banners system and declared himself khan of the Later Jin dynasty in 1616.
evt-ming-eight-banners: A Qing-era painting depicting bannermen of the Plain Blue Banner in formation — one of the eight color-coded military-administrative divisions Nurhaci organized to bind Jurchen, Mongol, and Han soldiers into a single conquest machine.
evt-ming-chongzhen-emperor: Bronze figure of the Chongzhen Emperor, the last Ming ruler, who inherited a dynasty wracked by fiscal collapse, peasant rebellion, and Manchu pressure and fought desperately to save it until the end.
evt-ming-li-zicheng: A 17th-century Dutch engraving depicting a Chinese ruler on horseback, possibly Li Zicheng — the former postal worker who led a peasant army out of Shaanxi and brought the Ming dynasty to its knees in 1644.
evt-ming-fall-beijing: Map illustrating Li Zicheng's rebel army closing on Beijing in April 1644, the campaign that ended with the gates opening and the last Ming emperor retreating to Coal Hill.
evt-ming-coal-hill-suicide: The Chongzhen Emperor's personal seal and signature — relics of the last Ming ruler, who hanged himself on Coal Hill on April 25, 1644, rather than surrender to Li Zicheng's rebels.
evt-ming-wu-sangui: Portrait of Wu Sangui, the Ming general commanding the Shanhai Pass garrison, whose fateful decision to open the gate to the Manchu Qing armies sealed Beijing's fate and ended the dynasty.
evt-ming-shanhai-pass: Map of the Battle of Shanhai Pass in 1644, where Wu Sangui's alliance with the Qing regent Dorgon routed Li Zicheng's rebel forces and opened China to Manchu conquest.
evt-ming-southern-ming: Map showing the fragmented Southern Ming resistance kingdoms holding out in southern China after the Qing took Beijing in 1644, their territory steadily shrinking as Qing armies pushed south.
evt-ming-koxinga: Official portrait of Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong), the half-Japanese, half-Chinese Ming loyalist admiral who expelled the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662 and established the last redoubt of Ming resistance.
evt-ming-wokou-pirates: A 16th-century painted scroll depicting a sea battle between Japanese pirates (wokou) and Chinese naval forces — vivid evidence of the coastal raids that terrorized Ming China's southeastern provinces for decades.
evt-ming-eight-legged-essay: A top-ranked imperial examination answer paper (zhuangyuan juan) written in the eight-legged essay format — the rigidly structured literary form that every Ming civil servant candidate had to master to win office.
evt-ming-lijia-system: The Yellow Register Archives in Nanjing, where the Ming government stored the household census rolls that underpinned the lijia rural control system — every farming family's obligations recorded and filed here.
evt-ming-ming-army: A Ming-dynasty painting of a military review, with an imperial commander enthroned on a hilltop dais while ranked columns of soldiers, cavalry, and banner-bearers assemble below — exactly the ceremonial display of the weisuo garrison system in action.
evt-tang-founds-shang: A traditional Chinese portrait painting of King Tang, founder of the Shang dynasty, shown in imperial robes with a white hare at his feet.
evt-shang-mingtiao: A woodblock illustration of Jie, the last king of the Xia dynasty, whom Tang defeated at the Battle of Mingtiao around 1600 BCE to establish the Shang.
evt-erligang-city: A large bronze ding (ritual cauldron) unearthed from the Erligang culture city ruins at Zhengzhou, one of the earliest monumental bronzes cast in China.
evt-rammed-earth: A Han-era rammed-earth watchtower at Dunhuang showing the durability of hangtu construction, the same compacted-earth technique used to build Shang city walls.
evt-bronze-casting-begins: A grouping of Chinese ritual bronzes at the Metropolitan Museum of Art illustrates the astonishing variety of vessels — ding cauldrons, jue tripods, and wine jars — that Shang piece-mold casters produced for royal ceremony.
evt-erligang-expansion: An Erligang-period bronze jue (wine-pouring vessel) at the Cernuschi Museum, a type found across Shang colonial sites as the dynasty expanded south and east.
evt-panlongcheng: The Lijiazui site marker at Panlong City National Archaeological Park near Wuhan, the southernmost known Shang colony and a major bronze-production outpost.
evt-yi-yin: A traditional portrait of Yi Yin, the legendary minister who helped King Tang found the Shang dynasty and later served as regent, depicted in court robes.
evt-bronze-foundry-org: A Shang bronze battle axe — its blade cut through with a glaring face design — is a product of the royal foundries that controlled every step of bronze production, from ore procurement to finished weapon.
evt-wang-yirong-discovery: Wang Yirong, the Qing scholar and official whose sharp eye in 1899 recognized that the characters on 'dragon bones' being sold at Beijing apothecaries were an ancient script, launching the study of oracle bone inscriptions.
evt-oracle-bones: Shang dynasty ox scapula oracle bones bearing dense columns of inscribed characters — the king's questions to his ancestors and the spirits, scratched into bone more than three thousand years ago.
evt-yinxu-excavations: The entrance to the Yinxu Museum at Anyang, built over the site where Chinese and international archaeologists began systematic scientific excavations of the Shang royal capital in 1928.
evt-anyang-capital: The ceremonial gate of the Yinxu royal palace ruins at Anyang, the last and greatest capital of the Shang dynasty, decorated with taotie motifs and dragon-jade medallions.
evt-chinese-writing-origin: An inscribed Shang ox scapula covered in oracle bone script — the earliest form of Chinese writing, a logographic system whose descendants are still used by over a billion people today.
evt-oracle-bone-preparation: The back face of a Shang oracle bone (British Library Or. 7694) showing the rows of oval pits drilled and chiseled by specialist craftsmen before the divination ritual — heat applied to a pit produced the cracks a diviner would read.
evt-shang-oracle-content: A Shang dynasty inscribed tortoise plastron bearing divination records — the oracle bone texts cover an extraordinary range of royal concerns, from harvest forecasts and military campaigns to the health of the king's toothache.
evt-taotie-motif: A taotie face — glaring eyes, prominent nose, and bared jaw — stands out in relief on this Shang bronze vessel at the Cernuschi Museum, Paris, embodying the motif that dominated ritual bronzes for centuries.
evt-ritual-bronzes: A pair of Shang Dynasty ritual bronze vessels, their surfaces dense with taotie mask decoration — objects that conveyed political authority as much as religious purpose.
evt-simuwu-ding: The Houmuwu (Simuwu) Ding, cast around 1250 BC and weighing 875 kg (1,929 lb), stands in the National Museum of China as the largest surviving bronze vessel from the ancient world.
evt-bronze-weapons: A bronze knife with an ibex-head pommel, cast along the Shang northern frontier, shows how state foundries extended their craft outward — producing weapons that mixed Chinese technique with steppe aesthetics.
evt-shang-music-bells: A complete set of bianzhong bronze bell chimes, the premier instrument of Chinese court ritual, traces its origins to the single nao bells the Shang cast as early as the 13th century BC.
evt-animal-bronzes: A Shang bronze ox-shaped zun from M54 Tomb — its body sheathed in taotie and scroll designs — shows how Shang casters merged animal form with ritual function in a single extraordinary object.
evt-wu-ding: The massive Houmuwu Ding bronze cauldron, cast during Wu Ding's reign and inscribed with the name of his consort Fu Hao, on display at a museum exhibition.
evt-fu-hao: An animal-shaped bronze gong vessel recovered from Fu Hao's tomb at Yinxu, one of hundreds of bronzes buried with the warrior queen.
evt-fu-hao-qiang-campaign: Modern statue of Fu Hao in military armor holding a battle axe at the Yinxu archaeological site in Anyang, commemorating her role as a Shang military commander.
evt-fu-hao-tomb: The excavated interior of Fu Hao's tomb at Yinxu, showing bronze ritual vessels and skeletal remains arrayed around the burial chamber as they were found.
evt-fu-yue: A traditional portrait painting of Fu Yue, the former laborer whom King Wu Ding elevated to chief minister after claiming to have found him in a dream.
evt-jade-carving: A finely carved white jade plaque depicting intertwined dragons, showcasing the intricate lapidary craftsmanship that made jade objects the premier prestige goods of the Shang elite.
evt-white-pottery: A Shang dynasty white pottery vessel with finely incised geometric patterns, exemplifying the high-fired kaolin clay ware produced exclusively for the Shang elite.
evt-shangdi-worship: The Circular Mound Altar at Beijing's Temple of Heaven, the imperial-era descendant of the Shang practice of offering sacrifices to Shangdi, the supreme sky deity.
evt-turtle-shell-trade: An inscribed Shang dynasty turtle plastron at the Ningxia Museum — the flat belly shell of a Reeves's turtle, sourced through long-distance trade networks and used for royal divination.
evt-shang-astronomy: The Dunhuang Star Map, an early Chinese astronomical chart that inherits the systematic constellation-naming tradition the Shang diviners began recording on oracle bones.
evt-silk-production: Raw silk threads reeled from silkworm cocoons and wound onto spindles — the same basic process the Shang refined into a state-controlled luxury industry more than three thousand years ago.
evt-lacquer-work: Chinese carved lacquerware vessels on display at a museum of Asian art, representing the millennia-old tradition of coating objects with layers of lacquer that the Shang pioneered.
evt-cowrie-currency: Cowrie shells used as currency in China during the 16th–8th century BCE — the same shells the Shang treated as the standard unit of exchange for everything from silk to slaves.
evt-shang-wine-culture: A Shang bronze guang — an elaborate lidded wine-pouring vessel in the form of a mythical beast — embodying the dynasty's obsession with ritual drinking and the prestige objects built around it.
evt-sanxingdui: The haunting gold-masked bronze heads of Sanxingdui — a civilization flourishing in Sichuan at the same time as the Shang, yet utterly unlike anything the Yellow River world produced.
evt-di-xin: A Japanese woodblock print of King Di Xin (殷紂王), the last ruler of the Shang, whose reputation for cruelty and excess became one of the foundational cautionary tales of Chinese political thought.
evt-daji: A stone relief at Ping Sien Si temple depicting Daji (妲己), the favorite consort of Di Xin, whose later legend cast her as a fox spirit whose seductions drove the last Shang king to ruin.
evt-king-wu-zhou: A traditional Chinese hanging-scroll painting of King Wu of Zhou (武王), the warrior-king who led the coalition armies that overthrew the Shang at Muye and founded the Zhou dynasty around 1046 BC.
evt-zhou-coalition: A map showing the Zhou coalition's march from its western base at Feng eastward across the Shang heartland to the battlefield at Muye, where the dynasty's fate was decided in a single day.
evt-song-state: A map of the Zhou dynasty principalities, with the state of Song visible in the central plain — the territory Zhou granted to Shang royal descendants to maintain their ancestral rites after the conquest.
evt-shang-proto-zhou: A traditional portrait of King Wen of Zhou, the ruler who built the small western state of Zhou into a credible rival of the Shang and laid the ideological groundwork for the dynasty his son would overthrow.
evt-pushyamitra-shunga: The reconstructed east gateway and railings of the Bharhut Stupa, the most celebrated monument of the Shunga dynasty Pushyamitra founded, now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.
evt-shunga-horse-sacrifice: A Rajput painting depicting the ashvamedha (horse sacrifice), the ancient Vedic rite Pushyamitra performed twice to legitimize his new dynasty after overthrowing the last Maurya.
evt-bharhut-stupa: A sandstone railing panel from the Bharhut Stupa (Shunga dynasty, early 2nd century BCE) showing a royal couple visiting the Buddha, now in the Freer Gallery of Art — among the earliest surviving narrative sculptures in Indian art.
evt-sanchi-gateways: The east torana (gateway) of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, its three crossbars carved with scenes from the Buddha's life and previous births — the most intact of the four gateways added during the Shunga period.
evt-kharavela-kalinga: The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri, Odisha — Kharavela's 17-line boast carved in Brahmi script that is the primary source for his reign and his campaigns against the Shunga empire.
evt-demetrius-invasion: A coin portrait of Demetrius I of Bactria wearing his distinctive elephant-scalp helmet, the headgear that announced his conquest of northwestern India to the Greek world.
evt-indo-greek-coins: A silver Indo-Greek coin of Hippostratos showing Greek on one side and Kharosthi on the other — the bilingual format that made Indo-Greek coinage the first in the world to carry text in two scripts.
evt-menander-reign: Portrait of Menander I reconstructed from his coinage — the Indo-Greek king whose philosophical debates with the Buddhist monk Nagasena became one of antiquity's most celebrated cross-cultural conversations.
evt-milindapanha: An illustrated Sinhalese palm-leaf manuscript with painted covers depicting scenes from the Buddhist tradition — the kind of text culture that preserved and transmitted the Milindapanha across centuries.
evt-heliodorus-pillar: The Heliodorus Pillar standing at Vidisha, erected around 113 BCE by a Greek ambassador who converted to Vaishnavism — one of the earliest non-Indian inscriptions dedicated to a Hindu deity.
evt-saka-migration: A map of Indo-Scythian (Saka) territory at its peak, showing the steppe migrants' new domain stretching from Gandhara into the Gangetic plains.
evt-maues-first-saka: Silver coin of Maues, the first Saka king of India, bearing his name in Greek letters alongside a Kharoshthi reverse — the bilingual calling card of a conqueror making himself at home.
evt-azes-era: Silver coin of Azes I showing the king on horseback — his reign became the anchor point for the Azes Era, a calendar system so widely used that scholars still argue about exactly when it started.
evt-gondophares: Silver coin of Gondophares, the Indo-Parthian king whose name turns up in early Christian tradition as the ruler Saint Thomas supposedly visited — though the legend grew long after the coins stopped circulating.
evt-satavahana-saka-wars: Coin of Vashishtiputra Sri Satakarni, the Satavahana king who reclaimed Deccan territory from the Western Sakas after generations of back-and-forth conflict along India's western coast.
evt-kushan-kujula: Bronze coin of Kujula Kadphises, founder of the Kushan Empire, showing his portrait on the obverse — one of the earliest unambiguous images of a Kushan ruler.
evt-vima-kadphises: Gold double stater of Vima Kadphises (Musée Guimet), showing the king enthroned and illustrating the empire's wealth at its territorial peak.
evt-kanishka-reign: Gold dinar of Kanishka I showing the emperor standing at an altar — his coinage advertised deities from three religions, a deliberate signal of the empire's cosmopolitan ambitions.
evt-ashvaghosha: Traditional portrait of Ashvaghosha, the poet-philosopher and Kanishka's court monk whose Buddhacharita gave the Buddha his first full literary biography.
evt-vasumitra-philosopher: 18th-century lacquered wood sculpture of Vasumitra at Tây Phương Pagoda, Vietnam — a later East Asian rendering of the great Kushan-era Buddhist philosopher and council president.
evt-silk-road-kushan: Map of the Kushan Empire at its height, spanning the key nodes of the Silk Road from Bactria through Mathura — the geographic basis of its commercial dominance.
evt-kushan-coinage: Gold dinar of Kushan king Huvishka (Cleveland Museum of Art) — the empire's standardized gold coinage became the trusted currency of the entire Silk Road.
evt-buddhism-central-asia: Buddhist mural from the Bezeklik Caves, Xinjiang — a vivid example of the Gandharan-influenced Buddhist art that spread across Central Asia in the Kushan era.
evt-lotus-sutra: Sanskrit manuscript of the Lotus Sutra in Brahmi script from South Turkestan — one of the oldest surviving copies of a text that reshaped Buddhist theology across Asia.
evt-pali-canon-written: Palm-leaf Burmese-Pali manuscript pages — representing the written tradition that began when Sri Lankan monks committed the oral Pali Canon to text around 29 BCE.
evt-kanishka-era: 1878 reconstruction drawing of the Ahin Posh stupa (Jalalabad Valley), a Kushan-era Buddhist monument whose relic casket inscription helped scholars pin down the Kanishka Era dating debates.
evt-gandhara-art: A Gandhara bodhisattva (Avalokitesvara) in bronze from the Musée Guimet, blending Hellenistic modeling with Buddhist iconography — the defining fusion of the Gandhara school.
evt-mathura-art: A seated Buddha in the Mathura red sandstone style, its full-bodied naturalism and flowing transparent robe marking the indigenous Indian answer to Gandhara's Greco-Buddhist aesthetic.
evt-bodhisattva-ideal: A bodhisattva relief at Plaosan temple, showing how the Mahayana ideal of the compassionate being who delays nirvana to aid others spread far beyond India into Southeast Asian Buddhist art.
evt-mahayana-buddhism: Maitreya, the future Buddha, depicted in a Pala-era illumination of the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita — the Perfection of Wisdom sutras at the heart of Mahayana's new vision of enlightenment.
evt-ajanta-early-caves: The Ajanta cave complex carved into a horseshoe-shaped basalt cliff in the Western Ghats, where the earliest chaitya halls and viharas were cut under Satavahana patronage around the 1st century BCE.
evt-karle-chaitya: The barrel-vaulted interior of the Karla Caves' great chaitya hall, whose rows of carved pillars and wooden-ribbed ceiling represent the finest surviving rock-cut prayer hall of the early Satavahana era.
evt-amaravati-stupa: A carved limestone slab from the Amaravati Stupa now in the British Museum, depicting the stupa itself ringed by worshippers — a masterpiece of the distinctive Amaravati school of Buddhist sculpture.
evt-gautamiputra-satakarni: Coins of Gautamiputra Satakarni bearing his name in Brahmi script, commemorating the king who drove out the Western Satraps and briefly reunited the Deccan under Satavahana rule.
evt-rudradaman: A silver coin of Rudradaman I, the Western Satrap who twice defeated Gautamiputra's successor and whose portrait coinage marks him as one of the most powerful rulers of 2nd-century CE India.
evt-satavahana-decline: The rock-cut facade of a Satavahana-era cave temple, representing the monumental Buddhist patronage the dynasty sustained even as regional successors began chipping away at its southern and western frontiers.
evt-roman-india-trade: A trade route map showing the vast network connecting Rome to Indian ports through the Arabian Sea, with goods like spices, textiles, and gems flowing in both directions.
evt-pliny-gold-drain: Roman gold solidus of Emperor Theodosius II found at Ajanta, India — tangible evidence of the gold coins Rome's treasury kept losing to the insatiable demand for Indian luxuries.
evt-muziris-port: Detail from the Tabula Peutingeriana, a medieval copy of a Roman road map, marking Muziris ("Muziris") on the Kerala coast as a known destination for Roman traders.
evt-periplus: Map reconstructing the trade routes described in the 1st-century CE Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, the Greek sailor's handbook that named every port from Egypt to southern India.
evt-arikamedu: A 1st–2nd century CE Roman-style terracotta figurine excavated at Arikamedu (Virampatnam), one of the many imported objects that prove Roman merchants lived and worked at this Tamil port.
evt-chera-chola-pandya: Map of Tamilakam in the Sangam period showing the territories of the three crowned kings — the Cheras on the west coast, the Cholas in the northeast, and the Pandyas in the deep south.
evt-sangam-literature: Palm-leaf manuscript preserving ancient and medieval Tamil literature from the Sangam era, the tradition of verse-making that produced some of the oldest surviving poetry in any language.
evt-tiruvalluvar: Title page of Charles Graul's 1865 Latin and Tamil edition of the Tirukkural, the 133-chapter ethical masterwork by Tiruvalluvar that Tamil culture has revered for two thousand years.
evt-pepper-trade: Botanical illustration of Piper nigrum, the black pepper vine native to Kerala's Malabar Coast, whose berries were so prized in Rome that they were accepted as currency and tribute.
evt-sassanid-pressure: A gold coin of Ardashir I Kushanshah, issued in the name of Vasudeva, marking the Sassanid seizure of western Kushan territories around 230–245 CE.
evt-vasudeva-kushan: Gold dinar of Vasudeva I, the last great Kushan emperor, whose reign saw the empire at its cultural peak before Sassanid pressure fractured it from the west.
evt-nagarjuna: Tibetan thangka painting depicting Nagarjuna, the 2nd-century philosopher whose Madhyamaka treatises on emptiness reshaped Buddhist thought across Asia.
evt-bhagavad-gita: A 19th-century illustrated Sanskrit manuscript of the Bhagavad Gita showing Krishna and Arjuna on their chariot at the moment of the great dialogue on duty and liberation.
evt-mahabharata-compilation: Ancient manuscript illustration of the Battle of Kurukshetra, the cataclysmic war at the heart of the Mahabharata, which reached its final compiled form around 400 CE.
evt-early-hindu-temples: The Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho, one of India's most celebrated examples of the nagara shikhara style that evolved from the earliest structural Hindu temples of the Gupta era.
evt-charaka-samhita: Manuscript pages from the Charaka Samhita's Sutrasthana section, the foundational Ayurvedic medical text compiled around the 1st–2nd century CE.
evt-indian-numerals: The Codex Vigilanus (976 CE), one of the earliest European manuscripts to record the Hindu-Arabic numerals — the decimal notation system that originated in India and transformed world mathematics.
evt-bamiyan-buddhas: The great standing Buddha of Bamiyan carved into the Afghan cliffs, one of two colossal figures begun in the 3rd–5th centuries CE and destroyed by the Taliban in 2001.
evt-gupta-founding: The Padmapani Bodhisattva fresco at Ajanta Caves, a masterwork of Gupta-era painting that embodies the artistic and spiritual flourishing the Gupta dynasty made possible.
evt-lapita-pottery: Archaeological drawings of Lapita pottery vessel types recovered from Taumako, showing the distinctive dentate-stamped decoration that marks sites across the Pacific.
evt-austronesian-dispersal: Map tracing the spread of the Austronesian language family from its Taiwan homeland outward through the Philippines, Indonesia, and across the Pacific to Hawaii and New Zealand.
evt-lapita-bismarck-expansion: Map of the Lapita pottery zone, showing the culture's rapid spread from the Bismarck Archipelago through Melanesia and into western Polynesia.
evt-lapita-outrigger: Nineteenth-century French lithograph of an Oceanian outrigger canoe under sail, showing the single-outrigger design and crab-claw sail that Lapita people refined into a deep-sea voyaging technology.
evt-lapita-obsidian-trade: A chunk of raw volcanic obsidian showing the glassy, razor-sharp fracture that made it the most prized cutting material in the prehistoric Pacific trade network.
evt-fiji-settlement: Nineteenth-century engraving of a traditional Fijian village gathering, depicting the ceremonial and communal life that took root when Lapita settlers first made landfall around 1000 BCE.
evt-tonga-settlement: Captain Cook's 1777 chart of the Friendly Isles — the island group that Lapita settlers reached around 900 BCE and transformed into the heartland of early Polynesian culture.
evt-samoa-settlement: 1896 map of the Samoan Islands, the archipelago where Lapita descendants settled around 800 BCE and developed the distinctively Polynesian language, customs, and social structures.
evt-polynesian-cultural-complex: The fifteen restored moai of Ahu Tongariki on Rapa Nui, one of the most powerful expressions of the shared religious and monumental architecture that defined the Polynesian Cultural Complex across the Pacific.
evt-kava-ceremony: Fijian men in traditional dress prepare kava around a carved tanoa bowl during a formal ceremony, a ritual of hospitality and chiefly rank that has united Polynesian societies for more than two thousand years.
evt-tapa-cloth: A Fijian wedding tapa (gatu vakaviti) from the LACMA collection, its intricate geometric patterns pressed into mulberry bark cloth — the same production tradition that spread with Polynesian settlers across the Pacific.
evt-polynesian-outliers: A map of the three major Pacific cultural zones — Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia — showing the geographic spread into which Polynesian outlier communities settled as isolated enclaves within Melanesian and Micronesian waters.
evt-double-hull-canoe: The Hokule'a, a modern reconstruction of a traditional Hawaiian double-hull voyaging canoe, demonstrates the open-ocean sailing technology that carried Polynesian settlers across thousands of miles of Pacific.
evt-stick-charts: A Micronesian stick chart woven from palm ribs and shells, encoding the patterns of ocean swells and island positions that Pacific navigators read by feel as much as by sight.
evt-marquesas-settlement: A museum reconstruction of a Marquesan war chief's ceremonial regalia — feathered headdress, tapa-fiber garment, and club — representing the warrior aristocracy that shaped early Marquesan society.
evt-cook-islands: The turquoise lagoon and white sand of Aitutaki's Motu Tapuaetai islet, one of the Cook Islands that Polynesian voyagers settled roughly a thousand years ago.
evt-tui-tonga-langi: The stepped stone terraces of Langi Tau'atonga at Mu'a, one of the massive royal burial mounds built by the Tu'i Tonga to announce dynastic power in coral and basalt.
evt-fijian-drua-canoe: Fijian sailing canoes under full lateen sail in a period photograph from Suva, capturing the speed and craftsmanship of the double-hulled drua tradition.
evt-marae-temples: The marae platform at Raiatea in French Polynesia, its flat stone pavement and upright basalt slabs overlooking the lagoon — the sacred gathering ground of chiefs and gods.
evt-breadfruit-cultivation: A ripe breadfruit hanging on the tree — the starchy, calorie-dense staple that Pacific islanders cultivated across thousands of miles of ocean to keep voyaging communities fed.
evt-taro-irrigation: Taro growing in a tropical garden on Réunion, its giant leaves channelling rainfall to the corms that Polynesian farmers learned to irrigate in terraced paddies across the Pacific.
evt-samoa-political: Three Samoan paramount chiefs, two of them bearing the orator's ceremonial staff, photographed on the beach — the visible embodiment of the fa'amatai chiefly hierarchy that ordered Samoan society.
evt-hawaii-settlement: Ancient Hawaiian petroglyphs carved into lava rock on the Big Island, among the earliest evidence of the settlers who reached these remote islands from the Marquesas.
evt-hawaiian-fishponds: The Alekoko (Menehune) fishpond on Kauai, one of the oldest surviving Hawaiian aquaculture systems, where stone walls channeling tidal flow let fish in to grow and blocked their exit.
evt-easter-island: A solitary moai stands against the Pacific shore of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), the most isolated landfall in the Polynesian world, settled around 800–1200 CE.
evt-moa-hunting: Skeleton of Dinornis maximus, the giant moa, at the Natural History Museum — the massive flightless bird that early Maori hunters drove to extinction within a few centuries of settlement.
evt-sweet-potato: Sweet potatoes (Ipomoea batatas), the South American crop whose presence across Polynesia is hard genetic proof that Polynesian voyagers reached the Americas and returned long before Europeans did.
evt-maori-kumara-cultivation: Kumara (taputini variety, Ipomoea batatas) growing in soil, the sweet potato cultivar Maori settlers carried to Aotearoa and painstakingly adapted to New Zealand's cooler climate.
evt-hawaiian-tahitian-voyages: John Webber's 1778 illustration of a heiau temple at Waimea, Kauai, drawn during Cook's third voyage — capturing Hawaiian religious architecture at the close of the great Hawai'i-Tahiti voyaging era.
evt-moai-construction: The fifteen restored moai of Ahu Tongariki stand in a row on Easter Island, each averaging 13 feet tall and weighing dozens of tons — the largest completed ahu on the island and a testament to the sheer organizational ambition of Rapa Nui society.
evt-ahu-tongariki: Ahu Tongariki as seen from the front, its fifteen moai gazing inland across the grassy plain — the platform was toppled in the 17th-century civil wars and collapsed by a 1960 tsunami before being painstakingly re-erected by a Chilean-Japanese team in the 1990s.
evt-hawaiian-heiau: An 1782 engraving by W. Ellis of a heiau at Kealakekua Bay, Hawai'i, showing the wooden ki'i akua figures and stone platform that formed the heart of Hawaiian ritual life long before European contact.
evt-makahiki-festival: Participants in traditional Hawaiian dress observe Makahiki rites, a four-month season of peace, games, and tribute to the god Lono that structured the Hawaiian year from roughly November to February.
evt-maori-pa: A museum model of a Maori pa built on a coastal headland shows the concentric wooden palisades and terraced earthworks that made these hilltop fortifications among the most sophisticated defensive architecture in the Pacific.
evt-maori-carving: A Maori carver at Whakarewarewa works the flowing koru spiral forms into a wooden panel in 1982, practicing a tradition that has encoded genealogy, cosmology, and identity into wood for centuries.
evt-maori-wharenui: The wharenui Tanenuiarangi displays the carved and painted facade typical of Maori meeting houses, where the building itself is understood as an ancestor's body — the ridgepole its spine, the rafters its ribs.
evt-arioi-society: A feather-wrapped to'o figure representing Oro, the Tahitian war god whose cult gave rise to the Arioi society — travelling performers, priests, and entertainers who carried Oro's sacred presence between islands.
evt-rapa-nui-birdman: An aerial view of Motu Nui (left) and Motu Iti off the southwest coast of Rapa Nui — the finish line of the annual birdman competition, where challengers swam through shark-patrolled waters to retrieve the first sooty tern egg of the season.
evt-rongorongo: The reverse of rongorongo tablet B (Aruku-Kurenga), one of only about two dozen surviving wooden tablets inscribed with the undeciphered rongorongo script — the only indigenous writing system known from Oceania.
evt-hula-tradition: A hula kahiko dancer performs the ancient form at Hawaii Volcanoes National Park, wearing the traditional lei po'o headpiece and wrist adornments — hula kahiko preserves chants and gestures that encode Hawaiian history and cosmology going back centuries.
evt-rapa-nui-collapse: The seven moai of Ahu Akivi — the only platform whose statues face the ocean — stand as monuments to the island society that exhausted its forests and its future raising them.
evt-hawaiian-unification-wars: A Hawaiian royal feather cape (ahu'ula), made from tens of thousands of birds' feathers, signals the chiefly mana that the island's warring ali'i staked everything to claim.
evt-mandate-of-heaven: The Ding cauldron of Duke Mao, a Western Zhou bronze bearing a 500-character inscription that repeatedly invokes the Mandate of Heaven — the doctrine Zhou rulers coined to explain why heaven had withdrawn its favour from the Shang and granted rule to them instead.
evt-tsc-emperor-wen-sui: A traditional painted portrait of Emperor Wen of Sui — Yang Jian — flanked by attendants, depicting the founder who reunified China after nearly four centuries of division.
evt-tsc-sui-reunification: A traditional portrait of Chen Feidi, the last emperor of the southern Chen dynasty, whose defeat by Sui forces in 589 CE completed China's reunification under Emperor Wen.
evt-tsc-emperor-yang-sui: A traditional painted portrait of Emperor Yang of Sui, the ambitious second emperor whose grand projects — canals, palaces, and disastrous Korean campaigns — exhausted the empire and triggered its collapse.
evt-tsc-grand-canal: A long convoy of cargo barges moves along the Jiangnan section of China's Grand Canal, the world's longest artificial waterway first built under the Sui dynasty to link the Yellow and Yangtze river basins.
evt-tsc-fall-of-sui: A map showing the widespread peasant and warlord uprisings that tore the Sui Empire apart between 613 and 618 CE, as overtaxed subjects and exhausted soldiers turned against Emperor Yang's regime.
evt-tsc-emperor-gaozu-tang: A traditional full-length portrait of Li Yuan, the Emperor Gaozu who founded the Tang dynasty in 618 CE after the Sui collapse.
evt-tsc-xuanwu-gate: A modern reconstruction of the Danfeng Gate at the Tang imperial Daming Palace complex — successor to the Xuanwu Gate where Li Shimin seized power in 626 CE.
evt-tsc-emperor-taizong: A traditional portrait of Emperor Taizong (Li Shimin) in imperial yellow dragon robes, the soldier-statesman whose Zhenguan era became the template for Tang greatness.
evt-tsc-civil-service-expansion: A historical illustration of candidates sitting the imperial civil service examinations in individual cells, the grueling system Tang Taizong dramatically expanded to open government service to talent.
evt-tsc-conquest-eastern-turks: A campaign map of the Tang war against the Eastern Türk Khaganate, showing the 629–630 CE offensive that broke Turkic power and made Taizong the 'Heavenly Khan' of the steppe.
evt-tsc-conquest-western-turks: A campaign map of the Tang conquest of the Western Turks under Emperor Gaozong, the 650s–660s campaigns that extended Chinese control deep into Central Asia.
evt-tsc-empress-wu-zetian: A portrait of Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name, shown in elaborate imperial court headdress.
evt-tsc-emperor-xuanzong: Emperor Xuanzong receives an audience in this Tang court painting, capturing the cultured imperial grandeur of the High Tang era he presided over for four decades.
evt-tsc-yang-guifei: Gu Jianlong's painting of Yang Guifei leaving the bath, depicting the legendary imperial consort whose romance with Xuanzong and tragic death at Mawei became the most famous love story of the Tang.
evt-tsc-tang-changan: A plan of Tang-era Chang'an showing the grid of wards, the twin markets, and the Imperial City at its heart — the world's largest city at nearly a million people.
evt-tsc-nestorian-stele: A 17th-century rubbing of the Nestorian Stele, erected in Chang'an in 781 CE to record the arrival of Christianity in China along the Silk Road.
evt-tsc-li-bai: A classic ink-wash portrait of Li Bai, the Tang dynasty's most celebrated poet, whose verse on wine, mountains, and the moon made him a legend in his own lifetime.
evt-tsc-du-fu: A traditional portrait of Du Fu, the 'Poet Sage' of the Tang dynasty, whose verse bore witness to the devastation of the An Lushan Rebellion.
evt-tsc-bai-juyi: A line drawing portrait of Bai Juyi, the Tang poet famous for writing verses plain enough that — legend says — even an illiterate old woman could understand them.
evt-tsc-chan-buddhism: Bodhidharma and Huike in a painting by Sesshu Toyo — the founding moment of Chan Buddhism, when Huike cut off his arm to prove his devotion and received the transmission.
evt-tsc-yan-zhenqing: A rubbing from the Yan Qinli Stele, showing the bold, upright brushwork of Yan Zhenqing — the Tang calligrapher whose style became a standard for Chinese writing for a thousand years.
evt-tsc-block-printing: The frontispiece of the Diamond Sutra (868 CE), the world's oldest dated printed book, produced by woodblock printing in Tang dynasty China.
evt-tsc-xuanzang-journey: A Tang-era portrait of the monk Xuanzang, shown laden with the Buddhist scriptures he carried back from India on his seventeen-year journey to the west.
evt-tsc-wild-goose-pagoda: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda in Xi'an, built in 652 CE to house the scriptures Xuanzang brought back from India and still standing after thirteen centuries.
evt-tsc-an-lushan-rebellion: Campaign map of the An Lushan Rebellion (755–763), showing rebel advances from Fanyang toward Luoyang and Chang'an and the Tang counteroffensive routes that eventually reclaimed the capitals.
evt-tsc-battle-talas: Map of the Battle of Talas (751 CE), where Tang forces clashed with the Abbasid Caliphate in Central Asia at the westernmost reach of Chinese imperial expansion.
evt-tsc-han-yu: Traditional portrait of Han Yu (768–824), the Tang essayist and philosopher whose vigorous Confucian revival and opposition to Buddhist influence shaped Chinese intellectual life for centuries.
evt-tsc-great-anti-buddhist-persecution: Portrait of Emperor Wuzong of Tang, whose Huichang Suppression (842–845) demolished thousands of monasteries and forced hundreds of thousands of monks and nuns back into secular life.
evt-tsc-loss-sixteen-prefectures: A map showing the Sixteen Prefectures — the strip of strategic northern territory ceded to the Khitan Liao, hemming the Song in and leaving the capital dangerously exposed.
evt-tsc-emperor-taizu-song: The imperial portrait of Zhao Kuangyin — Emperor Taizu — the former general who staged a coup in 960 and reunified China under the Song dynasty he would rule for sixteen years.
evt-tsc-song-kaifeng: The Dragon Pavilion in Kaifeng, built on the site of the Northern Song imperial palace complex that made this city the political and cultural heart of China for over a century.
evt-tsc-iron-pagoda: The Iron Pagoda of Kaifeng, completed in 1049, whose glazed brown brickwork resembles cast iron and has stood for nearly a thousand years as a testament to Northern Song engineering.
evt-tsc-along-river-scroll: A section of Zhang Zeduan's 'Along the River During the Qingming Festival,' showing the crowded city gate of Bianjing (Kaifeng) teeming with merchants, officials, and travelers in the early 12th century.
evt-tsc-wang-anshi-reforms: A portrait of Wang Anshi, the Song dynasty's boldest reformer, whose sweeping New Policies package of the 1070s—covering loans, taxes, and military recruitment—split the court into bitter factions.
evt-tsc-sima-guang: A surviving manuscript page of the Zizhi Tongjian (Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance), Sima Guang's monumental 294-volume chronicle of Chinese history from 403 BCE to 959 CE.
evt-tsc-wujing-zongyao: A page from the Wujing Zongyao (1044), the world's earliest known printed military encyclopedia, showing Song dynasty gunpowder formulas and weapon specifications in woodblock-printed text.
evt-tsc-song-fire-weapons: An 11th-century illustration of Song soldiers firing basketry fire-arrow launchers, one of the gunpowder-propelled weapons that gave Chinese armies a decisive technological edge in this era.
evt-tsc-gunpowder-formula: Black powder—the mixture of saltpeter, charcoal, and sulfur whose formula the Song dynasty first committed to writing, setting off a chain of military and technological consequences that would reshape the world.
evt-tsc-movable-type: A museum display of ceramic movable type in the style invented by Bi Sheng around 1040, the world's first movable-type printing system, which allowed individual characters to be set, printed, and reused.
evt-tsc-song-paper-money: A Song dynasty government-issued jiaozi note from 1023, the world's first state-backed paper currency, whose woodblock-printed design carried anti-counterfeiting marks and denominations in a single sheet.
evt-tsc-magnetic-compass: A Southern Song ceramic figure of an immortal holding a land compass, excavated from a tomb in Jiangxi Province—direct physical evidence of the Song dynasty's pioneering use of magnetic needle navigation.
evt-tsc-shen-kuo: A modern bust of Shen Kuo, the Song polymath whose 'Dream Pool Essays' (1088) described magnetic declination, movable type, and dozens of other scientific observations centuries before their Western equivalents.
evt-tsc-song-coal-iron: A historical woodblock illustration of Chinese iron fining and blast furnace operations, depicting the coke-fired industrial processes behind the Song dynasty's astonishing iron output of roughly 125,000 tons per year.
evt-tsc-champa-rice: Varieties of rice including the fast-ripening strains descended from Champa rice, the drought-resistant cultivar imported from Vietnam by Emperor Zhenzong around 1012 that enabled Song China's agricultural revolution and population boom.
evt-tsc-emperor-huizong: The formal seated imperial portrait of Emperor Huizong of Song, the painter-emperor whose refined court culture and catastrophic political misjudgments led to the Jurchen capture of Kaifeng and his own death in captivity.
evt-tsc-jurchen-conquest: Emperor Huizong of Song, the painter-emperor whose capture by Jurchen forces in 1127 became the defining humiliation of the Jingkang Incident.
evt-tsc-yue-fei: Traditional portrait illustration of Yue Fei, the Southern Song general whose campaigns against the Jurchen Jin dynasty made him China's most celebrated military martyr.
evt-tsc-zhu-xi-neoconfucianism: A traditional painted portrait of Zhu Xi, the Song philosopher whose synthesis of Confucian thought into Neo-Confucianism became the intellectual backbone of Chinese statecraft for the next seven centuries.
evt-tsc-li-qingzhao: A sculptural portrait of Li Qingzhao, the Song poet whose ci verse — sharp with longing and loss — established her as the greatest female writer in the Chinese literary tradition.
evt-tsc-su-shi: A traditional portrait of Su Shi (Su Dongpo), the Song polymath whose essays, poems, and paintings defined the era's cultural high-water mark and whose name still graces a famous braised pork dish.
evt-tsc-landscape-painting: Fan Kuan's 'Travelers Among Mountains and Streams' (c. 1000 CE), a towering ink-on-silk masterpiece that exemplifies the Song monumental landscape tradition — tiny human figures dwarfed beneath impossibly massive, mist-shrouded peaks.
evt-tsc-song-maritime-trade: A Northern Song dynasty 'Daguan Tongbao' bronze coin from Emperor Huizong's reign, one of the standard currencies that flowed through the Song's vast maritime trade networks stretching from Japan to the Persian Gulf.
evt-tsc-quanzhou-port: An aerial view of Quanzhou's old city, the port that medieval Arab traders called Zaytun and that Marco Polo declared one of the greatest commercial harbors in the world during its Song-era peak.
evt-tsc-mongol-conquest: A campaign map tracing the Mongol advance into the Song Empire, with dated invasion arrows from the north, west, and south converging on the dynasty's final coastal refuges between 1234 and 1279.
evt-tattoo-tradition: A traditional Polynesian tattoo being applied in Tahiti, the artist working bold geometric patterns into the recipient's leg using hand-tapping tools — a practice that has encoded rank, lineage, and identity on Pacific bodies for more than two thousand years.
evt-tonga-tu-i-tonga: The Ha'amonga 'a Maui trilithon on Tongatapu — three massive coral-limestone slabs fitted together to form a ceremonial gateway — built by the 11th Tu'i Tonga around 1200 CE and still the most imposing monument of the empire's power.
evt-tui-manu-a: A Samoan chief photographed in traditional dress on Manu'a, wearing the whale-tooth ornament that marked the highest-ranking ali'i — the Tui Manu'a title held by this lineage was considered the most ancient and sacred paramount chieftaincy in all of Samoa.
evt-rapa-nui-ahu-platforms: The precisely fitted basalt blocks of Ahu Vinapu on Rapa Nui, whose Inca-like mortarless masonry has long intrigued researchers — one of dozens of ceremonial platforms that clans built along the coastline to seat and venerate their ancestor statues.
evt-hawaiian-ali-i: A Hawaiian feather cloak (ahu'ula) and feather helmet (mahiole) displayed in a museum case — garments made from tens of thousands of honeyeater feathers that only the highest-ranking ali'i could commission or wear.
evt-kumulipo: Queen Liliuokalani photographed around 1891 — she translated and published the Kumulipo in 1897, the 2,102-line Hawaiian creation chant that traces the genealogy of the cosmos from primordial darkness through the first chiefs.
evt-piilani-maui: The towering lava-stone terraces of Pi'ilanihale Heiau on Maui's Hamoa coast — the largest heiau in the Hawaiian Islands, built in stages from roughly the 14th century, with its final form credited to the conquering chief Pi'ilani.
evt-hawaiian-ahupuaa: The entrance to Ahupua'a O Kahana State Park on O'ahu — Kahana Valley is one of the last surviving intact ahupua'a, the wedge-shaped land divisions that ran from mountain ridge to reef and gave each community complete access to every resource zone.
