evt-umar-ii: A gold dinar struck during the reign of Umar II, the reform-minded caliph who tried to ease the tax burden on non-Arab converts and briefly narrowed the gap between Arab and mawali Muslims.
evt-tariq-spain: A medieval depiction of Tariq ibn Ziyad, the Umayyad commander who led the Muslim crossing into Iberia in 711 and gave his name to Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq, "Mountain of Tariq").
evt-battle-guadalete: The Battle of Guadalete (711), where Tariq ibn Ziyad's forces shattered the Visigothic army of King Roderic, opening all of Iberia to Arab and Berber conquest within a few years.
evt-conquest-sind-711: The ruins of the mosque at Kot Diji in Sind (modern Pakistan), named for Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, the seventeen-year-old Umayyad general who conquered the Indus Valley in 711 and carried Islam to the edge of the subcontinent.
evt-qutayba-transoxiana: A silver coin of the Sogdian ruler of Sawashfan in Transoxiana, the prosperous region beyond the Oxus River that Qutayba ibn Muslim systematically subdued between 705 and 715, bringing Bukhara and Samarkand under Umayyad control.
evt-battle-tours: Charles de Steuben's 19th-century painting of the Battle of Tours (Poitiers), 732, where the Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel halted the Umayyad advance into Western Europe.
evt-conquest-north-africa: A painting of Uqba ibn Nafi, the Arab general who drove across North Africa to the Atlantic coast around 682, reportedly riding his horse into the surf and declaring he would press on if not for the sea.
evt-dome-rock: The Dome of the Rock on Jerusalem's Temple Mount, completed by Abd al-Malik around 692 CE, remains one of the oldest surviving works of Islamic architecture and a deliberate statement of Umayyad ambition in the holy city.
evt-great-mosque-damascus: The arcaded courtyard facade of the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, built by al-Walid I around 706–715 CE on the site of a Byzantine cathedral, its golden mosaics and soaring arches signaling a new Islamic monumental vision.
evt-aqsa-mosque: Al-Aqsa Mosque on the southern end of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, rebuilt and expanded under the early Umayyads and second only to Mecca and Medina in sanctity for Muslims worldwide.
evt-early-hadith: An early Islamic manuscript page from a hadith collection, illustrating the careful written transmission of the Prophet's reported sayings and deeds that scholars began systematically gathering in the Umayyad period.
evt-early-fiqh: A world map showing the distribution of the four main Sunni law schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) and the Shia Jafari school, all rooted in the early jurisprudential debates that began during the Umayyad era.
evt-hisham: A silver dirham struck in the name of Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, the longest-reigning Umayyad caliph, whose fiscally disciplined rule kept the empire solvent for two decades.
evt-abu-muslim: A 1598 Ottoman genealogical portrait of Abu Muslim, the Khorasan organizer whose black-bannered revolt dismantled Umayyad power and handed the caliphate to the Abbasids.
evt-battle-zab: The Greater and Lesser Zab rivers of northern Iraq, where Abbasid forces crushed the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II in 750 CE and ended Umayyad rule in the east.
evt-abd-al-rahman-spain: Abd al-Rahman I, the young Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasid massacres, crossed into Spain, and founded an independent emirate at Córdoba that kept Umayyad rule alive in the west.
evt-arabic-science-translation: A folio from an Arabic translation of Dioscorides' De Materia Medica, an early example of the Graeco-Arabic translation movement that brought Greek scientific knowledge into the Islamic world.
evt-vs-dust-veil-536: A temperature reconstruction of the Common Era showing the sharp cold anomaly of 536–550, the deepest sustained cooling in the past 2,000 years, driven by volcanic aerosols that dimmed the sun across the Northern Hemisphere.
evt-vs-536-sun-dimming: A Latin stone inscription from Nosedo, Italy, dated 536 AD — one of the few contemporary records from the year the sky turned dark and the harvests failed across the Mediterranean and northern Europe.
evt-vs-bracteates: A gold Migration Period bracteate from Funen, Denmark (DR BR42), stamped with a commanding figural scene — these thin gold pendants were worn by the Scandinavian elite and deposited in hoards as the 536 catastrophe unfolded.
evt-vs-sosdala-style: The Sutton Hoo shoulder clasp, a masterpiece of Migration Period gold-and-garnet cloisonné featuring intertwined animal bodies — the same Germanic animal-style tradition that originated in Sösdala-era Scandinavia and spread across northern Europe.
evt-vs-depopulation-recovery: The Vendel I helmet, excavated from the elite boat grave at Vendel in Uppland, Sweden — a defining artifact of the post-536 recovery era when a new warrior aristocracy rebuilt Scandinavian society around prestige, war gear, and feasting halls.
evt-vs-vendel-graves: A 7th-century iron helmet with bronze fittings from one of the Vendel boat graves, now in the Swedish History Museum — the defining grave goods of Uppland's warrior elite.
evt-vs-valsgarde: The burial mounds at Valsgärde, near Uppsala, where a continuous series of boat graves spanning the Vendel Period and into the Viking Age were interred side by side across generations.
evt-vs-sutton-hoo-link: The burial mounds at Sutton Hoo, Suffolk, where the famous Mound 1 ship burial of c. 625 AD yielded treasure strikingly parallel to the Vendel boat graves just across the North Sea.
evt-vs-boat-burial-ritual: The 1880 excavation of the Gokstad ship burial in Norway lays bare the clinker-built vessel used to carry a chieftain into the afterlife — the same ritual logic that drove the Vendel and Valsgärde boat graves a century and a half earlier.
evt-vs-old-uppsala: The three royal burial mounds at Old Uppsala, Sweden, where Vendel-era kings of the Svear were interred and where the great sacrificial cult was centered.
evt-vs-hrolf-kraki: Hrólf Kraki scattering gold on the Fyrisvellir to slow his pursuers — the defining act of generosity in the most celebrated legend of the legendary Danish heroic age.
evt-vs-ynglings: Hugo Hamilton's 19th-century depiction of the Yngling king Ingjald the Ill-Ruler burning his rival kings alive — one of the dynasty's many violent succession episodes preserved in the sagas.
evt-vs-three-great-mounds: Museum reconstruction model of the Old Uppsala royal complex, showing the three great barrows alongside the temple precinct and surrounding settlement as archaeologists believe it appeared in the Vendel period.
evt-vs-ynglingatal: The Rök runestone in Östergötland, one of Scandinavia's longest runic inscriptions, representing the same oral-to-written transmission tradition through which the Ynglingatal king-list poem was eventually recorded.
evt-vs-beowulf: The opening folio of the Beowulf manuscript (Cotton MS Vitellius A XV, c. 1000 AD), the sole surviving copy of the Old English epic poem that preserves memory of the Geats and Swedes in the Vendel period.
evt-vs-geats-swedes: Map of the tribal territories in Beowulf-era Scandinavia, showing the Geats in southern Sweden, the Swedes to their north, and the Jutes and Danes to the south — the peoples whose conflicts dominate the epic.
evt-vs-danish-kingdoms-legendary: Interior of the reconstructed great hall at Lejre, the legendary seat of the Scylding dynasty and the Heorot of Beowulf, where the Danish kings hosted their warriors around a central hearth.
evt-vs-ring-swords: A Lombard ring-sword pommel from the 6th–7th century, showing the distinctive attached ring that made these weapons symbols of alliance and loyalty among the Vendel-era elite across northern Europe.
evt-vs-blot-sacrifice: A 19th-century depiction of the dísablót, the Norse seasonal sacrifice held indoors in the great hall, with worshippers raising offerings before statues of the gods.
evt-vs-norse-religion: A detail from the Ardre VIII Gotland picture stone showing a rider on an eight-legged horse, interpreted as Odin on Sleipnir — one of the earliest surviving images of Norse mythology.
evt-vs-odin-war-god: Georg von Rosen's 1886 painting of Odin as the wandering one-eyed god, hooded and staff in hand — the archetype of the warrior-king deity who demanded sacrifice in exchange for victory.
evt-vs-thor-freyr: The Rällinge statuette, an 11th-century Swedish bronze figurine of Freyr, god of fertility and plenty — one of the few surviving three-dimensional images of a Norse deity.
evt-vs-gotland-stones: The Hammars I picture stone from Gotland, its layered panels filled with warriors, ships, and mythological scenes painted in red ochre — among the finest surviving examples of Vendel-era stone carving.
evt-vs-picture-stone-valhalla: Max Brückner's 1896 stage painting of Valhalla, the hall of slain warriors high above the world — the destination that Gotland's picture stones promised to every warrior who died with honor.
evt-vs-ship-symbolism: The Gettlinge stone ship on Öland, Sweden, where standing stones were arranged in the outline of a vessel — a burial monument that physically anchored the ship as the pre-Viking symbol of the journey to the afterlife.
evt-vs-uppsala-temple: Olaus Magnus's 16th-century woodcut of the Temple at Uppsala, showing the great pagan sanctuary that Adam of Bremen described as decorated in gold, where every nine years kings and subjects alike made sacrifice.
evt-vs-helgo: The island of Helgö on Lake Mälaren, the sheltered waterway that made it Scandinavia's first great long-distance trading site from the 5th century onward.
evt-vs-helgo-workshops: The village road sign at Helgö, the island settlement on Lake Mälaren where archaeologists have uncovered bronze-casting moulds and craft-production debris spanning several centuries.
evt-vs-malaren-network: Lake Mälaren's island-studded western reaches, the sheltered inland sea whose interconnected waterways formed the backbone of Vendel-period Scandinavian trade.
evt-vs-grobina: The medieval castle ruins at Grobiņa in Latvia, built on the same commanding promontory where Scandinavian settlers established their overseas colony in the 7th century.
evt-vs-frisian-trade: The historical Frisian homeland along the North Sea coast, the middlemen traders whose emporium at Dorestad funnelled Frankish silver and Rhineland goods north into Scandinavian hands.
evt-vs-amber-trade: The ancient Amber Road linking Baltic shores to the Roman Empire, the same corridor that kept Baltic amber flowing south while silver and prestige goods moved north into Scandinavia.
evt-vs-ribe: The ancient town of Ribe, Denmark, seen from its river — one of northern Europe's oldest market towns, founded around 700 CE as a seasonal trading post where craftsmen and merchants gathered each spring.
evt-vs-sceattas: Obverse and reverse of a silver sceat, the small hammered pennies that became the first true coinage circulating through the North Sea emporia, including Ribe, in the early eighth century.
evt-vs-wodan-monster-coin: A 'porcupine' sceat of the Wodan-monster series, its obverse showing a stylised face framed by spiky lines — the distinctive coinage type minted at Ribe and widely copied across the North Sea trading zone.
evt-vs-silver-economy: The Cuerdale hoard at the British Museum displays the kind of Viking-age hacksilver — chopped arm-rings, ingots, and coin fragments — that Scandinavians used as weighed currency once silver began flowing north from Frankish and Arab trade networks.
evt-vs-thrall-economy: Erik Werenskiold's illustration 'Erling Sets His Thralls to Daywork' captures the Norse institution of thralldom, where enslaved people performed the agricultural and craft labour that underpinned the emerging emporium economy.
evt-vs-dorestad: A Carolingian silver denier minted at Dorestad under Lothair I, with 'DOR·ES·TAT' clearly struck on the reverse — the coins that Frankish merchants brought north along the Rhine to trade wine, cloth, and glass for Scandinavian furs and amber.
evt-vs-ahus-emporium: The central square and medieval church of Åhus in Scania, a coastal site that archaeological finds show was already serving as a small emporium — a seasonal gathering point for exchange — before the Viking Age proper began.
evt-vs-clinker: The overlapping strakes of a clinker-built wooden boat, the construction technique Scandinavian shipwrights perfected in the Vendel period and carried into the Viking Age.
evt-vs-the-sail: The Gokstad ship in the Viking Ship Museum, Oslo — a clinker-built vessel whose mast step and hull form show the sail-ready design that transformed Scandinavian seafaring.
evt-vs-hull-evolution: A clinker-built boat under oars, showing the overlapping plank construction that gave Scandinavian hulls their flexible, seaworthy character as builders moved from rivers to open water.
evt-vs-younger-futhark: A painted replica runestone from Öland displays the reduced 16-rune Younger Futhark alphabet that replaced the Elder Futhark as Scandinavian writing spread in the late Vendel period.
evt-vs-elder-futhark: The Einang stone inscription, one of the oldest surviving Elder Futhark texts, its 24-character alphabet carved in red paint visible against the rock surface.
evt-vs-runestones: The Lingsberg runestone (U 240) in Uppland, its serpentine body filled with runic text and a central cross — an example of the memorial stone tradition that flourished from the Vendel period onward.
evt-vs-danish-border-fortification: The Danevirke earthwork at Krummwall stretches across the Jutland peninsula — the great Danish border rampart begun around 737 to hold Frankish expansion at arm's length.
evt-vs-petty-kingdoms-norway: A map of the Norwegian petty kingdoms around 860 CE shows the patchwork of coastal and inland chieftaincies that Harald Fairhair would later force into a single realm.
evt-vs-salme: The excavated Salme boat burial site in Estonia, where two early 8th-century Scandinavian ships were found packed with warriors killed in battle far from home.
evt-vs-salme-ship-two: A sword recovered from the Salme II ship burial — one of many weapons found with the 33 warriors interred in the larger of the two Estonian Salme boats.
evt-vs-frankish-pressure: A 19th-century engraving depicts Charlemagne leading his Frankish forces against the Saxons — the decades-long Saxon Wars that pushed the Frankish frontier to Denmark's doorstep.
evt-vs-restless-aristocracy: A Gotland picture stone from Smiss depicting warriors and a ship, capturing the restless martial culture of the pre-Viking Scandinavian elite.
evt-vs-ottar: A page from the Old English Orosius manuscript containing Ohthere's firsthand account of his voyages around northern Norway and the White Sea, one of the earliest written descriptions of the Arctic north.
evt-vs-portland-incident: Coins of King Beorhtric of Wessex, in whose reign a small Norse fleet landed at Portland around 789 and killed his reeve — the first recorded Viking attack on English shores.
evt-vs-eve-of-vikings: The Tjängvide picture stone from Gotland, carved around the start of the Viking Age, showing a ship under sail crewed by armed warriors — an image that captures Scandinavia on the cusp of its explosive outward surge.
evt-vs-lindisfarne-launch: Lindisfarne (Holy Island) at sunrise, the isolated Northumbrian monastery struck by Norse raiders on 8 June 793 — the attack that announced the Viking Age to the Christian world.
evt-songhai-za-dynasty: A mounted guardsman of the Djermakoye, photographed in colonial Niger — the horseback warrior tradition of the Niger Bend chieftaincies stretches back to the Za dynasty lords who ruled Gao before Islam arrived.
evt-songhai-sonni-dynasty: A 19th-century engraving of a Niger Bend settlement, with mud-brick towers and flat-roofed compounds clustered above the floodplain — the landscape the Sonni dynasty ruled for generations before Sonni Ali transformed it into an empire.
evt-songhai-capture-timbuktu: A 19th-century engraving of Timbuktu from a rooftop, the Djinguereber Mosque's pyramid rising above a sea of mud-brick courtyards — the fabled city Sonni Ali seized from the Tuareg in 1468 after a brutal assault.
evt-songhai-scholar-massacres: A manuscript page from al-Maghili's political treatise addressed to Askia Muhammad — written in the aftermath of Sonni Ali's persecutions, it advised the new ruler on how a Muslim king should treat the scholars his predecessor had terrorized.
evt-songhai-niger-fleet: Traditional pirogues lining the Niger bank at Gao in 1990 — the same slender wooden craft that Sonni Ali organized into a war fleet, turning the river into both a supply line and a weapon.
evt-songhai-religious-heterodoxy: Drummers perform a traditional ceremony on the Niger bank — the kind of pre-Islamic ritual Sonni Ali refused to abandon, outraging Muslim scholars who condemned him as a hypocrite and sorcerer.
evt-songhai-judar-pasha: Ahmad al-Mansur, the Moroccan sultan whose obsession with Songhai's gold sent Judar Pasha and 20,000 soldiers on a four-month crossing of the Sahara — the most audacious military expedition in West African history.
evt-songhai-ahmed-baba-exile: A Portuguese architectural survey of the Saadian Kasbah of Marrakesh, the Moroccan capital where Ahmed Baba was imprisoned and then, grudgingly permitted to teach — his 14-year exile in this city becoming a center of Islamic scholarship despite itself.
evt-mawali-discontent: An Arab-Sasanian silver dirham issued in the eastern caliphate during Abd al-Malik's reign — coins like this, blending Sasanian imagery with Arabic script, circulated in the Persian heartland where mawali resentment of Arab privilege ran deepest.
evt-vs-gold-hoards-536: The Sorte Muld gold hoard from Bornholm — Roman-era gold medallions, bracteates, and beads spilling from their bone container, exactly the kind of prestige gold that Scandinavian elites buried in the ground as the 536 catastrophe unfolded and the old social order buckled.
evt-vs-fimbulwinter-echo: Lorenz Frølich's illustration of Líf and Lífþrasir, the sole human survivors of the Fimbulwinter, sheltering in the forest of Hoddmímis holt while the world freezes around them — the mythological memory of a real catastrophe encoded in Norse cosmology.
evt-vs-warrior-retinue: The Torslunda bronze dies from Öland, 6th–7th century, showing armoured Vendel warriors side by side — the most direct surviving image of the warrior retinue culture that defined Scandinavian aristocratic life in the centuries before the Viking Age.
evt-vs-uppland-aristocracy: A Vendel-era iron helmet with bronze fittings and a spectacle-frame face guard, excavated from Uppland — the prestige war gear that marked a man as part of the elite warrior aristocracy who dominated central Sweden between 550 and 800 CE.
evt-vs-baltic-networks: The Varangian trade routes map shows the Baltic and river corridors linking Scandinavia to Byzantium and the Caspian — the same network of sea lanes and portages that Vendel-period Scandinavians were already working a century before the Viking Age proper began.
evt-6d-cao-cao: Traditional portrait of Cao Cao labeled 魏太祖像 (Portrait of Wei Taizu), the warlord-poet who unified the north and laid the foundation for the Wei dynasty.
evt-6d-battle-red-cliffs: The Red Cliffs rock face on the Yangtze River, bearing the characters 赤壁 (Red Cliffs), site of the decisive 208 CE battle that ended Cao Cao's bid to unify China.
evt-6d-liu-bei: Tang-era painting of Liu Bei (labeled 蜀主劉備) flanked by attendants, founder of the Shu Han kingdom and the warlord whose claim to Han legitimacy made him a central figure of the Three Kingdoms era.
evt-6d-sun-quan: Tang-era painting of Sun Quan (labeled 吳主孫權), founder of the Wu kingdom and the ruler whose alliance with Liu Bei at Red Cliffs stopped Cao Cao's southern advance.
evt-6d-cao-pi-founds-wei: Map of the Three Kingdoms as of 262 CE, showing the Wei, Shu Han, and Wu territories that emerged after Cao Pi formally founded Wei in 220 CE by accepting the Han emperor's abdication.
evt-6d-zhuge-liang: Ming-era full-length portrait of Zhuge Liang, the brilliant strategist and chancellor of Shu Han whose Northern Expeditions became legendary long after his death in 234 CE.
evt-6d-cao-zhi: Traditional portrait of Cao Zhi, the gifted poet-prince of Wei whose rivalry with his brother Cao Pi and tragic marginalisation produced some of the most celebrated verse of the Three Kingdoms era.
evt-6d-seven-sages: Hanging scroll from the Metropolitan Museum depicting the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, the freewheeling scholars who retreated into Daoist philosophy and wine to escape the dangers of Wei court politics.
evt-6d-sima-yi: Traditional illustration of Sima Yi's swift defeat of the rebel general Meng Da in 228 CE, a campaign that demonstrated the military genius that would eventually give the Sima family control of the Wei court.
evt-6d-jin-dynasty-founded: Map of the Jin dynasty at its greatest extent in 280 CE, when Sima Yan's forces finally destroyed Wu and reunified China under the dynasty Sima Yi's ambitions had made possible.
evt-6d-chen-shou: A surviving manuscript fragment from Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, the definitive 3rd-century history that remains the primary written source for the entire Three Kingdoms era.
evt-6d-war-eight-princes: A campaign map of the War of the Eight Princes (291–306 AD), showing the competing Sima princes and the contested cities of Luoyang, Chang'an, and Ye that became flashpoints in the dynasty-destroying civil war.
evt-6d-liu-yuan-han-zhao: A map of the Sixteen Kingdoms in 317 AD labels Liu Yuan's Han (Han-Zhao) kingdom occupying the central northern plains, the first of the non-Han successor states to seize former Jin heartland.
evt-6d-eastern-jin-founded: A celadon stoneware ram vessel from the Western or Eastern Jin dynasty, 4th century CE — the kind of refined southern craft that flourished in Jiankang after the court fled north China's chaos.
evt-6d-former-qin-fu-jian: A map of the Sixteen Kingdoms in 376 AD shows Former Qin under Fu Jian dominating nearly all of northern China, the closest any ruler had come to reunifying the north since the Jin collapse.
evt-6d-fei-river: The Battle of Fei River (383 CE): the front line before and after Eastern Jin's surprise rout of Fu Jian's massive Former Qin army, halting the north's last serious bid to reunify China for two centuries.
evt-6d-northern-wei: A museum model of the Yongning Pagoda, the Northern Wei dynasty's most ambitious architectural statement — a nine-story Buddhist tower reportedly visible for miles around Luoyang.
evt-6d-xie-lingyun: Xie Lingyun, who invented Chinese landscape poetry by turning the Zhejiang mountains around his estate into verse and proving that wilderness itself was a worthy subject.
evt-6d-wang-dao: Wang Dao, the Eastern Jin's indispensable statesman, whose steady hand kept the refugee court together at Jiankang and whose family dominated southern politics for generations.
evt-6d-wang-xizhi: Wang Xizhi, the Sage of Calligraphy, whose brushwork set the standard for every Chinese literatus who came after him.
evt-6d-orchid-pavilion: A Tang-dynasty copy of Wang Xizhi's Orchid Pavilion Preface — the most celebrated piece of calligraphy in Chinese history, dashed off at a wine-floating poetry party in 353 CE.
evt-6d-portrait-painting: A scene from Gu Kaizhi's Admonitions of the Court Instructress, the earliest surviving attributed Chinese painting and the founding text of the tradition that inner spirit matters more than outward likeness.
evt-6d-tao-yuanming: Chen Hongshou's painting of Tao Yuanming smelling chrysanthemums — China's most beloved recluse-poet, who quit official life to farm, drink wine, and write verses about marigolds and country silence that Chinese readers have memorized ever since.
evt-6d-guo-pu: Guo Pu, the polymathic Jin scholar who systematized feng shui geomancy, compiled the Erya dictionary, and predicted (correctly) his own death at the hands of a warlord.
evt-6d-yue-ware-celadon: A Yue ware celadon ewer — the distinctive grey-green stoneware whose kilns near Shaoxing made southern China the center of fine ceramics and helped bankroll the refugee aristocracy's new economy.
evt-6d-southern-dynasties: China divided at 440 CE: the Southern Dynasties (Liu Song, red) holding the Yangtze basin and the south, while the Northern Wei (blue) consolidated the old heartland — the split that would last 170 years.
evt-6d-kumarajiva: A modern bronze statue of Kumarajiva at the Kizil Caves near Kuqa, the Central Asian oasis city that was his birthplace and the gateway through which he first absorbed Buddhism before his forced journey to Chang'an.
evt-6d-faxian: A bronze statue of Faxian, staff in hand, at the Maritime Experiential Museum in Singapore — memorializing the elderly monk who walked overland to India and sailed home through Southeast Asian waters carrying Sanskrit scriptures.
evt-6d-pure-land-buddhism: Donglin (East Forest) Temple on Mount Lu in Jiangxi, the monastery Huiyuan founded in 386 CE and from which he launched the Pure Land movement, teaching that calling on Amitabha Buddha's name could carry any believer to the Western Paradise.
evt-6d-huiyuan: A traditional line-drawing portrait of Huiyuan, the monk who spent the last thirty years of his life on Mount Lu and refused to cross the Tiger Ravine bridge — a self-imposed vow to remain within his sacred mountain retreat.
evt-6d-bodhidharma: Bodhidharma seated in moonlit meditation, as imagined in an 1887 woodblock print by Tsukioka Yoshitoshi — the legendary Indian monk credited with bringing Chan (Zen) Buddhism to China around 520 CE.
evt-6d-buddhism-arrives: The colossal Leshan Buddha carved into a Sichuan cliff — begun in 713 CE, it stands as the ultimate expression of the Buddhist rock-carving tradition that began spreading across southern China during the Six Dynasties period.
evt-6d-ge-hong: A Chinese woodcut portrait of Ge Hong (Baopuzi), the Eastern Jin alchemist-scholar whose writings on Daoist inner cultivation, elixirs, and talismanic magic became the foundational texts of religious Daoism.
evt-6d-tao-hongjing: A hanging scroll depicting Tao Hongjing at his mountain retreat listening to the wind in the pines — the reclusive Daoist scholar who systematized the Maoshan revelations and turned down the Liang emperor's repeated calls to court.
evt-6d-celestial-masters: A traditional painting of Zhang Daoling, founder of the Celestial Masters, riding a tiger — the charismatic second-century Daoist patriarch whose southern Chinese movement survived the chaos of the Six Dynasties by moving its headquarters to the north under imperial patronage.
evt-6d-shaolin-monastery: The main hall of Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song, founded in 495 CE under Northern Wei imperial patronage to house the Indian monk Buddhabhadra.
evt-6d-emperor-wu-liang: A traditional painted portrait of Emperor Wu of Liang (r. 502–549), the longest-reigning ruler of the Southern Dynasties, who famously embraced Buddhism and founded a culturally brilliant court at Jiankang.
evt-6d-yungang-grottoes: The massive seated Buddhas of the Yungang Grottoes near Datong, carved into the sandstone cliffs by Northern Wei craftsmen starting around 460 CE.
evt-6d-longmen-grottoes: The Longmen Grottoes outside Luoyang as seen from across the Yi River, with the colossal Vairocana Buddha of the Fengxian Temple cave dominating the cliff face.
evt-6d-emperor-xiaowen: A stone relief from the Central Binyang Cave at Longmen depicting Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei and his court in a Buddhist procession, carved shortly after his death.
evt-6d-northern-wei-capital-move: A museum model of Luoyang's imperial city layout, showing the grid-planned capital that Emperor Xiaowen rebuilt as the Northern Wei's new cultural and political center in 494 CE.
evt-6d-six-garrison-rebellions: Map of the Six Garrison uprisings that erupted across Northern Wei territory from 523 CE, showing the overlapping regional revolts that ultimately shattered the dynasty.
evt-6d-dunhuang-caves: The multi-storey wooden facade built into the cliff face of the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang, where Buddhist monks began excavating and painting chambers in the late fourth century CE.
evt-6d-northern-qi-northern-zhou: A Chang Ping Wu Zhu bronze coin issued by the Northern Qi dynasty, one of the two rival successor states that divided the former Northern Wei territories after 550 CE.
evt-6d-liang-wudi-patronage: Map of the Liang dynasty at its height, showing the southern realm centered on Jiankang where Emperor Wu's Buddhist patronage transformed the capital into one of the great religious and intellectual centers of sixth-century East Asia.
evt-6d-liu-xie: Title inscription of the Wenxin Diaolong ("The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons"), Liu Xie's landmark fifth-century treatise that laid down the first systematic theory of Chinese literary criticism.
evt-6d-xiao-tong: A later printed edition of the Wen Xuan ("Selections of Refined Literature"), the literary anthology compiled by Crown Prince Xiao Tong around 520 CE that became the definitive canon of classical Chinese prose and poetry for a thousand years.
evt-6d-zu-chongzhi: A traditional portrait of Zu Chongzhi, the fifth-century mathematician and astronomer who calculated pi to seven decimal places — a level of precision not matched in Europe for another thousand years.
evt-6d-gupta-contact: A Central Indian ambassador depicted in the Tang-era painting "The Gathering of Kings" (c. 650 CE), illustrating the kind of diplomatic and Buddhist cultural exchange between India and China that flourished during the Southern Dynasties period.
evt-6d-northern-zhou-reforms: A gilded relief from the Northern Zhou tomb of An Jia (Xi'an, 579 CE) depicts a diplomatic feast — evidence of the era's militarized alliances with Turkic steppe powers that shaped the Northern Zhou reforms.
evt-6d-yang-jian: A Tang-era portrait of Emperor Wen of Sui (Yang Jian), the general who united China in 589 CE and founded the short-lived Sui dynasty that ended three centuries of division.
evt-6d-grand-canal-begins: Barges convoy along the Jiangnan section of the Grand Canal, the vast waterway whose construction Yang Jian's son Yangdi began in the early 600s to link China's north and south.
evt-6d-pipa-music: Tang-era relief sculpture of court musicians playing flutes, a pipa lute, and other instruments — the Central Asian pipa arrived via the Silk Road during the Northern Dynasties and quickly became a staple of Chinese court music.
evt-saul-king: A brooding painted portrait of Saul wearing his royal crown — Israel's first and ill-fated king.
evt-david-goliath: Osmar Schindler's painting captures the moment of confrontation: the slight shepherd boy facing the armored giant Goliath as the two armies watch.
evt-battle-gilboa: Mount Gilboa as it looks today — the ridge where Saul and his sons fell in battle against the Philistines, ending the first Israelite monarchy.
evt-david-king: A Baroque portrait of King David wearing his crown and holding his famous harp, symbols of the poet-king who united the tribes of Israel and made Jerusalem his capital.
evt-conquest-jerusalem: An 1899 topographical map of Jebus — the Jebusite stronghold on its ridge between the valleys of Hinnom and the Kidron that David captured and renamed the City of David.
evt-ark-jerusalem: James Tissot's watercolor shows priests prostrating before the Ark of the Covenant in the Tabernacle, the sacred object David brought to Jerusalem to cement his new capital's religious authority.
evt-bathsheba: Willem Drost's intimate portrait shows Bathsheba holding David's letter summoning her to the palace — a pivotal moment that set off a chain of court intrigue and succession struggles.
evt-tel-dan-stele: The Tel Dan Stele fragments in the Israel Museum — a 9th-century BCE Aramaic inscription that contains the earliest known reference to the 'House of David' outside the Bible.
evt-mesha-stele: The Mesha Stele in the Louvre — a 9th-century BCE black basalt stone on which the Moabite king Mesha boasted of throwing off Israelite domination, corroborating the biblical account of the Omride dynasty.
evt-solomon-king: Simeon Solomon's 1872 portrait of King Solomon, robed and crowned, conveys the legendary grandeur of Israel's builder-king.
evt-proverbs: A 1497 incunabulum Bible open to the Book of Proverbs, one of the earliest printed editions of the wisdom texts attributed to Solomon's court.
evt-ezion-geber: A 19th-century photograph of the Red Sea coast near Ezion-Geber, the port Solomon built on the Gulf of Aqaba to launch his legendary trading fleets.
evt-ophir-gold: An early 19th-century map showing the biblical table of nations, with 'Ophir' marked in the Arabian peninsula — one of many proposed locations for the legendary land whose gold filled Solomon's treasury.
evt-queen-sheba: Edward Poynter's 1890 masterpiece depicts the Queen of Sheba arriving at Solomon's magnificent court, her retinue bearing the spices, gold, and jewels described in the biblical account.
evt-rehoboam: Hans Holbein the Younger's fragment from Basel Town Hall depicts Rehoboam, the king whose arrogance split the united monarchy in two.
evt-ahab-king: The death of Ahab at the Battle of Ramoth-Gilead, in a 19th-century engraving by Gustave Doré — the arrow that found the gap in his armor ended the most powerful king of the Omride dynasty.
evt-kingdom-split: The prophet Ahijah tears his cloak into twelve pieces before Jeroboam, telling him he will rule ten of the twelve tribes — the dramatic moment that foretold the kingdom's division.
evt-jeroboam: The archaeological remains of Jeroboam I's royal sanctuary at Bethel, one of the two rival shrines he established to keep his subjects from worshipping in Jerusalem after the kingdom split.
evt-dan-bethel-shrines: A 19th-century chromolithograph illustrates the crowd worshipping before a golden calf on an altar, the rival cult Jeroboam established at Dan and Bethel to keep his subjects from returning to Jerusalem.
evt-shishak-invasion: Ippolito Rosellini's 19th-century rendering of a Karnak relief shows Pharaoh Shoshenq I (the biblical Shishak) in triumphal pose, commemorating his campaign through Canaan around 925 BCE.
evt-omri-dynasty: An engraving depicting the civil conflict between Omri and Tibni for control of the northern kingdom, the power struggle Omri won to found Israel's most internationally recognized dynasty.
evt-samaria-built: Excavated ruins at Tel Shomron (ancient Samaria) preserve the stone walls and terraces of the hilltop city Omri built from scratch as the northern kingdom's brand-new capital around 880 BCE.
evt-gezer-calendar: A close-up of the Gezer Calendar, a small limestone tablet inscribed with an early Hebrew agricultural cycle, one of the oldest known Hebrew inscriptions and a window into everyday Israelite life.
evt-megiddo-stables: Aerial view of Tel Megiddo, where excavations have revealed the massive stables, gate complex, and grain silo that made this city one of the most impressive fortified centers in Iron Age Israel.
evt-elijah: Elijah Fed by the Raven, painted by Giovanni Gerolamo Savoldo around 1510 — depicting the moment the prophet hid in the wilderness, sustained by ravens, as he defied Ahab and Jezebel.
evt-mount-carmel: El-Mohraka on Mount Carmel — the traditional site of Elijah's contest with the 450 prophets of Baal, depicted here in a 19th-century lithograph showing the ruins where fire from heaven supposedly settled the argument.
evt-kuntillet-ajrud: Ink drawing of the famous Kuntillet Ajrud pithos, showing the Bes figures and inscriptions that mention 'Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah' — key evidence that Israelite religion in this period was far more complex than later texts suggest.
evt-arad-temple: The standing stones (masseboth) inside the Holy of Holies at the Arad temple — a functioning Israelite sanctuary in the Negev that mirrored the layout of Solomon's Temple and operated for centuries before being decommissioned.
evt-elisha: Elisha raising the son of the Shunammite woman, painted by Jean-Baptiste Despax — one of the many miracle stories that established Elisha as Elijah's successor and the most politically active prophet of the northern kingdom.
evt-jehu-coup: A relief panel from the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III showing Jehu — or his envoy — prostrating before the Assyrian king and paying tribute, the earliest surviving image of an Israelite monarch.
evt-black-obelisk: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III in the British Museum — the 9th-century BC Assyrian monument that records tribute from five kings including Jehu of Israel, making it one of the most important artifacts for biblical archaeology.
evt-jeroboam-ii: Jeroboam II of Israel, in a woodcut from Guillaume Rouillé's Promptuarium iconum (1553) — the king whose 41-year reign brought the northern kingdom to its greatest territorial extent and prosperity, even as the prophets raged about inequality.
evt-amos: The prophet Amos, depicted in a Russian Orthodox icon — the shepherd from Tekoa whose written oracles against wealth and injustice in the prosperous northern kingdom launched the tradition of written biblical prophecy.
evt-hosea: Hosea by James Tissot — the prophet who used his troubled marriage as an extended metaphor for Israel's unfaithfulness to God, giving the northern kingdom its most intimate and emotionally raw indictment before its fall.
evt-tiglath-pileser-tribute: King Menahem of Israel, who bought off the Assyrian invasion of Tiglath-Pileser III by levying a crushing silver tribute on his own wealthy subjects.
evt-isaiah: Michelangelo's Isaiah from the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted c. 1509 — the prophet who counseled Judah's kings through the Assyrian crisis and left behind one of the ancient world's most influential bodies of writing.
evt-micah: Russian Orthodox icon of the prophet Micah, whose oracles against injustice and his famous vision of swords beaten into plowshares made him one of the most quoted voices of the 8th-century prophetic age.
evt-fall-samaria: The hilltop site of ancient Samaria (modern Sebastia), capital of the northern Kingdom of Israel, which fell to the Assyrian army of Sargon II in 722 BC after a three-year siege.
evt-lost-ten-tribes: A 1695 Hebrew map of the Land of Israel showing the traditional territories of the twelve tribes — the northern ten of which vanished from history after Assyria deported the population of Samaria.
evt-samaritan-origins: Samaritan priests leading the community's Passover ceremony on Mount Gerizim — a ritual the Samaritans have maintained continuously, tracing their origins to the mixed population that emerged in Samaria after the Assyrian conquest.
evt-hezekiah: A Swedish church portrait of Hezekiah, the reform-minded king of Judah who dismantled pagan shrines and prepared Jerusalem against Assyrian attack.
evt-lmlk-seals: A close-up of an LMLK seal impression stamped into a jar handle, the royal storage jars Hezekiah used to stockpile supplies ahead of Sennacherib's invasion.
evt-siloam-tunnel: The interior of Hezekiah's Siloam Tunnel, hand-cut through solid bedrock to channel the Gihon Spring into Jerusalem — one of the ancient world's most impressive engineering feats.
evt-sennacherib-invasion: The Taylor Prism, a six-sided clay cylinder inscribed with Sennacherib's own account of his 701 BCE campaign in Judah, boasting that he shut Hezekiah up 'like a bird in a cage.'
evt-lachish-siege: A detail from Sennacherib's palace reliefs at Nineveh showing an Assyrian siege engine battering the walls of Lachish, Judah's second city, during the 701 BCE campaign.
evt-covenant-theology: Joseph Anton Koch's painting of Noah's covenant, with the rainbow as a symbol of God's binding promise — the template for the covenant theology that defined Israel's relationship with its deity.
evt-manasseh: A 19th-century Bible card depicting Manasseh in Assyrian chains, praying for forgiveness — the king whose 55-year reign undid Hezekiah's reforms and filled Jerusalem with foreign altars.
evt-josiah-reforms: A Swedish church portrait of Josiah, the boy-king who launched the most sweeping religious purge in Judah's history after a lost scroll of the Law was discovered in the Temple.
evt-passover-reinstituted: A traditional Passover Seder table set with matzah and ritual foods — the celebration that Josiah reinstated with a national assembly in Jerusalem for the first time since the judges era.
evt-deuteronomy: Papyrus Fouad 266, one of the oldest surviving copies of Deuteronomy, preserving the text of the scroll whose discovery in Josiah's Temple triggered a religious revolution.
evt-ketef-hinnom: The reconstructed Ketef Hinnom burial cave on display at the Israel Museum, where excavators found the two tiny silver scrolls inscribed with the Priestly Blessing — the oldest known biblical text.
evt-battle-megiddo-josiah: A kneeling statue of Pharaoh Necho II at the Brooklyn Museum — the Egyptian king whose army killed Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BCE, ending the reform era and putting Judah under Egyptian control.
evt-jeremiah: Horace Vernet's 1844 painting of Jeremiah writing his lamentations amid the ruins of Jerusalem, the city burning in the distance behind him.
evt-jehoiakim: A Babylonian cuneiform tablet recording the conquest of Jerusalem and the surrender of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, in 597 BCE — one of the few contemporary records of the event outside the Bible.
evt-first-deportation: The Babylonian Chronicle tablet recording Nebuchadnezzar's early campaigns, including the 597 BCE siege of Jerusalem and the first deportation of Judeans to Babylon.
evt-zedekiah: Gustave Doré's engraving of Nebuchadnezzar's troops executing Zedekiah's sons before the blinded king — the last thing the last king of Judah would ever see.
evt-lachish-letters: Lachish Letter 4, an ostracon written in ancient Hebrew script during the final weeks before the Babylonian destruction — the soldier reports he can no longer see the fire signals from Azekah.
evt-fall-jerusalem: An 1896 illustration depicting Jerusalem in flames as Nebuchadnezzar's forces destroy the city and Solomon's Temple in 587 BCE, ending four centuries of Judahite kingship.
evt-hebrew-calendar: A printed Hebrew calendar showing the intercalary month of Adar II, a feature of the lunisolar system that ancient Judean scribes systematically codified during the late monarchy period.
evt-ten-commandments: An elaborately illuminated manuscript of the Ten Commandments in Hebrew, arranged in the traditional two-column format with decorative floral borders and a crown motif.
evt-psalms: A Psalms scroll (Tehilim) open on a velvet stand — the Book of Psalms, assembled from poems composed across centuries of Israelite and Judahite history, became the great hymnal of ancient worship.
evt-toyotomi-hideyoshi-death: A contemporary portrait of Toyotomi Hideyoshi painted around 1598, the year of his death, held at Kodai-ji Temple in Kyoto.
evt-korean-invasions: A Korean painting depicting the Japanese assault on Busan fortress in 1592, the opening strike of Hideyoshi's first Korean invasion.
evt-battle-sekigahara: The Battle of Sekigahara folding screen, painted shortly after the 1600 battle, shows the full chaos of the clash that decided who would rule Japan.
evt-tokugawa-ieyasu: The formal portrait of Tokugawa Ieyasu, painted in the early 17th century, shows Japan's first Tokugawa shogun seated in full court regalia.
evt-osaka-castle-siege: A Meiji-era woodblock print depicts mounted warriors storming the walls of Osaka Castle during the 1614–1615 sieges that ended the Toyotomi line.
evt-nikko-toshogu: The ornate torii gate and Yomeimon Gate precinct of Nikkō Tōshō-gū, the lavish mausoleum shrine built to deify Tokugawa Ieyasu after his death in 1616.
evt-himeji-castle: Himeji Castle rises above its stone ramparts and surrounding greenery, its gleaming white plastered towers earning it the nickname 'White Heron Castle.'
evt-tokugawa-iemitsu: Tokugawa Iemitsu, the third Tokugawa shogun, whose long rule (1623–1651) hardened the isolation edicts and locked the bakuhan system into its final form.
evt-sankin-kotai: A daimyo's sankin-kotai procession arrives at Edo in this woodblock triptych — hundreds of retainers, horses, and lacquered palanquins making the point that attendance at the shogun's court was a statement of submission as much as loyalty.
evt-gokaido: The post town of Magome on the Nakasendo, one of the Five Great Roads — a well-preserved slice of the network that stitched Edo to the provinces and made the sankin-kotai system physically possible.
evt-terauke-system: A shumon aratamecho — the temple registration document every household was required to hold — the paper trail through which the Tokugawa government tracked and stamped out hidden Christianity.
evt-ise-shrine-rebuild: The Naiku inner shrine at Ise — rebuilt every twenty years in unpainted cypress and thatch, a ritual of renewal that the Tokugawa shoguns patronized to bind their regime to the divine legitimacy of the imperial house.
evt-christianity-banned: A wooden notice board from 1682 bearing the Tokugawa shogunate's anti-Christian edict, posted publicly to warn that harboring Christians was a crime punishable by death.
evt-fumi-e: A woodblock print depicting the fumi-e ritual in which a suspected Christian steps on a sacred image under the watchful eyes of shogunate officials, with a bronze crucifix plaque displayed in the upper corner.
evt-shimabara-rebellion: A 17th-century Japanese battle map of the Shimabara siege, showing the rebel stronghold at Hara Castle surrounded by the shogunate's encircling forces.
evt-amakusa-shiro: A woodblock portrait of Amakusa Shiro, the teenage Christian rebel leader who commanded tens of thousands of peasants during the Shimabara Rebellion before being killed at its defeat in 1638.
evt-sakoku-edict: An Edo-period woodblock print of a Chinese junk entering a Japanese harbor, representing the tightly controlled foreign trade that the sakoku edicts permitted only at Nagasaki under strict shogunate supervision.
evt-portuguese-expelled: A small Japanese Buddhist figure with a cross secretly carved on its back, one of the crypto-Christian devotional objects that proliferated after the Portuguese were expelled and open worship became a capital crime.
evt-dejima-trade: An Edo-period painting showing the fan-shaped island of Dejima in Nagasaki Bay, the sole portal through which Dutch merchants conducted Japan's only sanctioned European trade for over two centuries.
evt-kakure-kirishitan: A kakure kirishitan devotional image depicting the Madonna and Child in a deliberately Buddhist visual style, used by hidden Christians to practice their faith while evading the shogunate's informers.
evt-tokugawa-hidetada: A period portrait of Tokugawa Hidetada, the second Tokugawa shogun whose aggressive persecution of Christianity in the 1610s–20s laid the groundwork for the full sakoku closure that followed.
evt-genroku-culture: A 1696 (Genroku 9) Japanese map of Kyoto, produced at the height of the Genroku cultural flourishing when urban merchants were commissioning art, literature, and printed works on an unprecedented scale.
evt-tokugawa-tsunayoshi: Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, the fifth shogun whose infamous Edicts on Compassion for Living Things made it a capital offense to harm a dog — earning him the sardonic nickname 'the Dog Shogun.'
evt-floating-world: A bathhouse scene by Torii Kiyonaga captures the sensuous, pleasure-seeking spirit of the ukiyo floating world.
evt-yoshiwara: Cherry blossom season along Nakanocho, the central avenue of the Yoshiwara licensed quarter, in a Hiroshige woodblock print.
evt-great-meireki-fire: A contemporary screen painting depicts the chaos of the 1657 Meireki Fire, which consumed most of Edo and killed over 100,000 people.
evt-kabuki-theater: A woodblock print by Shunkōsai Hokushū shows an aragoto kabuki warrior in full dramatic pose, the bold style that made the theater a sensation.
evt-bunraku: A richly costumed bunraku puppet from the National Bunraku Theatre in Osaka, the art form's historic home.
evt-chikamatsu: A period scroll portrait of Chikamatsu Monzaemon, whose domestic tragedies for the bunraku stage earned him the title of Japan's Shakespeare.
evt-matsuo-basho: Matsuo Bashō depicted as a traveling poet by his disciple Morikawa Kyoriku, painted during the master's lifetime.
evt-ihara-saikaku: A period portrait of Ihara Saikaku, the Osaka novelist who turned merchant-class life and erotic comedy into literary art.
evt-hishikawa-moronobu: Hishikawa Moronobu's iconic "Beauty Looking Back," one of the defining masterworks of the early ukiyo-e tradition he founded.
evt-rice-market-osaka: A woodblock panorama of the Dōjima Rice Exchange in Osaka, the world's first commodity futures market, bustling with traders.
evt-mitsui-house: Hiroshige's print of Surugacho shows the Mitsui Echigoya dry-goods store, the retail innovation that launched Japan's greatest merchant dynasty.
evt-kitagawa-utamaro: Utamaro's close-up bijinga of the courtesan Karagoto exemplifies his signature style — intimate, psychological, and technically dazzling.
evt-hokusai-wave: A portrait of Katsushika Hokusai in old age — he produced the Great Wave at around 70, still driven by an obsessive pursuit of artistic mastery.
evt-hiroshige: A print from Hiroshige's "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo" series, whose rain, snow, and seasonal light transformed landscape woodblock printing forever.
evt-ako-incident: A dramatic Meiji-era painting by Yasuda Raishu depicts the 47 rōnin huddled in the snow outside Kira's compound on the night of their revenge raid, December 1702.
evt-bushido: The Hagakure, the early 18th-century text dictated by samurai Yamamoto Tsunetomo, became the definitive written codification of bushido — the way of the warrior.
evt-sugita-genpaku: A reproduction of Kaitai Shinsho (1774), the landmark anatomy text Sugita Genpaku co-translated from Dutch, opening Japan's first direct window into Western medical science.
evt-tokugawa-yoshimune: Tokugawa Yoshimune, the eighth shogun whose Kyōhō Reforms cut government waste, expanded sweet-potato cultivation, and quietly cracked open the door to Western scientific learning.
evt-rangaku: Shiba Kokan's late-18th-century painting of a Japanese, Chinese, and Western scholar gathered around a table captures the intellectual curiosity at the heart of Rangaku, Japan's movement to absorb Dutch scientific knowledge.
evt-aoki-konyo: Aoki Konyō, the Edo-period scholar who pioneered Dutch-language study in Japan and promoted sweet-potato cultivation as a famine remedy, in a contemporary portrait.
evt-hiraga-gennai: Hiraga Gennai, the polymathic Rangaku inventor who built Japan's first static-electricity generator, the Elekiter, portrayed by Nakamaru Seijuro and held in the Waseda University Library.
evt-ino-tadataka: One of Ino Tadataka's large-scale Edo-period coastal survey maps of Kyushu, color on paper, now held at the Tokyo National Museum — a testament to his decade-long effort to chart Japan's entire coastline by foot.
evt-tanuma-okitsugu: Tanuma Okitsugu, the shogun's powerful senior councilor who steered Edo Japan toward mercantilist policies in the mid-18th century before scandal brought him down.
evt-kansei-reforms: Matsudaira Sadanobu, the reform-minded regent who cracked down on luxury, expelled heterodox thought from the official academy, and tried to put the Tokugawa house back on a frugal footing in the 1790s.
evt-tenmei-famine: A contemporary Japanese artwork depicting the catastrophic Tenmei Famine of the 1780s, when volcanic eruption and cold summers pushed the northeast into mass starvation.
evt-mount-asama-eruption: Mount Asama in Nagano, the active stratovolcano whose devastating 1783 eruption buried villages, choked crops with ash, and helped trigger the Tenmei Famine.
evt-tenpo-famine: A period illustration showing famished commoners crowding outside a famine relief station (sukuioya) during the Tenpō Famine of the 1830s, one of the worst food crises of the Edo era.
evt-morrison-incident: A contemporary Japanese brush drawing of the American merchant ship Morrison, which sailed to Japan in 1837 to return castaways and was fired upon under the sakoku exclusion edicts.
evt-perry-arrival: A Japanese contemporary watercolor of one of Perry's steam-powered black ships, drawn by a Japanese artist in 1854 as the foreign squadron anchored in Uraga Bay.
evt-treaty-kanagawa: The Japanese ratification copy of the Convention of Kanagawa, the 1854 agreement that opened Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships and cracked Japan's two-century isolation.
evt-ansei-treaties: The 1858 Ansei treaty booklets covering Japan's agreements with the Netherlands, Britain, France, Russia, and the United States — the unequal commercial treaties that humiliated the shogunate.
evt-sakuradamon-incident: A contemporary woodblock print depicting the March 1860 assassination of Great Elder Ii Naosuke in the snow outside Edo Castle's Sakurada Gate, the act that destabilized the shogunate.
evt-bombardment-shimonoseki: Western warships bombard the Choshu domain's shore batteries at the Shimonoseki Strait in 1864, the combined Anglo-French-Dutch-American punitive expedition that silenced Choshu's cannon.
evt-choshun-war: Rifle-armed Takada domain troops marching during the Second Choshu Expedition of 1866, one of the many shogunal forces the bakufu assembled in its ultimately failed campaign to punish the rebel domain.
evt-sakamoto-ryoma: A portrait of Sakamoto Ryoma, the Tosa samurai-turned-revolutionary whose back-channel diplomacy brokered the Satsuma-Choshu Alliance and helped end the shogunate.
evt-tokugawa-yoshinobu: Tokugawa Yoshinobu photographed in formal court dress in Osaka in 1867, the year he became the fifteenth and final shogun before returning power to the emperor.
evt-cyrus-cylinder: The Cyrus Cylinder, a baked-clay barrel inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform around 539 BCE, in which Cyrus presents himself as a liberator chosen by the god Marduk.
evt-late-intermediate-period: A map of the competing regional powers — Chimor, the Aymara kingdoms, Cuzco, and others — that filled the Andean political landscape after Tiwanaku's collapse around 1000 CE.
evt-chimor-kingdom: A montage of Chimu artifacts — blackware ceramics, gold work, and a map of the kingdom's coastal territory — capturing the sophistication of Chimor at its height.
evt-chan-chan: Intricately carved adobe friezes at Chan Chan, the Chimu capital near modern Trujillo, where geometric and figurative patterns covered nearly every wall of the city's royal compounds.
evt-killke-culture: The massive polygonal stone walls of Sacsayhuaman above Cuzco, whose earliest courses were laid by the Killke people generations before the Inca empire took shape.
evt-manco-capac: A colonial-era Cuzco School portrait of Manco Capac, labeled "Primer Rey Del Cuzco," from the Brooklyn Museum's series of fourteen Inca king portraits.
evt-mama-ocllo: A circa-1840 Peruvian painting of Mama Ocllo, first Coya and co-founder of the Inca dynasty alongside Manco Capac, holding the ritual mask of her mummy cult.
evt-cuzco-founded: A nineteenth-century engraving of Cuzco's main plaza and cathedral, built over the very spot where Inca legend says Manco Capac drove his golden staff into the earth to found the city.
evt-origin-myths: A chakana (Andean stepped cross) woven into an Inca tunic, a symbol that encoded the Inca cosmological worldview — the layered heavens, earth, and underworld at the heart of their origin myths.
evt-eight-legendary-rulers: A colonial-era painting of an early Sapa Inca holding the sun disk, representing the legendary rulers who — by tradition — expanded Inca territory and consolidated power in the Cuzco valley before Pachacuti.
evt-viracocha-inca: The Brooklyn Museum's colonial-era portrait of Viracocha Inca, eighth Sapa Inca, who expanded the empire's reach before famously fleeing Cuzco when the Chanka confederation attacked.
evt-chanka-war: A section of the Mural of the History of Cusco depicting the ferocious Inca–Chanka war, the defining crisis that the young Pachacuti turned into the founding moment of the Inca empire.
evt-pachacuti: The Brooklyn Museum's colonial-era portrait of Pachacuti, labeled "Décimo Ynoa," the ninth Sapa Inca who defeated the Chanka, rebuilt Cuzco as a puma-shaped city, and launched the empire's greatest era of conquest.
evt-coricancha: The Coricancha's curved Inca stonework base still stands in Cusco, its precision-fitted blocks supporting the colonial-era Santo Domingo church built atop it by the Spanish.
evt-sacsayhuaman: Sacsayhuamán's zigzagging outer rampart near Cusco, built from limestone blocks that can weigh over 100 tons and yet interlock without mortar.
evt-machu-picchu: Machu Picchu perched on its Andean saddle at 7,970 feet, the best-preserved example of an Inca royal estate and now the most recognized symbol of the civilization.
evt-bingham-1911: Hiram Bingham III photographed at an Inca ruin site in 1911, the year his Yale expedition brought Machu Picchu to the attention of the outside world.
evt-qhapaq-nan: A map of the Qhapaq Ñan, the vast Inca road network running the length of South America along both the Andes and the Pacific coast.
evt-qollqa-storehouses: Rows of qollqa storehouses built into the hillside at Ollantaytambo, designed with ventilated walls to preserve freeze-dried food and goods for the empire's redistribution system.
evt-inti-cult: A Guaman Poma illustration showing the December Capac Inti Raymi solar festival, with the Inca king gesturing toward the sun and moon — the state religion of Inti worship made visible.
evt-topa-inca: Topa Inca Yupanqui, the tenth Inca, depicted in a colonial-era illustrated chronicle — the ruler who stretched the empire from Ecuador to Chile.
evt-huayna-capac: Huayna Capac, the eleventh and last undivided Sapa Inca, as drawn by Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala in his 1615 chronicle — the emperor whose death without a clear heir fractured the empire.
evt-chimu-metallurgy: A Chimu gold ritual headdress and pectoral from the Museo Larco, representing the metalworking mastery that made Chimu craftsmen so prized by the Inca after the conquest.
evt-maule-river-frontier: An aerial view of the Maule River in central Chile, the southern boundary where Topa Inca's army halted and the Inca Empire reached its greatest extent.
evt-cieza-de-leon: The title page of Pedro Cieza de León's Crónica del Perú, first published in Seville in 1553 — the earliest and most detailed Spanish eyewitness account of Inca civilization.
evt-garcilaso-vega: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, the mestizo historian whose Comentarios Reales de los Incas (1609) gave the world its richest insider account of Inca society and legend.
evt-rope-bridges: A surviving Inca-style rope bridge spanning a deep Andean gorge, woven from twisted grass fibers and rebuilt annually by local communities.
evt-chasqui-runners: A chasqui relay runner blowing a pututu horn to announce his arrival, as depicted by the Indigenous chronicler Felipe Guamán Poma de Ayala around 1615.
evt-tambos: The ruins of Conchamarka, an Inca tambo way station with its cooking facilities still visible, set alongside the ancient road in the Peruvian highlands.
evt-cumbi-textiles: A scholarly compilation of tocapu geometric patterns from Inca cumbi cloth, the elite woven textile whose abstract symbols carried encoded meaning legible only to the initiated.
evt-acllawasi: The acllacunas — chosen women selected from across the empire — depicted by Guamán Poma de Ayala in his early 17th-century chronicle, gathered in the acllawasi compound.
evt-quipu: An actual Inca quipu, its hundreds of knotted and color-coded cords fanning out from the main cord — each knot encoding numerical data in a decimal system with no written equivalent.
evt-quipucamayoc: A quipucamayoc — the empire's official knot-keeper and accountant — reading a quipu, as depicted by Guamán Poma de Ayala; the title above reads 'Contador Mayor Tesorero.'
evt-llama-economy: A Quechua girl in traditional Andean dress with her llama in the highlands near Cusco, an image of the human-llama bond at the heart of Inca pastoral and transport economy.
evt-sapa-inca-divine: Colonial portrait of Atahualpa in full Sapa Inca regalia — the royal headdress, ear spools, and scepter marking a ruler believed to be the living son of the sun god Inti.
evt-viracocha-god: A pre-Columbian stone head identified as Viracocha, the Inca creator deity who was said to have risen from Lake Titicaca to shape the world and its people, now held in the Museo de América in Madrid.
evt-panaca-mummies: An 18th-century Cusco school painting depicting the royal Inca lineage — each panaca clan traced its descent from a deified ancestor whose mummy was paraded, housed, and consulted as a living presence.
evt-wakas: A museum panel at the Coricancha in Cusco explaining the Inca waka network — the system of sacred shrines, stones, springs, and temples that the Incas wove into every corner of the landscape.
evt-inti-raymi: The modern Inti Raymi reenactment at Sacsayhuaman in Cusco, where a costumed Sapa Inca is carried on a golden litter — echoing the June solstice festival at which the Inca emperor offered llamas and prayers to the sun.
evt-capacocha: One of the Llullaillaco child mummies recovered from the summit of Volcán Llullaillaco in Argentina — a preserved capacocha sacrifice, a child selected as a divine offering to the sun god and the mountain spirits.
evt-ceque-system: A diagram at the Coricancha museum in Cusco showing the ceque system — 41 imaginary lines radiating outward from the temple of the sun, each linking a sequence of sacred waka shrines across the Inca landscape.
evt-mortarless-masonry: The famous twelve-angled stone in a Cusco wall — each face fitted to its neighbor without a drop of mortar, a signature of Inca polygonal masonry.
evt-trapezoidal-style: Coricancha's precisely coursed andesite wall, where each stone's face is ground to a subtle inward batter — the same trapezoidal geometry that defined Inca doorways and niches across the empire.
evt-pisac: The town and Sacred Valley floor below Pisac, where Pachacuti's royal estate terraced the ridgeline above into one of the empire's most dramatic highland retreats.
evt-ollantaytambo: Ollantaytambo's temple terrace rising above the Sacred Valley town — both a royal estate and a working quarry site where massive pink granite blocks were ferried across the Urubamba River.
evt-moray-laboratory: Moray's concentric circular terraces descend nearly 100 feet into a natural depression, creating a series of microclimates that the Inca may have used to test and adapt crops from across the empire.
evt-stone-moving: An Inca courtyard interior in Ollantaytambo showing the characteristic trapezoidal niches and stone-on-stone construction, the finished product of a stone-moving operation that required no wheels, no iron, and no draft animals larger than a llama.
evt-smallpox-1524: Smallpox pustules cover a child in Bangladesh — the same disease that swept ahead of European contact, killing Huayna Capac and millions across the Andes before a single conquistador reached Cuzco.
evt-civil-war: A modern illustration of the armies of Huascar and Atahualpa clashing — the five-year civil war that split the empire north and south and left it fatally weakened when Pizarro arrived.
evt-huascar: A painted portrait of Huascar, labeled Huascar Inca XIII — the Cuzco-based claimant who held the imperial capital but lost the civil war to his half-brother Atahualpa.
evt-atahualpa: A 17th-century anonymous oil portrait of Atahualpa, labeled 'Atabalipa Roy du Peru' — the northern claimant whose victory in the civil war made him emperor just as Pizarro's ships appeared on the coast.
evt-pizarro-arrives: A colonial-era portrait of Francisco Pizarro in armor — the Spanish conquistador who led the expedition that brought down the Inca Empire.
evt-cajamarca-ambush: Juan Lepiani's early 20th-century painting depicts the chaotic ambush at Cajamarca's plaza, where Pizarro's men seized Atahualpa from the center of his vast court.
evt-manco-inca: A historical illustration of Manco Inca Yupanqui in full royal regalia — the Inca nobleman the Spanish installed as a puppet ruler who would later lead a massive rebellion against them.
evt-siege-cuzco-1536: Guaman Poma's drawing records Manco Inca setting fire to Cuzco during the 1536 siege — a desperate act to deny the Spanish their stronghold in the Inca heartland.
evt-tupac-amaru-i: A colonial-era portrait of Tupac Amaru I, the last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State at Vilcabamba, who was captured and publicly beheaded in Cuzco's plaza in 1572.
evt-spanish-encomienda: A Guaman Poma drawing from his Nueva Corónica shows an encomendero brutalizing an indigenous Andean — the encomienda system granted Spaniards the right to extract labor and tribute from the people of assigned territories.
evt-tupac-amaru-ii: A period watercolor labeled 'El Rebelde Tupac Amaro' depicts the 18th-century rebel leader on horseback — José Gabriel Condorcanqui, who took the name Tupac Amaru II and launched the largest indigenous uprising in colonial Andean history.
evt-bakuhan-system: A bird's-eye view painting of Edo Castle and its concentric moats — the shogun's seat of power and the administrative heart of the bakuhan system that governed Japan for two and a half centuries.
evt-shoheiko: Hayashi Razan, the Confucian scholar who founded the private academy in 1630 that the Tokugawa government would later formalize as the Shōheikō, Japan's official school for samurai officials.
evt-caranqui-conquest: Yahuarcocha — the 'Lake of Blood' near Ibarra in northern Ecuador — where Inca forces under Huayna Capac allegedly threw the bodies of thousands of slaughtered Caranqui warriors after their final defeat, giving the lake its grim name.
evt-temujin-birth: The Yuan-era imperial portrait of Genghis Khan, painted shortly after his death and considered the most authoritative likeness of Temüjin, the boy who would unite the Mongol clans.
evt-genghis-khan: Modern Mongolia's 20,000-tögrög note bears the face of Chinggis Khaan — a nation's testament to the 1206 kurultai that proclaimed a shepherd's son ruler of the steppe.
evt-uighur-script: Flowing vertical Mongolian calligraphy, written in the traditional script adapted from the Uyghur alphabet that Genghis Khan ordered adopted as the empire's official writing system.
evt-alliance-toghrul: A medieval illuminated manuscript depiction of Toghrul (Wang Khan), the powerful Kereit ruler who became Temüjin's early patron and military ally.
evt-defeat-naimans: The Mongol Empire's territorial extent in 1206, the year Temüjin crushed the Naimans and united the steppe — the map that shows what he had just won.
evt-kurultai-1206: A medieval Mongol enthronement assembly scene from the Diez Albums, capturing the ceremonial pageantry of the great kurultai at which Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan.
evt-great-yasa: Temüjin enthroned as Genghis Khan in 1206, from the Jami' al-tawarikh manuscript — the very occasion on which the Great Yasa, his law code, was first proclaimed.
evt-religious-tolerance: A 1312 Nestorian Christian tombstone from Issyk-Kul, a tangible relic of the diverse faiths that flourished under Mongol religious tolerance across Central Asia.
evt-hoelun: The monument to Hoelun at the Mother Hoelun Memorial Complex in Tsonjin Boldog, Mongolia, honoring the resilient mother who kept her children alive on the steppe after Yesügei's death.
evt-western-xia-first-campaign: A campaign map showing the Mongol invasion of Western Xia in 1209, with advance routes converging on the Tangut heartland.
evt-conquest-jin: A Persian miniature depicting the Mongol and Jin cavalry clash of 1211, the opening battle of Genghis Khan's campaign to bring down the Jin dynasty.
evt-capture-zhongdu: Campaign map of the Mongol invasion of Jin 1211–1215, showing the converging advances that bottled up and eventually fell Zhongdu (Beijing).
evt-yelü-chucai: A classical Chinese portrait of Yelü Chucai, the Khitan scholar-official who persuaded Genghis Khan that ruling farmers was more profitable than razing them.
evt-khwarezmian-campaign: Map of the Khwarazmian Empire at its height (1190–1220), the vast Central Asian power that Genghis Khan set out to destroy after the Otrar massacre.
evt-sack-bukhara: A Persian miniature showing Genghis Khan addressing the assembled citizens of Bukhara from the pulpit of the Friday mosque after its capture in 1220.
evt-destruction-khwarezmia: A Persian miniature depicting Mongol cavalry in battle near Valiyán (1221), part of the relentless campaign that shattered the Khwarazmian Empire.
evt-sack-urgench: A 1480 manuscript painting of a siege of Urgench — the great Khwarazmian capital endured repeated destruction, first by Genghis Khan's forces in 1221.
evt-battle-indus: A Mughal-era miniature showing Jalal al-Din Khwarazm-Shah plunging his horse into the Indus to escape Genghis Khan after his defeat at the river in 1221.
evt-battle-kalka: A Russian medieval chronicle illustration of Princes Daniil Romanovich and Mstislav Mstislavich leading their forces — the Russian coalition that was routed by Mongol scouts at the Kalka River in 1223.
evt-genghis-death: Map of the Mongol Empire at Genghis Khan's death in 1227, stretching from the Pacific coast to the Caspian Sea — the largest contiguous land empire any single person had ever built.
evt-tolui-regent: Tolui Khan, youngest son of Genghis and regent of the Mongol Empire in the two years between his father's death and Ögedei's coronation, depicted in a Persian miniature.
evt-ogedei-khan: Official Yuan dynasty portrait of Ögedei Khan, Genghis's chosen successor, who expanded the empire further than his father ever had.
evt-karakorum-built: Erdene Zuu Monastery, built in 1586 directly atop the ruins of Karakorum, preserves the outline of Ögedei's great walled capital on the Mongolian steppe.
evt-silver-tree-karakorum: A later engraving depicting the famous Silver Tree Fountain of Karakorum, the automaton built by the French craftsman Guillaume Boucher to dispense wine, koumiss, and honey mead from four spouts at the Khan's command.
evt-yam-postal: A yam relay station in Siberia, illustrating the network of horse-post stations that allowed official riders to cover up to 200 miles a day across the Mongol Empire.
evt-pax-mongolica-paiza: The Polo caravan crossing Central Asia, from a 14th-century Catalan Atlas — merchants traveling under the protection of the Pax Mongolica and the paiza safe-conduct tablet.
evt-sorghaghtani-beki: Tolui and Sorghaghtani Beki enthroned together, from a Persian manuscript; Sorghaghtani outlived her husband and masterminded the rise of four sons who would each rule a corner of the empire.
evt-fall-jin: The final Mongol campaigns against the Jin dynasty, 1230–1234, showing the pincer advance that destroyed the last Jin resistance and ended a dynasty that had ruled northern China for over a century.
evt-invasion-europe: Ögedei Khan's invasion of Europe, 1236–1242, tracing Batu Khan and Subutai's campaigns from the Volga steppes through Russia, Poland, and Hungary to the Adriatic coast.
evt-batu-khan: Batu Khan enthroned, from Rashid al-Din's Jami' al-tawarikh — the grandson of Genghis who led the western campaigns and founded the Golden Horde on the Pontic steppe.
evt-sack-vladimir: Mongol cavalry before the wooden walls of Vladimir in February 1238, painted by Vasily Maximov; the city fell within days and its population was massacred or enslaved.
evt-sack-kiev: The Mongol assault on Kyiv in 1240, depicted in a medieval Russian chronicle; the city that had been the heart of Kievan Rus was reduced to rubble and its population nearly wiped out.
evt-battle-legnica: The Battle of Legnica, 9 April 1241, from the 14th-century Legend of Saint Hedwig — Mongol horse archers routing the combined Polish and Teutonic Knight force under Duke Henry II.
evt-battle-mohi: The Battle of Mohi (Sajó River), 11 April 1241, depicted in a medieval manuscript; Subutai's flanking maneuver across the river destroyed the Hungarian royal army and opened the road to Vienna.
evt-toregun-khatun-regency: A bilingual Chinese-Mongolian inscription issued under Töregene Khatun's authority in 1240, one of the few surviving documents from her five-year regency that kept the empire intact until Güyük's election.
evt-guyuk-khan: Güyük Khan, son of Ögedei and third Great Khan of the Mongol Empire, depicted in a Persian miniature; his reign lasted barely two years before his death in 1248 on the road to a likely showdown with Batu.
evt-mongke-khan: Möngke Khan, fourth Great Khan and first of Tolui's sons to hold the throne, whose energetic rule launched simultaneous campaigns against China and the Islamic world before his death at the siege of Diaoyu in 1259.
evt-alamut-taken: A Persian miniature depicting the storming of Alamut, the Nizari Ismaili mountain fortress that fell to Hulagu's Mongols in 1256, ending the Assassins' two-century grip on the region.
evt-nasir-al-din-tusi: An Iranian commemorative stamp bearing the portrait of Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, the polymath astronomer and mathematician who survived the fall of Alamut and went on to found the Maragheh Observatory under Mongol patronage.
evt-fall-baghdad: A medieval Islamic miniature from the Jami al-Tawarikh showing Mongol forces outside the walls of Baghdad during the catastrophic 1258 siege that ended five centuries of Abbasid caliphate rule.
evt-house-of-wisdom: A 13th-century illumination from al-Hariri's Maqamat showing scholars gathered before shelves of books — an image of the Islamic world's great library culture that the destruction of Baghdad's House of Wisdom in 1258 obliterated.
evt-ain-jalut: A campaign map showing the movements of Mamluk and Mongol forces leading to the Battle of Ayn Jalut in 1260, the first major Mongol defeat that halted their westward advance into Egypt.
evt-kitbuqa: A medieval illumination depicting the Mongol siege of Sidon in 1260, part of Kitbuqa's Levant campaign that ended with his defeat and death at Ayn Jalut the same year.
evt-ariq-boke: Ariq Böke, Kublai's younger brother, whose rival kurultai in Karakorum plunged the empire into civil war from 1260 to 1264.
evt-toluid-civil-war: A Persian miniature from Rashid al-Din's chronicle depicting Ariq Böke defeating his rival Alghu, a clash that typified the fratricidal Toluid Civil War.
evt-yuan-founded: The Yuan dynasty at its height around 1290, showing the vast Chinese territories Kublai Khan ruled after proclaiming the dynasty in 1271.
evt-xiangyang-siege: A medieval manuscript illustration of a trebuchet siege, the same Islamic engineering used by the Mongols to finally crack Xiangyang's walls in 1273 after five years of stalemate.
evt-battle-yamen-proto-firearms: The崖門 (Yamen) battle site memorial in Guangdong, marking where the last Song fleet was destroyed in 1279 in one of history's earliest battles to feature gunpowder firearms.
evt-japan-invasion: Map of the two Mongol naval invasions of Japan, showing the 1274 and 1281 fleets that were both ultimately destroyed — the second by the typhoon the Japanese called the kamikaze, or divine wind.
evt-invasion-java: The Mongol naval expedition to Java in 1293, tracing the fleet's route from southern China — an overextended campaign that ended in ambush and an embarrassing retreat.
evt-paper-money: A Yuan-dynasty chao banknote and its copper printing plate from 1287, the world's first government-issued paper currency at imperial scale.
evt-guo-shoujing: A commemorative bust of astronomer-engineer Guo Shoujing outside his memorial hall in Beijing, where he built instruments and computed the Shoushi calendar accurate to within 26 seconds of the modern solar year.
evt-yuan-drama-flourishes: A painted scene of Yuan zaju performers in costume, capturing the vibrant theatrical culture that flourished under Mongol rule when elite Chinese scholars turned to popular drama.
evt-ilkhan-islam: A Persian miniature depicting Ghazan Khan's conversion to Islam in 1295, the moment that made the Ilkhanate an officially Muslim state and reshaped Persian cultural patronage.
evt-rashid-al-din: A folio from Rashid al-Din's Jami' al-tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles), the monumental illustrated world history commissioned by the Ilkhanate that remains one of the greatest medieval encyclopedic works.
evt-observatory-maragheh: The excavated ruins of the Maragheh Observatory in northwestern Iran, founded in 1259 under Nasir al-Din al-Tusi and for decades the most advanced astronomical facility in the world.
evt-sultaniyya: The soaring double-shelled turquoise dome of Sultaniyya in Iran, built as the Ilkhanid capital's crown jewel and, at 50 meters (164 ft) high, the largest brick dome in the world when completed around 1313.
evt-abu-said-death-ilkhanate-end: A gold dinar struck under Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, the last Ilkhan to rule a unified realm — his death in 1335 without an heir set off a decade of fragmentation and ended Mongol rule in Persia.
evt-sarai-capital: Sarai depicted in the 1375 Catalan Atlas as a fortified city on the Volga, the wealthy Golden Horde capital that Ibn Battuta described as one of the largest and most beautiful cities he had ever seen.
evt-berke-khan-islam: A silver coin struck at the Crimea mint under Berke Khan (r. 1257–1267), the first Mongol ruler to embrace Islam, whose conversion opened the Golden Horde to Muslim scholars, merchants, and diplomats.
evt-oz-beg-khan: A medieval portrait of Öz Beg Khan (r. 1313–1341), whose long reign saw the Golden Horde reach its territorial and commercial peak and Islam formally established as the khanate's state religion.
evt-ibn-battuta-golden-horde: A 19th-century illustration of Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan traveler who visited the Golden Horde around 1332 and left one of the most vivid outside accounts of Sarai, Öz Beg's court, and life on the steppe.
evt-chagatai-khanate-kebek: Kebek Khan enthroned, as depicted in the 1375 Catalan Atlas — he overhauled the Chagatai Khanate's coinage with a new silver dinar (the kebeki) that became the standard trade currency of Central Asia.
evt-caffa-plague-siege: The Genoese towers of Caffa (modern Feodosia, Crimea), the Black Sea colony besieged by the Golden Horde in 1346, whose fleeing sailors carried plague west into Europe.
evt-black-death: A mass grave of plague victims excavated at Martigues, France — one of many across Europe left by the Black Death that followed Mongol trade routes out of Central Asia.
evt-red-turban-rebellion: Map of major rebel factions and warlords at the end of the Yuan dynasty, showing the fractured landscape of the Red Turban uprising that would eventually topple Mongol rule in China.
evt-toghon-temur-flees: Portrait of Toghon Temür (Emperor Shun of Yuan), the last Yuan emperor, who fled Khanbaliq for Mongolia in 1368 as Zhu Yuanzhang's forces closed in on the capital.
evt-ghazan-reforms: A Persian miniature depicting Ghazan Khan at court with his wife — the reforming Ilkhanid ruler who standardized taxes, weights, and measures across his realm while converting the khanate to Islam.
evt-timur: A forensic facial reconstruction of Timur, built from his exhumed skull in 1941, capturing the fierce Central Asian warlord who would carve a new empire from the ruins of the Mongol world.
