evt-mughal-babur: Babur, founder of the Mughal dynasty, depicted reading in a garden alongside his court — a Mughal miniature that captures both the scholar-king and the cultured world he built.
evt-mughal-ferghana-loss: A detail portrait of Babur from the Late Shah Jahan Album, showing the young prince in the years before he lost Ferghana and began his long road to India.
evt-mughal-first-panipat: A Mughal miniature depicting the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and the death of Sultan Ibrahim Lodi — the clash that ended the Delhi Sultanate and opened India to Babur.
evt-mughal-ibrahim-lodi: Ibrahim Lodi on horseback amid the chaos of Panipat, from a Mughal-era miniature — the last sultan of Delhi, killed on the field as Babur's artillery shattered his army.
evt-mughal-khanwa: Babur's forces clash with Rana Sanga's Rajput confederacy at Khanwa (1527) in this Mughal miniature — the battle that confirmed Mughal rule over Hindustan.
evt-mughal-rana-sanga: Rana Sanga of Mewar, the formidable Rajput warrior-king who united northern India's chiefs against Babur — depicted in a painting held at the Udaipur Museum.
evt-mughal-baburnama: A page from an illuminated manuscript of the Baburnama recording the deer and cattle Babur observed in Hindustan — evidence of his remarkable eye for natural detail and the literary ambition that made his memoir a masterpiece.
evt-mughal-humayun: A 1590 Mughal miniature showing Humayun routing an Afghan force — vivid evidence of the second emperor's early military campaigns before his catastrophic losses to Sher Shah Suri.
evt-mughal-humayun-tahmasp: A contemporary portrait of Humayun painted in Kabul around 1550–55, during the years when he was rebuilding Mughal power after his decade-long exile at Shah Tahmasp's Safavid court.
evt-mughal-humayun-tomb: Humayun's Tomb reflected in the garden water channel — the 1570s Delhi mausoleum that set the template for Mughal garden-tomb architecture and directly prefigured the Taj Mahal.
evt-mughal-grand-trunk-road: The full route of the Grand Trunk Road, stretching from Kabul to Bengal — Sher Shah Suri's great infrastructure project that knit together northern South Asia and outlasted the dynasty that built it.
evt-mughal-painting-workshop: A richly detailed Mughal miniature from the Khamsa of Nizami, painted in Akbar's imperial workshop — a showcase of the Persian-Indic fusion style that defined the atelier's golden output.
evt-mughal-akbar: Map of the Mughal Empire in 1605 at the end of Akbar's 49-year reign, showing the vast territory he consolidated across northern and central India.
evt-mughal-bairam-khan: Bairam Khan, the Turkic-Persian general who served as Akbar's regent and chief military commander during the early years of his reign, depicted in a Mughal miniature.
evt-mughal-second-panipat: The defeat of Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556, from the Akbarnama — a chaotic melee of cavalry and war elephants that secured Akbar's hold on the Delhi throne.
evt-mughal-hemu: Hemu, the Hindu general who briefly declared himself emperor of Delhi before being captured and executed after the Second Battle of Panipat, depicted in a Mughal miniature.
evt-mughal-rajput-marriages: A royal Rajput procession fresco, evoking the martial aristocracy whose alliance with Akbar through marriage transformed the political landscape of Mughal India.
evt-mughal-jizya-abolition: A jizya tax document — the kind of non-Muslim poll tax that Akbar controversially abolished in 1564, a landmark act of religious tolerance that set his reign apart.
evt-mughal-fatehpur-sikri: The Buland Darwaza (Gate of Magnificence) at Fatehpur Sikri, the sandstone imperial city Akbar built in 1571 and abandoned barely a decade later when the water supply failed.
evt-mughal-akbar-conquests: Akbar depicted with a divine halo in a Mughal miniature of c. 1630, reflecting the near-sacred authority he wielded as he brought Gujarat, Bengal, and much of the subcontinent under Mughal rule.
evt-mughal-mansabdari: A Mughal mansabdar official holding a scroll, representing the rank-based imperial service system Akbar formalized in which every officer held a numbered grade tying his salary, cavalry quota, and status to a single number.
evt-mughal-todar-mal: Raja Todar Mal, Akbar's finance minister, whose meticulous land surveys and standardized revenue assessments gave the Mughal state a reliable fiscal foundation for the first time.
evt-mughal-din-i-ilahi: Akbar holding a falcon in a Mughal miniature — the emperor whose syncretic faith Din-i-Ilahi blended elements of Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, and Christianity into a personal spiritual experiment centered on himself.
evt-mughal-ibadat-khana: Jesuit missionaries debating with Muslim scholars and other religious figures at Akbar's Ibadat Khana (House of Worship) in Fatehpur Sikri, in this scene from the Akbarnama.
evt-mughal-abul-fazl: Abu'l Fazl presenting the Akbarnama to Emperor Akbar — the court historian's monumental chronicle that shaped how Akbar's reign has been understood ever since.
evt-mughal-tansen: Tansen of Gwalior, the legendary court musician of Akbar whose mastery of Hindustani classical ragas made him one of the most celebrated performers in Indian history, in a Mughal miniature of c. 1585–90.
evt-mughal-sirhindi: Ahmad Sirhindi, the Sufi scholar who spearheaded an Islamic renewal movement in response to Akbar's religious experiments, depicted in a Mughal-era miniature painting.
evt-mughal-jahangir: A Mughal portrait of Emperor Jahangir — shown in profile with his characteristic solar halo — painted at the height of his reign in the early seventeenth century.
evt-mughal-nur-jahan: A contemporaneous Mughal miniature portrait of Nur Jahan, the empress who effectively ran the empire while her husband Jahangir withdrew from affairs of state.
evt-mughal-jahangir-painting: Govardhan's depiction of Jahangir visiting the ascetic Jadrup, painted around 1616–20, captures the Mughal atelier's mastery of landscape, portraiture, and spiritual narrative at its peak.
evt-mughal-thomas-roe: Sir Thomas Roe, the English diplomat sent by James I to Jahangir's court in 1615, whose three-year embassy opened formal trade negotiations between England and the Mughal Empire.
evt-mughal-east-india-company: A copper pice of the Bombay Presidency bearing the East India Company's initials — a tangible artifact of the commercial foothold the Company established on the Mughal coast from 1608 onward.
evt-mughal-shah-jahan: Shah Jahan enthroned and receiving his eldest son Dara Shikoh, in a Mughal miniature from the Late Shah Jahan Album, c. 1650.
evt-mughal-mumtaz-mahal: A Mughal-era portrait of Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan's beloved empress, painted on ivory.
evt-mughal-taj-mahal: The Taj Mahal at Agra, the white marble mausoleum Shah Jahan built for Mumtaz Mahal, completed around 1653.
evt-mughal-red-fort: The Lahori Gate of the Red Fort in Delhi, the massive red sandstone citadel Shah Jahan built as the seat of Mughal imperial power.
evt-mughal-shahjahanabad: An 1863 plan of Delhi showing the walled city of Shahjahanabad — Shah Jahan's purpose-built imperial capital — hugging the Yamuna River.
evt-mughal-jama-masjid: The Jama Masjid of Delhi, commissioned by Shah Jahan and completed in 1656, remains one of the largest mosques in India.
evt-mughal-peacock-throne: A Mughal miniature depicting an emperor seated on the jeweled Peacock Throne beneath its gilded canopy crowned with peacock motifs.
evt-mughal-koh-i-noor: A replica of the Koh-i-Noor diamond, the storied gem that passed through Mughal hands before its eventual seizure by the British.
evt-mughal-aurangzeb: A Mughal miniature portrait of Aurangzeb, painted during his Deccan campaigns in the mid-seventeenth century.
evt-mughal-war-of-succession: A contemporary painting depicting the Battle of Samugarh in 1658, where Aurangzeb defeated his brother Dara Shukoh to seize the Mughal throne.
evt-mughal-shah-jahan-imprisoned: A portrait of Shah Jahan at the height of his power, painted by Bichitr around 1630 — the same emperor Aurangzeb would lock away in Agra Fort nearly three decades later.
evt-mughal-dara-shukoh: A Mughal miniature portrait of Dara Shukoh, Shah Jahan's eldest and favourite son, whose liberal religious views put him on a collision course with his orthodox brother Aurangzeb.
evt-mughal-shivaji: A period portrait of Shivaji held in the British Museum, showing the Maratha chieftain who turned guerrilla warfare and strategic alliances into the foundation of an independent kingdom.
evt-mughal-shivaji-coronation: A 1974 Indian commemorative stamp marking the 300th anniversary of Shivaji's coronation as Chhatrapati — sovereign king — at Raigad Fort in 1674.
evt-mughal-deccan-wars: A collage of paintings depicting scenes from the Deccan Wars, the grinding decades-long campaign that consumed Aurangzeb's final years and overstretched the Mughal empire.
evt-mughal-bijapur-golconda: Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II of Bijapur venering a Sufi saint, painted around 1620–30 — a ruler of one of the two Deccan sultanates Aurangzeb would finally annex in the 1680s.
evt-mughal-sambhaji: A late seventeenth-century miniature portrait of Sambhaji, Shivaji's son and successor, whose capture and execution by Aurangzeb in 1689 only hardened Maratha resistance.
evt-mughal-fatawa-alamgiri: A manuscript copy of the Fatawa-i-Alamgiri, the massive compendium of Hanafi Islamic law commissioned by Aurangzeb and compiled by hundreds of scholars over decades.
evt-mughal-badshahi-mosque: The Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, completed in 1673 on Aurangzeb's orders — one of the largest mosques in the world and a monument to his vision of an orthodox Mughal empire.
evt-mughal-bahadur-shah-i: Bahadur Shah I in a Mughal miniature portrait, the last emperor to hold the empire together before the fratricidal succession wars shattered central authority.
evt-mughal-sayyid-brothers: Sayyid Abdullah Khan holding court, early 18th century — one of the two Sayyid Brothers who made and unmade four emperors in a decade of back-room kingmaking.
evt-mughal-muhammad-shah: Muhammad Shah in a jharokha portrait by Nidha Mal, ca. 1730 — the emperor whose long, pleasure-loving reign presided over the empire's steady unraveling.
evt-mughal-marathas-rise: India in 1760, showing the Maratha Confederacy at its greatest territorial reach, encircling the rump Mughal domains from Gujarat to Bengal.
evt-mughal-nizam-hyderabad: Asaf Jah I, the Mughal viceroy who founded the Hyderabad dynasty in 1724 and never came back — the first great breakaway that proved the empire could no longer hold its own governors.
evt-mughal-bengal-nawabs: Murshid Quli Khan, the first Nawab of Bengal, whose fiscal genius turned the province into a self-sufficient power that merely paid lip service to Delhi.
evt-mughal-nader-shah: Nader Shah in battle — the Iranian conqueror who sacked Delhi in 1739, carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor, and left the Mughal treasury empty for good.
evt-mughal-karnal: The battle fresco in Isfahan's Chehel Sotoun palace, depicting Nader Shah's campaigns — the same army that crushed Muhammad Shah at Karnal in February 1739 in under three hours.
evt-mughal-third-panipat: The Third Battle of Panipat, 13 January 1761, in a contemporary Mughal panoramic painting — the day the Maratha bid for empire ended and the subcontinent's fate was sealed.
evt-mughal-black-hole: A 19th-century illustration of the Black Hole of Calcutta, 20 June 1756 — when Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah's troops locked 146 British prisoners into a tiny cell and outrage back home gave the East India Company its moral pretext.
evt-mughal-plassey: Lord Clive meets Mir Jafar on the field at Plassey in 1757, the encounter that handed Bengal — and the Company's future empire — to Britain.
evt-mughal-mir-jafar: Mir Jafar (left) and his son Mir Miran in a contemporary portrait — the nawab whose secret deal with Clive cost Siraj ud-Daula his throne and Bengal its independence.
evt-mughal-buxar: General Sir Hector Munro, who commanded the Company's forces at Buxar in 1764, the battle that transformed Plassey's coup into permanent British military supremacy.
evt-mughal-diwani: Shah Alam II hands the diwani — the right to collect Bengal's revenues — to Robert Clive in 1765, the moment the East India Company became a sovereign tax-collecting power.
evt-mughal-shah-alam: Shah Alam II reviews Company troops in 1781, a scene that captures the emperor's increasingly hollow authority as the British became the real power behind his throne.
evt-mughal-tipu-sultan: A circa-1790 portrait of Tipu Sultan, the 'Tiger of Mysore,' whose fierce resistance to the East India Company made him the last serious check on British expansion in southern India.
evt-mughal-textile-trade: Francois Renaldi's 1787 painting of a woman in translucent Bengali muslin — the gossamer fabric that made Mughal Bengal's textile exports the envy of European markets.
evt-mughal-1857-rebellion: A period map of Northern India charting the principal centres of the 1857–59 Mutiny, including the routes the rebels held and the line of march on Cawnpore.
evt-mughal-greased-cartridges: A contemporary engraving of rebel sepoys storming a British battery at Lucknow in July 1857, one of the bloodiest engagements of the uprising that the greased-cartridge controversy had ignited.
evt-mughal-bahadur-shah-zafar: A period miniature portrait of Bahadur Shah II (Zafar), the last Mughal emperor, shown in imperial regalia — the man whose reluctant proclamation as leader of the 1857 revolt sealed both his fate and the dynasty's.
evt-mughal-delhi-siege-1857: A contemporary photograph of the battered Kashmiri Gate of Delhi taken shortly after the 1857 siege, showing the breach that British engineers blew open to retake the city.
evt-mughal-mirza-ghalib: A rare photograph of Mirza Ghalib, the greatest Urdu and Persian poet of the Mughal twilight, who survived the fall of Delhi in 1857 to record its destruction in verse.
evt-mughal-dynasty-ended: The text of Queen Victoria's 1858 proclamation to the princes and peoples of India, the document that dissolved the East India Company's rule and transferred the subcontinent to the British Crown, formally extinguishing Mughal sovereignty.
evt-yesugei-poisoned: Young Temüjin at his father's deathbed — Yesügei had been poisoned by Tatars on his way home from arranging his son's betrothal, leaving the family abandoned on the steppe with no clan to protect them.
evt-norse-clinker-ships: A diagram of a clinker-built Viking longship, showing the overlapping strake planks, single square sail, and row of shields along the gunwale that made these vessels the terror of European coastlines.
evt-oseberg-ship-burial: The Oseberg ship displayed in Oslo's Viking Ship Museum — unearthed in 1904, it is the world's best-preserved Viking vessel and the burial chamber of a high-ranking Norse woman interred around 834.
evt-lindisfarne-raid: Lindisfarne Castle rises above the rocky Northumberland shore at sunrise — the tidal island that Viking raiders struck in 793, sending shockwaves through the Christian world.
evt-great-heathen-army: A Viking sword and grave goods from a warrior killed in battle, recovered from a Derby burial site — material evidence of the Great Heathen Army's campaign through England.
evt-william-conqueror-normandy: The Bayeux Tapestry scene depicting the death of King Harold at the Battle of Hastings, inscribed 'HAROLD REX INTERFECTUS EST' — the moment William of Normandy, grandson of the Viking Rollo, conquered England and ended the Anglo-Saxon era.
evt-hedeby-trade: Reconstructed timber-and-thatch buildings at the Hedeby open-air museum mark where the bustling emporium once stood at the base of Jutland.
evt-dublin-founded: A silver penny of Sihtric Silkbeard, the Viking king of Dublin, minted in the city the Norse founded and turned into one of the wealthiest slave-trading ports in the British Isles.
evt-settlement-iceland: Norwegian settlers rowing ashore in Iceland in 872, as depicted in a 19th-century painting capturing the beginning of the Viking Age's most ambitious colonization effort.
evt-norse-greenland: A reconstruction of the small church at Brattahlíð, the farm established by Erik the Red in Greenland around 985, which became the hub of the Norse Western Settlement.
evt-lanse-aux-meadows: Reconstructed Norse sod longhouses at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland — the only confirmed Viking settlement in North America, occupied briefly around 1000 CE.
evt-ladby-ship-burial: The Ladby ship, preserved in situ beneath a burial mound on Funen, Denmark — the only ship burial found on Danish soil, where a Viking chieftain was interred with horses, dogs, and hunting equipment.
evt-volga-trade-route: Nicholas Roerich's painting of Varangian traders portaging their boats overland, capturing the grueling but lucrative river-route commerce that connected Scandinavia to Baghdad.
evt-runestone-memorial-tradition: Runestone U 240 at Lingsberg, Uppland, Sweden — a well-preserved Viking-age memorial stone bearing carved runic text and serpent interlace, raised to commemorate the dead.
evt-charlemagne-coastal-defense: A silver denier struck at Mainz (812–814) bearing Charlemagne's portrait — the emperor who spent his final years organizing Frankish coastal defenses against Norse raids.
evt-iona-raids: Iona Abbey seen from the island's shore, the sacred monastery founded by Columba that Viking raiders repeatedly targeted from 795 onward.
evt-paris-siege-845: A 19th-century engraving depicting the Viking fleet of Ragnar pressing upriver past the Frankish fortifications during the 845 siege of Paris.
evt-hastein-mediterranean: A 19th-century illustration of Hastein (Hasting) raising his standard at Luna, the Italian city his fleet attacked in 859 during the famous Mediterranean raid.
evt-birka-trade: A Celtic-style stone cross monument at Birka, Sweden, marking the site of the Viking-age trading town where merchants from across Scandinavia and the Frankish world converged.
evt-waterford-limerick-wexford: Map showing the main Viking-founded towns of Ireland — Dublin, Wexford, Waterford, Cork, and Limerick — the coastal longphort settlements that became permanent trading cities.
evt-danelaw-established: A map of England showing the Danelaw territory and the campaigns of the Great Heathen Army, with the Danelaw boundary of 886 marked in black.
evt-battle-edington: The memorial stone at Edington, Wiltshire, marking the site of Alfred's decisive 878 victory over the Danish leader Guthrum that saved the kingdom of Wessex.
evt-treaty-wedmore: A statue of King Alfred the Great, under whose leadership the Treaty of Wedmore was agreed with the Viking leader Guthrum, drawing a boundary across England.
evt-hafrsfjord: Ole Peter Hansen Balling's dramatic 19th-century painting of the Battle of Hafrsfjord, where Harald Fairhair crushed rival chieftains to become the first king of a unified Norway.
evt-ingolfr-arnarson: P. Raadsig's 1850 painting of Ingólfr Arnarson planting his high-seat pillars upon landing in Iceland around 874, the traditional founding moment of permanent Norse settlement.
evt-althing-founded: A 19th-century painting depicting the Althing assembly at Þingvellir, where Icelandic settlers gathered each summer to settle disputes and pass laws under the open sky.
evt-aud-the-deep-minded: Krosshólar (Cross Hills) in Iceland's Dalir district, where Aud the Deep-Minded — one of Iceland's most powerful early settlers — reportedly had crosses erected, marking her Christian faith.
evt-vinland: The bronze statue of Leif Erikson in Duluth, Minnesota, commemorating the Norse explorer who led the first known European voyage to North America around 1000 CE.
evt-rurik-novgorod: Rurik depicted on the Millennium of Russia monument in Novgorod, sword and shield in hand, commemorating his role as founder of the Rus' dynasty.
evt-oleg-of-kiev: A Radzivill Chronicle miniature showing conquered peoples bringing tribute to Prince Oleg, who unified the Rus' lands from Novgorod to Kiev.
evt-rus-attack-constantinople: A Moscow Kremlin fresco depicting the 860 Rus' attack on Constantinople, showing the city's walls and towers as Patriarch Photius leads prayers against the fleet at the gates.
evt-olga-of-kiev: Mikhail Nesterov's 1892 portrait of Saint Olga of Kiev, the regent-grandmother who converted to Christianity and is venerated as the first Russian saint.
evt-varangian-guard: A Byzantine Skylitzes Chronicle miniature explicitly depicting Varangian guardsmen, the Norse mercenary elite who served as the emperor's personal bodyguard in Constantinople.
evt-disablot-midwinter: August Malmström's 19th-century engraving of a dísablót — the midwinter festival held in honour of the dísir, female spirits whose goodwill the Norse sought before the farming season began.
evt-temple-at-uppsala: Olaus Magnus's 1555 woodcut depicting the great temple at Uppsala, the foremost pagan sanctuary in Scandinavia, where offerings to Odin, Thor, and Freyr were held every nine years.
evt-conversion-denmark-bluetooth: Dalby Holy Cross Church in Scania, one of the earliest surviving stone churches in Scandinavia, built in the generation after Harald Bluetooth declared Denmark a Christian kingdom.
evt-jelling-stones: The two Jelling runestones standing in their protective glass enclosure at Jelling, Denmark — the larger, raised by Harald Bluetooth around 965, is sometimes called Denmark's birth certificate.
evt-battle-svolder: Otto Sinding's panoramic painting of the Battle of Svolder (c. 1000), where Olaf Tryggvason's flagship the Long Serpent was overrun by a coalition fleet, ending Norway's brief first Christian kingship.
evt-olaf-ii-norway: A contemporary coin bearing the image of Olaf Haraldsson — later venerated as Saint Olaf — struck during his reign as King of Norway from 1015 to 1028.
evt-stiklestad: Peter Nicolai Arbo's painting of the fall of Olaf Haraldsson at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030, where the exiled king's attempt to retake Norway ended in death and the making of a martyr-saint.
evt-norse-mythology-eddas: The ornate title page of Olive Bray's 1908 edition of the Elder Edda — the primary written source for Norse mythology, preserving the cosmological poems that Viking-Age skalds recited from memory for centuries.
evt-younger-futhark: A painted replica of a Younger Futhark runestone from Resmo, Öland, showing the vivid red-on-black animal interlace and runic border that defined the Viking-age script tradition.
evt-skaldic-poetry: A skald performs in a Viking chieftain's hall, reciting verses of famous deeds before an assembled audience — the living heart of the skaldic oral tradition.
evt-egil-skallagrimsson: A 17th-century Icelandic manuscript portrait of Egil Skallagrímsson, the fearsome warrior-poet whose verses ranged from grief-stricken laments to thunderous praise-songs.
evt-rune-stones: The Rök Runestone in Östergötland, Sweden — carved around 800 CE with the longest known runic inscription, its dense text fills every face of the stone in a tour de force of early Norse literacy.
evt-trelleborg-fortress: The near-perfect circular earthwork of Trelleborg seen from the air reveals the geometric precision Harald Bluetooth's engineers achieved when they built his network of ring fortresses around 980.
evt-danegeld-ethelred: The Lingsberg runestone U 241, raised by a Swedish warrior's family to commemorate his service in England, is one of dozens of 'Danegeld stones' recording the silver that flowed back from Æthelred's desperate payments.
evt-battle-maldon: A 1922 illustration of the Battle of Maldon captures the moment the Viking force crossed the causeway after ealdorman Byrhtnoth fatally allowed them to land — a decision the Old English poem would mourn for centuries.
evt-sweyn-forkbeard-england: A medieval manuscript portrait of Sweyn Forkbeard as king, from the Chronica Roskildensis, depicts the Danish ruler who became the first Viking conqueror to hold the English throne.
evt-cnut-great: The Winchester Liber Vitae illumination shows Cnut and his queen Ælfgifu placing a gold cross on the altar of New Minster — a deliberate act of Christian kingship from the man who ruled England, Denmark, and Norway.
evt-harald-bluetooth: A gilded copper-alloy plaque likely from the twelfth century depicts a baptism scene, reflecting the conversion of Denmark that Harald Bluetooth proclaimed on the great Jelling runestone around 965.
evt-rollo-normandy: A medieval manuscript portrait of 'Rollo le premier duc de Normandie,' the Viking chieftain who received Normandy from the Frankish king in 911 and founded the dynasty that would conquer England.
evt-tostig-godwinson: A medieval manuscript illumination from a Cambridge University Library manuscript depicting a court scene from the era of Tostig Godwinson, whose banishment by his brother Harold in 1065 set the catastrophic chain of events in motion.
evt-harald-hardrada: A coin struck during the reign of Harald Hardrada (Harald III of Norway), the last great Viking warlord whose claim to the English throne brought him south in 1066 to die at Stamford Bridge.
evt-stamford-bridge: Peter Nicolai Arbo's 1870 painting of the Battle of Stamford Bridge, where Harald Hardrada's Norwegian army was crushed by Harold Godwinson's English forces on 25 September 1066, ending the Viking Age's last major invasion of England.
evt-muawiya-caliphate: An Arab-Sasanian silver coin struck in Muawiya I's name at the Fasa mint in Darabjird, the earliest physical evidence of his governance over the eastern provinces.
evt-battle-of-zab: The Greater and Lesser Zab rivers in northern Iraq, where Abbasid forces crushed the last Umayyad army in January 750 and ended a dynasty.
evt-abbasid-revolution: A medieval illumination from Balami's Tarikhnama showing Abu al-Abbas as-Saffah surrounded by his court at the moment he was proclaimed the first Abbasid caliph in 749.
evt-abu-al-abbas-saffah: A silver dirhem struck during the reign of as-Saffah (AH 132–136), one of the first coins minted under the new Abbasid dynasty.
evt-umayyad-emirate-cordoba: A gilded painted panel from the Alhambra depicting Andalusian court figures, reflecting the sophisticated Islamic culture that flourished under Umayyad rule in Spain.
evt-al-mansur-caliph: A portrait of Caliph al-Mansur from the 1598 Ottoman genealogical manuscript Zübdet-üt Tevarih, showing the man who built the Abbasid state into a lasting empire.
evt-founding-baghdad: The Abbasid Palace in Baghdad, one of the few surviving structures from the city's golden age as the caliphate's imperial capital on the Tigris.
evt-round-city-design: Guy Le Strange's scholarly reconstruction of the Round City of Madinat al-Salam, showing the perfectly circular walled city al-Mansur built as Baghdad's original core.
evt-harun-al-rashid: Harun al-Rashid seated on his throne (takht), the caliph whose reign became synonymous with the Abbasid golden age and the world of the Thousand and One Nights.
evt-battle-of-talas: A campaign map of the Battle of Talas (751), where Abbasid and allied forces halted Tang Chinese expansion into Central Asia and — through captured papermakers — gained the secret of paper production.
evt-paper-samarkand: Workers at the Konigil paper mill near Samarkand stripping mulberry bark, the same traditional technique used at the mill the Abbasids established there in the 8th century.
evt-paper-production: A Chinese woodblock illustration depicting the paper-making process, the technology that spread from Samarkand across the Islamic world and eventually to Europe.
evt-bayt-al-hikma: A 13th-century manuscript illustration from al-Hariri's Maqamat showing scholars gathered in a library, evoking the learned atmosphere of Baghdad's House of Wisdom.
evt-ibn-al-muqaffa: A portrait sketch of Ibn al-Muqaffa by Khalil Gibran, depicting the Persian-Arab scholar whose translations of Pahlavi wisdom literature into Arabic helped launch the great translation movement.
evt-al-mamun-caliph: A gold dinar struck in the name of Caliph al-Ma'mun, whose reign turned Baghdad into the intellectual capital of the medieval world.
evt-hunayn-ibn-ishaq: An illuminated initial from a Latin manuscript of the Isagoge, translated by Hunayn ibn Ishaq, showing a seated scholar with a book — an emblem of the transmission of Greek knowledge into Arabic and then into Latin Europe.
evt-banu-musa-hiyal: A technical illustration from the Banu Musa brothers' Book of Ingenious Devices, a 9th-century compendium of nearly a hundred self-operating machines that astounded the Abbasid court.
evt-hanbali-law-school: A miniature portrait of Ahmad ibn Hanbal from a Chester Beatty manuscript, depicting the scholar whose refusal to submit to the Mihna inquisition made him a hero of traditionalist Islam.
evt-al-khwarizmi-algebra: A bronze statue of al-Khwarizmi at the Universidad Complutense de Madrid honors the ninth-century mathematician whose treatise on al-jabr gave algebra its name.
evt-al-khwarizmi-algorithm: A 1983 Soviet commemorative stamp marks the 1200th anniversary of al-Khwarizmi, whose Latinized name — Algoritmi — became the word 'algorithm.'
evt-thabit-ibn-qurra: An Arabic manuscript of Apollonius's Conics, preserved through the translation work of Thabit ibn Qurra, whose renderings of Greek geometry kept ancient mathematics alive in the Islamic world.
evt-al-battani: The frontispiece of al-Battani's De scientia stellarum — his monumental astronomical tables, translated into Latin and used by European astronomers for six centuries.
evt-al-kindi: A 1962 Iraqi postage stamp commemorates al-Kindi, the ninth-century polymath known as the 'Philosopher of the Arabs,' who wrote on mathematics, music, optics, and cryptography.
evt-al-farabi: A Soviet stamp honoring al-Farabi, the tenth-century philosopher and music theorist whose commentaries on Aristotle earned him the title 'the Second Teacher' after the great Greek.
evt-arabic-numerals-spread: The Codex Vigilanus of 976 AD contains the earliest known European depiction of the Arabic-Indic numeral set — the moment the new number system first appeared in the Latin West.
evt-ibn-sina-canon: A colorized portrait of Ibn Sina (Avicenna), the Persian polymath whose Canon of Medicine became the standard medical textbook across Europe and the Islamic world for five centuries.
evt-ibn-sina-philosophy: A monument to Ibn Sina in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, commemorating the philosopher-physician who argued that the rational soul survives the body — an idea that sparked debate from Baghdad to Paris.
evt-al-razi-medicine: Al-Razi depicted as a physician examining a urine flask in a 13th-century illuminated manuscript, reflecting his pioneering emphasis on clinical observation and empirical diagnosis.
evt-hospital-system: The courtyard of the Bimaristan Argun in Aleppo, one of the best-preserved examples of the Islamic hospital system that provided free care to all patients regardless of religion or social standing.
evt-ibn-al-haytham-optics: An Arabic manuscript diagram showing Ibn al-Haytham's analysis of the optic nerves and visual system, from the work that overturned a millennium of Greek theory by proving that eyes receive light rather than emit it.
evt-al-jazari: Al-Jazari's famous elephant clock, illustrated in his 1206 Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices — a water-powered timekeeping automaton that blended Indian, Chinese, Byzantine, and Arab engineering in a single machine.
evt-ibn-al-nafis: A leaf from Ibn al-Nafis's Commentary on the Canon of Avicenna, the work in which he described pulmonary circulation — blood passing through the lungs — three centuries before European anatomists reached the same conclusion.
evt-hanafi-law-school: A Chester Beatty Library miniature portrait of Abu Hanifa, the 8th-century jurist whose rulings became the foundation of the Hanafi school.
evt-maliki-law-school: A Chester Beatty Library miniature portrait of Malik ibn Anas, the Medinan scholar whose legal teachings spread across North Africa and became the Maliki school.
evt-rabia-al-adawiyya: A traditional artistic depiction of Rabia al-Adawiyya, the 8th-century mystic poet from Basra whose devotional love poetry helped shape early Sufi spirituality.
evt-al-hallaj: A 19th-century Kashmiri manuscript illustration of the execution of al-Hallaj in 922 CE, the Sufi mystic put to death for his ecstatic declaration 'I am the Truth.'
evt-al-ghazali: The final page of al-Ghazali's autobiographical 'Deliverance from Error,' the deeply personal account of his spiritual crisis and eventual return to faith.
evt-al-ghazali-ihya: An illuminated medieval manuscript of al-Ghazali's 'Revival of the Religious Sciences,' the monumental work that reconciled Islamic law with Sufi spirituality.
evt-ibn-rushd: Ibn Rushd (Averroes) as depicted in Andrea di Bonaiuto's 14th-century fresco in Florence's Santa Maria Novella — a telling sign of how deeply the Córdoban philosopher's commentaries on Aristotle had penetrated European intellectual life.
evt-ibn-rushd-incoherence: The statue of Averroes outside the walls of Córdoba, the city where Ibn Rushd was born and where he wrote his systematic defense of Aristotelian philosophy against al-Ghazali's attacks.
evt-sufism-growth: A Persian miniature from the LACMA collection depicting a Sufi mystic absorbed in ecstatic prayer, capturing the inward, devotional intensity that drew millions to the Sufi path across the Islamic world.
evt-umayyad-caliphate-cordoba: The Caliphate of Córdoba at its peak under al-Mansur around 1000 CE, stretching across almost all of Iberia and asserting Umayyad rival caliphal authority against Baghdad.
evt-fatimid-founding: The Fatimid Caliphate's expansion from its North African heartland outward, showing the Ismaili Shia dynasty's rise from a regional power to a rival caliphate challenging both the Abbasids and Umayyads.
evt-al-azhar: The courtyard of Al-Azhar mosque and university in Cairo, founded by the Fatimids in 970 CE as a center for Ismaili theology that grew into one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world.
evt-almoravid-dynasty: A page from a Quran manuscript produced in 1190 CE under the Almoravid cultural sphere, its distinctive Maghrebi script and illumination reflecting the North African Berber dynasty's strict Islamic piety and patronage.
evt-ibn-tumart-almohad: The Almohad movement's expansion outward from its origin in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, showing how Ibn Tumart's reformist theology translated into a conquering state that swept aside the Almoravids and unified the Islamic west.
evt-umayyad-conquest-spain: A bilingual Arabic-Latin gold dinar minted in al-Andalus in 715–717 AD, within two years of the Umayyad conquest, bears witness to the new regime's attempt to legitimize itself in both worlds.
evt-madinat-al-zahra: The restored Salon Rico at Madinat al-Zahra near Córdoba, with its signature red-and-white horseshoe arches and intricate carved stucco, gives a sense of the dazzling palace city Abd al-Rahman III built as the physical statement of Umayyad power in the West.
evt-cordoba-library: A modern statue of al-Hakam II in Córdoba commemorates the caliph who turned the Great Mosque library into one of the largest collections of books anywhere in the medieval world, reportedly amassing some 400,000 volumes.
evt-ibn-hazm: The manuscript title page of Ibn Hazm's Tawq al-Hamama (Ring of the Dove) in the Leiden University Library, one of the oldest surviving copies of the 11th-century Córdoban scholar's celebrated meditation on love.
evt-ibn-tufayl-hayy: The title page of Simon Ockley's 1708 English translation of Ibn Tufayl's Hayy ibn Yaqzan, the 12th-century Andalusian philosophical novel that imagined a child raised alone in nature reasoning his way to truth without society or religion.
evt-maimonides: An 18th-century engraved portrait of Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon), the Córdoba-born Jewish philosopher and physician whose Guide for the Perplexed wrestled Aristotelian reason and Jewish scripture into an uneasy accord, influencing Christian and Islamic thinkers alike.
evt-silk-road-peak: The Abbasid caravanserai at Nishapur, one of the rest-house chains that sustained merchant traffic along the Silk Road through the Islamic heartland.
evt-volga-trade-dirham: A hoard of Abbasid silver dirhams of the kind that flooded north along the Volga route, turning Islamic coinage into the de facto currency of Viking-age Scandinavia.
evt-muhtasib-trade: An Ottoman-era illustration of a muhtasib — the market inspector who carried scales and enforced fair weights, a role that traced directly back to the Abbasid commercial code.
evt-ibn-hauqal: Ibn Hawqal's world map from his Book of Roads and Kingdoms, a richly annotated geographic survey that documented the trading cities and routes of the tenth-century Islamic world.
evt-al-masudi: Al-Mas'udi's circular world map, a visual companion to his encyclopedic Meadows of Gold that ranged across the geography, peoples, and customs of the known world.
evt-buyid-amirs: Silver coin of 'Adud al-Dawla, the most powerful of the Buyid amirs, who made the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad his figurehead while ruling the caliphate in all but name.
evt-seljuk-conquest-baghdad: Turkoman soldiers depicted in a mid-13th-century Iraqi manuscript, representative of the Seljuk warrior elite whose sudden arrival upended Baghdad's political order in 1055.
evt-nizam-al-mulk: A medieval Persian manuscript illustration of the assassination of Nizam al-Mulk in 1092, the killing that ended the career of the Seljuk Empire's most consequential administrator.
evt-first-crusade: A medieval illumination of the 1099 Crusader siege of Jerusalem, the climactic event of the First Crusade that ended nearly five centuries of Muslim rule over the city.
evt-saladin-ayyubid: The Ayyubid Sultanate at Saladin's death in 1193, showing the vast domain he assembled across Egypt, Syria, and the Hejaz that made him the dominant power in the Islamic world.
evt-saladin: A silver dirham struck at Damascus in Saladin's name in AH 583 (1187–88 CE), the same year he recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders — the high-water mark of his career.
evt-third-crusade: Map of the Third Crusade (1189–1192), showing the routes of the European kings who set out to retake Jerusalem after Saladin's stunning victory at Hattin.
evt-al-biruni: A 1973 Soviet commemorative stamp honoring al-Biruni on the thousandth anniversary of his birth, depicting the polymath scholar who mapped India, calculated the earth's circumference, and catalogued dozens of fields of knowledge.
evt-mongol-advance: A 13th-century manuscript painting captures the ferocity of the Mongol assault on Khwarezm in 1221, the opening wave of the campaign that would shatter the Islamic world's eastern heartland.
evt-mongol-sack-baghdad: A medieval illumination from Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh depicts Hulagu Khan's forces storming Baghdad in 1258, the catastrophic event that ended five centuries of Abbasid rule and left the city in ruins.
evt-nasir-al-din-al-tusi: An Iranian commemorative stamp honors Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, the polymath who turned the Mongol catastrophe into a scientific lifeline by founding the Maragha Observatory and saving generations of astronomical knowledge.
evt-maragha-observatory: The surviving stone foundations of the Maragha Observatory in northwest Iran, built in 1259 under al-Tusi's direction and for decades the most advanced astronomical facility in the world.
evt-firdawsi-shahnameh: Sultan Muhammad's breathtaking illumination of the Court of Gayumars, from a 16th-century Shahnameh manuscript, shows the timeless power of Firdawsi's epic verse — composed around 1010 and still inspiring artists five centuries later.
evt-uyghur-001: Territory of the Second Turkic Khaganate, the steppe empire the Uyghurs and their allies rose up against in 744 to claim the Mongolian plateau.
evt-uyghur-002: Museum display of artifacts from Uyghur-era Durvuljin archaeological sites in central Mongolia, dating to the period of the Khaganate's founding.
evt-uyghur-004: Remains of Ordu-Baliq on the Mongolian steppe, the capital city founded by Bayanchur Khan and the most enduring monument of his reign.
evt-uyghur-005: Reconstruction drawing of the Karabalgasun inscription stele erected at Ordu-Baliq, one of the great commemorative monuments of the Uyghur capital built by Bayanchur Khan.
evt-uyghur-007: Map of the Battle of Talas, 751 CE, showing the clash between Tang China's westward expansion and the Abbasid Caliphate at the river that marked the limit of Chinese power in Central Asia.
evt-uyghur-072: A silver Turkic plaque showing two mounted warriors, reflecting the steppe horseman culture of the Karluk tribes who relocated to Semirechye after being expelled from the Uyghur orbit in the mid-8th century.
evt-uyghur-009: A campaign map tracing An Lushan's rebel advance from the northeast against the Tang heartland in 755, the crisis that gave the Uyghurs their opening.
evt-uyghur-010: Wall paintings from the Bezeklik caves depicting Sogdian merchants and court figures — the diplomatic and mercantile networks through which the Tang appeal for Uyghur military aid traveled.
evt-uyghur-014: A detail from a Manichaean manuscript painting showing Bögü Qaghan in armour kneeling before a Manichaean high priest — the moment that would reshape the entire Uyghur court.
evt-uyghur-013: A Silk Road caravanserai at Nishapur — a waystation on the trade routes along which Uyghur horses moved east in exchange for bolts of Tang silk.
evt-uyghur-012: Tang-era donor figures from the Dunhuang Mogao caves showing a noblewoman in elaborate court dress — the visual world of the imperial women sent north as diplomatic brides to steppe rulers.
evt-uyghur-015: A Manichaean manuscript painting depicting the 762 CE conversion of Bögü Qaghan, the pivotal scene in which a Persian religion took root on the Mongolian steppe.
evt-uyghur-016: A 3rd-century seal bearing the image of Mani, founder of the religion the Uyghurs would elevate to state faith — one of the few surviving artifacts linked to Manichaeism's origins.
evt-uyghur-008: The 7th-century Afrasiab murals from Samarkand show Sogdian courtiers and diplomats in procession — the world these merchants brought with them when they entered Uyghur service.
evt-uyghur-017: A Manichaean devotional fresco from Central Asia depicting a paradise scene with the characteristic Cross of Light — the kind of image that would have adorned the monasteries at Ordu-Baliq.
evt-uyghur-018: A medieval funerary tablet inscribed in Old Uyghur script alongside a cross and lotus, showing the alphabet at work in a real steppe community.
evt-uyghur-020: A gold 12-petalled flower ornament from the Sogdian heartland, typical of the luxury goods and courtly taste that Sogdian advisers carried with them into the Uyghur capital.
evt-uyghur-026: The Elegest I runic inscription, a Yenisei Kyrgyz memorial stele from the upper Yenisei region — one of the primary written records left by the people who would destroy the Uyghur empire.
evt-uyghur-027: Iron agricultural and combat tools from the Yenisei Kyrgyz, now in the State Historical Museum in Moscow, showing the material culture of the warriors who sacked Ordu-Baliq in 840.
evt-uyghur-029: A traditional portrait of Emperor Tang Wuzong, the Tang ruler who in 843 ordered the systematic suppression of Manichaean temples and the execution of their clergy throughout the empire.
evt-uyghur-096: The Orkhon River winding through the arid Mongolian steppe — the heartland valley where the Uyghur capital once stood, silent and empty after the Kyrgyz conquest of 840.
evt-uyghur-031: A map showing the Xizhou Uyghurs (Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom) and the Guiyi Circuit during the Five Dynasties period, marking the territory the Uyghur successor state carved out in the Hexi Corridor after the steppe collapse.
evt-uyghur-032: The Qocho Uyghur Kingdom at its height in the Turfan Basin, the settled oasis state the steppe refugees built between the Kara-Khanid Khanate and the Liao Empire.
evt-uyghur-034: The Bezeklik Thousand Buddha Caves cut into the cliffs above Turfan, where Qocho Uyghur patrons funded some of Central Asia's finest Buddhist cave-temple art.
evt-uyghur-097: The interior tunnel of a traditional qanat (karez) irrigation channel — the same underground gravity-flow technology that brought mountain snowmelt beneath the desert to the fields of Turfan.
evt-uyghur-039: A silver dirham struck in the name of Ali-Tegin, one of the early Kara-Khanid rulers whose dynasty emerged from the Karluk and related Turkic tribes to dominate Transoxiana from the mid-10th century onward.
evt-uyghur-040: The mausoleum of Satuq Bughra Khan at Artush in Xinjiang, built to honor the Kara-Khanid prince whose conversion to Islam in the early 10th century made him the first Turkic Muslim ruler.
evt-uyghur-083: A 19th-century engraving of the mausoleum of Satuq Bughra Khan in Artush, the holy war leader whose campaigns against pagan Turkic neighbors established Islam's foothold on the eastern steppe.
evt-uyghur-042: The Ismail Samani mausoleum in Bukhara, the jewel of the Samanid capital the Kara-Khanids captured around 999, ending one of the great Persian dynasties and making Bukhara a Turkic Islamic city.
evt-uyghur-045: A page from the Vienna manuscript of the Kutadgu Bilig, the 1069 Turkic-language mirror-for-princes composed by Yusuf Khass Hajib for the Kara-Khanid ruler of Kashgar — the first great work of Turkic Islamic literature.
evt-uyghur-046: The circular world map drawn by Mahmud al-Kashgari in his Diwan Lughat al-Turk (1072–74), placing the Turkic-speaking world at its center and preserving the earliest known cartographic record of Turkic geography.
evt-uyghur-047: The Bobrinsky Bucket, a 12th-century Seljuk bronze vessel inlaid with Arabic inscriptions and courtly scenes, epitomizing the Central Asian Islamic material culture the Kara-Khanids entered as Seljuk vassals after 1089.
evt-uyghur-048: The Registan in Samarkand, the most famous madrasa complex of the Turkic-Islamic world, heir to the tradition of Quranic learning that spread eastward into Kara-Khanid lands in the 11th century.
evt-uyghur-049: A map showing the five circuits of the Liao Dynasty at its height — the empire Yelü Dashi would flee when the Jurchen Jin swept it away in 1125.
evt-uyghur-050: The Lake Balkhash basin — the steppe and river corridor through which Yelü Dashi led his followers on the long march west after the Liao collapse.
evt-uyghur-052: A map of the Battle of Qatwan (1141), where the Qara Khitai under Yelü Dashi decisively crushed the Seljuk Sultan Sanjar and redrew the balance of power across Central Asia.
evt-uyghur-053: A Chinese ink depiction of a Kara-Khitan man — subjects and rulers of the Western Liao, a Buddhist dynasty that held power over a predominantly Muslim population.
evt-uyghur-054: The Western Liao (Qara Khitai) empire at its peak, a patchwork of vassal states and tribute relationships stretching from the steppe to the edge of the Islamic world.
evt-uyghur-055: A crowned Prester John enthroned, as depicted on a late-medieval Portuguese portolan chart — the legendary Christian king that Europeans conjured partly from garbled reports of the Buddhist Gurkhan's victories over Muslim rulers.
evt-uyghur-059: A map of the Naiman Khanate at its height, the steppe confederacy that Genghis Khan destroyed in 1204 to consolidate his grip on Mongolia.
evt-uyghur-060: The iconic Yuan dynasty portrait of Genghis Khan, painted after his death — the face of the man proclaimed universal ruler of the Mongols at the great kurultai of 1206.
evt-uyghur-067: The Mongol Empire's expansion from its 1206 core across Eurasia, showing how the steppe heartland and the Tarim Basin — long governed by Uyghurs and Qara-Khitai — became the launching pad for the greatest land empire the world has ever seen.
evt-gupta-collapse: The Padmapani fresco from the Ajanta caves, painted at the height of Gupta patronage — the last great flourishing before the empire fell apart.
evt-yashodharman: A 19th-century illustration depicting the defeat of the Hephthalite (White Huns) forces at the Battle of the 528, when Yashodharman halted the nomadic advance into India.
evt-pushyabhuti-dynasty: A sandstone lion capital from Gwalior dated to the 7th century CE, one of the few surviving artifacts directly attributable to the Vardhana (Pushyabhuti) dynasty that produced Emperor Harsha.
evt-pallava-dynasty: The 7th-century Sri Kailasanathar temple at Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital and one of the finest surviving monuments of the dynasty's golden age.
evt-pandya-dynasty: An aerial view of Madurai from the Meenakshi Amman Temple, the ancient Pandya capital whose towering gopurams still dominate the city skyline.
evt-chera-dynasty: Roman amphorae and sherds from the Pattanam excavations on the Kerala coast, material evidence of the thriving long-distance trade the Cheras controlled through their ports.
evt-chalukya-dynasty: A 6th-century Kannada inscription carved into the sandstone cliff at Badami (Vatapi), the Chalukya capital hewn from the rock above the sacred tank.
evt-chola-dynasty: A Chola-dynasty bronze Ganesha from the Cleveland Museum of Art, showing the dynasty's mastery of lost-wax casting at its medieval peak.
evt-buddhism-decline: The ruins of Nalanda, once the greatest university in Asia, whose burning by Bakhtiyar Khalji's forces around 1200 CE effectively extinguished institutional Buddhism on the Indian subcontinent.
evt-vikramashila-monastery: The excavated ruins of Vikramashila monastery in Bihar, the great Pala-era Buddhist university that rivaled Nalanda until its destruction in 1203.
evt-harsha-empire: A historical illustration of Emperor Harsha's royal elephant procession, depicting the Buddhist-patron king in the grand ceremonial style that defined his court at Kannauj.
evt-xuanzang-pilgrimage: A Tang-dynasty-era portrait painting of Xuanzang, the Chinese monk who spent sixteen years traveling India collecting Buddhist texts and left behind one of the most vivid accounts of Harsha's empire.
evt-pulakeshin-ii: The Aihole inscription of court poet Ravikirti, carved in 634 CE into a temple wall at Aihole, which records Pulakeshin II's decisive defeat of Harsha and his northern ambitions.
evt-kannauj-capital: An early 19th-century watercolor view of Kannauj, the ancient city on the Ganges that every dynasty — Pratihara, Pala, and Rashtrakuta — fought to hold as the symbolic prize of north Indian supremacy.
evt-narasimhavarman-i: A rock-cut relief figure at Mahabalipuram, carved under Narasimhavarman I, whose reign launched the great stone-carving program at this coastal site.
evt-mahabalipuram: The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram, built by the Pallavas in the 8th century, stands where the Bay of Bengal meets some of the earliest free-standing stone temples in South India.
evt-vesara-style: The Nageshvara and Chennakeshava temples at Mosale, Karnataka, show the Vesara hybrid style blending the curvilinear Nagara shikhara of the north with the tiered Dravida base of the south.
evt-rashtrakuta-dynasty: A towering relief of Parshvanatha carved in the Jain caves at Ellora, commissioned under Rashtrakuta patronage in the 8th–9th century.
evt-cheraman-juma-mosque: The Cheraman Juma Mosque at Kodungallur, Kerala, claimed as the first mosque in India and built in the traditional Kerala timber style rather than the domed forms of later Islamic architecture.
evt-nagara-temple-style: The Kandariya Mahadeo temple at Khajuraho, its clustered shikharas rising in a mountain-like silhouette, is the defining example of the North Indian Nagara style at its height.
evt-dravida-temple-style: The Arunachalesvara temple at Thiruvannamalai, its four massive gopuram gate-towers soaring above the Tamil plain, exemplifies the Dravida style's monumental pyramid-gateways over a walled sacred precinct.
evt-tripartite-struggle: A map of the three rival powers — Gurjara-Pratiharas, Palas, and Rashtrakutas — each pushing toward Kannauj in the 9th-century tripartite struggle.
evt-pratihara-dynasty: A 9th–10th-century Pratihara stone panel from Kannauj depicting the Saptamatrikas (seven mother goddesses), showcasing the dynasty's artistic patronage at their imperial capital.
evt-mihira-bhoja: A silver coin of Mihira Bhoja, the greatest Gurjara-Pratihara ruler, whose horse-rider type coinage circulated widely across north India during his long 9th-century reign.
evt-pala-dynasty: The Pala Empire at its height, stretching across Bengal and Bihar as the last great Buddhist dynasty of the Indian subcontinent.
evt-dharmapala: A Pala-dynasty phyllite sculpture of Durga slaying the buffalo demon, representing the fine stone carving tradition that flourished under Pala royal patronage in Bengal.
evt-arab-conquest-sindh: A map of Sindh showing the key cities — Daybul, Brahmanabad, Roar, and Multan — that fell to Muhammad ibn Qasim's Arab forces in 711–713 CE.
evt-mahmud-ghazni: A 14th-century miniature from Rashid al-Din's universal history showing Mahmud of Ghazni on horseback during his Indian campaigns.
evt-chandela-dynasty: A ruined Chandela temple at Ajaigarh fort, Madhya Pradesh — the dynasty that ruled Jejakabhukti from the 9th to 13th centuries left dozens of temples across Bundelkhand, Khajuraho being only the most famous.
evt-khajuraho-temples: The Chandela-era temples at Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh — built between roughly 950 and 1050 CE, their soaring shikhara towers and densely carved walls represent the high-water mark of the Nagara temple tradition in north-central India.
evt-chaulukyas-gujarat: A silver coin of the Chaulukya-Paramara period, circa 950–1050 CE — the Chaulukyas of Gujarat (also called Solankis) ruled from Anhilwara and built some of medieval India's finest temples, including the Modhera Sun Temple.
evt-paramara-bhoja: The unfinished Bhojeshwar temple at Bhojpur — a colossal Shiva shrine begun by King Bhoja of the Paramaras in the early 11th century, left incomplete when his kingdom collapsed.
evt-rajput-rise: A Mughal-era fresco depicting a royal Rajput procession, capturing the pageantry and martial splendor of the clans who dominated northern and central India for five centuries.
evt-rajaraja-chola: A stone portrait detail of Rajaraja Chola I, the warrior-king who transformed the Chola realm from a regional power into a maritime empire.
evt-brihadeeswara-temple: The Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur illuminated at dusk, its 216-foot vimana tower still the tallest medieval temple tower in India.
evt-srivijaya-raid: A 17th-century Dutch map of the Indian Ocean showing the sea lanes linking Tamil Nadu to the island kingdoms of Southeast Asia that Rajendra Chola's fleet struck in 1025.
evt-chola-administration: The temple gopuram at Uttaramerur, the Tamil Nadu village whose stone-inscribed assembly rules are the oldest known written constitution for local self-governance.
evt-chola-bronzes: A Chola Nataraja bronze from the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the definitive icon of the dynasty's lost-wax casting tradition — Shiva dancing in a ring of fire.
evt-chola-trade-china: The Airavateswara Temple at Darasuram, built by Rajaraja II with wealth flowing from the Chola trading network that extended as far as Song-dynasty China.
evt-bhakti-movement: Mirabai, the 16th-century Rajput poet-saint, is shown with Krishna above her — a devotional painting capturing the Bhakti ideal of direct, personal love for god over ritual or priestly hierarchy.
evt-alvars-nayanars: Shrine statues of Alvar saints at Thiruthankal temple, each identified by Tamil name plaques — these Tamil poet-devotees composed the Nalayira Divya Prabandham that became the scripture of Vaishnava bhakti in South India.
evt-andal-poet: A devotional painting of Andal, the 8th-century Tamil woman poet and the only female Alvar, depicted as a divine figure — her Tiruppavai and Nachiyar Tirumozhi remain sung in Vaishnava temples every morning.
evt-jayadeva-gita-govinda: The original palm-leaf manuscript of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, preserved at the Odisha State Museum in Bhubaneswar — written in the 12th century, it became the defining lyric poem of Krishna devotion across South and Southeast Asia.
evt-konark-sun-temple: The Konark Sun Temple in Odisha, built by Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I around 1250 CE — conceived as a colossal stone chariot for the sun god Surya, it is one of the most ambitious architectural feats of medieval India.
evt-eastern-ganga: The Mukhalingeswara temple complex at Mukhalingam, Andhra Pradesh — built under early Eastern Ganga patronage, these temples illustrate the Kalinga architectural style the dynasty would later push to its apex at Konark.
evt-hoysala-dynasty: An apsara holding a mirror, carved in the densely detailed Hoysala style on the outer wall of the Chennakesava Temple at Belur, Karnataka — the Hoysalas turned temple surfaces into a continuous encyclopedia of celestial figures, each unique.
evt-shankara: Raja Ravi Varma's painting of Adi Shankara teaching his four main disciples, capturing the philosopher who unified Hindu doctrine into Advaita Vedanta — the teaching that the individual soul and Brahman are one.
evt-ramanuja: A painted portrait of Ramanuja, the 11th-century Vaishnava theologian whose Vishishtadvaita philosophy argued that the individual soul, though real, exists within and depends entirely on Brahman.
evt-madhva: The sacred vigraha of Madhvacharya at Pajaka, his birthplace near Udupi, honoring the 13th-century philosopher who broke sharply from both Shankara and Ramanuja to argue that souls and God are eternally and absolutely distinct.
evt-bahubali-statue: The 57-foot monolithic statue of Gomateshwara (Bahubali) at Shravanabelagola, carved in 983 CE and still the world's largest free-standing monolithic statue, a testament to the ambition of Jain royal patronage under the Ganga dynasty.
evt-jainism-medieval: The Thousand-Pillar Jain temple at Moodbidri in Karnataka, built under the patronage of local Jain chiefs and illustrating how Jainism survived and flourished in the Deccan long after Buddhism had faded from the subcontinent.
evt-bhaskara-ii: A page from Lilavati, the first volume of Bhaskara II's masterwork Siddhanta Shiromani, showing Sanskrit mathematical verse alongside a geometric proof — the 12th-century text that would define Indian mathematics for centuries.
evt-lilavati: A problem from Bhaskara II's Lilavati, framed as a riddle about bees and lotus flowers — mathematics taught as poetry, in a tradition where problems were composed in verse so students could memorize them.
evt-sanskrit-cosmopolis: An 1863 palm-leaf manuscript of Vedic Sanskrit texts in the Southern Grantha script, copied in Kerala — one glimpse of how Sanskrit functioned as a cosmopolitan literary language unifying courts, scholars, and temples across South and Southeast Asia for over a millennium.
evt-sack-somnath: Archive photographs from 1869 and 1895 showing the Somnath temple in ruins, still bearing the scars of repeated sackings across the centuries.
evt-muhammad-ghor: Gold coins struck in the name of Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghor, the sultan whose armies ended Rajput independence and opened the subcontinent to permanent Islamic rule.
evt-prithviraj-chauhan: A posthumous Kota-school portrait of Prithviraj Chauhan, the last great Rajput king of Delhi, shown in the warrior-archer pose that became his legendary signature.
evt-second-tarain: A 19th-century painting depicting the Rajput cavalry's doomed last stand at the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192, the engagement that ended Hindu political dominance of northern India.
evt-bakhtiyar-khalji-bengal: A Victorian-era illustration depicting Bakhtiyar Khalji's sack of Nalanda in 1193, the destruction of India's greatest Buddhist monastery and a blow from which Indian Buddhism never recovered.
evt-qutb-al-din-aibak: The tomb of Qutb al-Din Aibak in Lahore, the former slave-general who founded the Delhi Sultanate and became the first sultan to rule India from a permanent Islamic capital.
evt-qutb-minar: The Qutb Minar framed through a ruined arch of the Quwwat ul-Islam mosque, the 73-meter sandstone tower begun by Aibak as a proclamation of Islam's arrival in the heart of India.
evt-uyghur-100: A 1287 Yuan dynasty paper banknote and its printing plate — the paper-money infrastructure of the Mongol commercial world in which the ortoq merchant partnership system channelled trade credit across the empire.
evt-uyghur-064: A Persian miniature depicting Mongol horsemen in full charge — the kind of swift, relentless cavalry pursuit that Jebe led against Küchlüg across the Tarim Basin in 1218.
evt-dar-al-ilm: A double-page world map from the Book of Curiosities (Kitab Gharaib al-Funun), an 11th-century Fatimid cosmographic manuscript produced in Cairo — exactly the kind of scientific work the Dar al-Ilm was founded to house and sponsor.
evt-uyghur-085: A balbal stone memorial figure from Burana in Kyrgyzstan, typical of the steppe warrior culture shared by the Uyghurs and their Tang allies in the mid-eighth century.
evt-mp-huns-europe: A map showing the vast sweep of Hunnic political control under Attila around 450 CE, with subject peoples — Goths, Gepids, Herules, and more — ringed around the Hunnic core in the Pannonian basin.
evt-mp-hunnic-society: A gold-hilted spatha sword from the Hunnic-era princely burial at Jakuszowice, Poland — the kind of prestige weapon that marked elite status in a society built on mounted raiding and personal loyalty to a warlord chief.
evt-mp-gothic-refugees: A map tracing the migration routes of the Gothic peoples and other groups into the Roman Empire between 100 and 500 CE, with the Hunnic advance from the east visible as the pressure that set everything else in motion.
evt-mp-pontic-steppe-goths: An engraving depicting the Gothic king Athanaric and the Roman emperor Valens meeting on boats in the middle of the Danube — the uneasy diplomacy that defined the Gothic-Roman borderland before the Hunnic shockwave shattered it.
evt-mp-adrianople: A re-enactor in late Roman infantry officer kit — the chainmail, ridge helmet, and oval shield of the kind of soldier who marched out from Adrianople in August 378 and did not come back.
evt-mp-clovis-rises: Ary Scheffer's 1836 painting of the Battle of Tolbiac, where Clovis's victory over the Alamanni set him on the path to uniting the Franks under a single crown.
evt-mp-radagaisus: Giorgio Vasari's ceiling fresco in Florence's Palazzo Vecchio depicts Stilicho's forces routing the Gothic army of Radagaisus at Fiesole in 406.
evt-mp-vandals-gaul: A Vandal cavalryman in full gallop, preserved in a mosaic pavement near Carthage — the people who poured across the frozen Rhine into Gaul on New Year's Eve 406 and never went home.
evt-mp-constantine-iii: A gold solidus struck at Lugdunum (Lyon) bearing the portrait of Constantine III, the British soldier who declared himself emperor in 407 and briefly held Gaul against both barbarians and a suspicious Honorius.
evt-mp-britain-abandoned: A map tracing the phased Roman withdrawal from Britain between 383 and 410, showing Pictish and Saxon raids pressing in from every direction as the legions departed for the last time.
evt-mp-stilicho: The ivory diptych of Stilicho, carved around 395, shows the half-Vandal general in military dress alongside his wife Serena and son Eucherius — one of the few contemporary likenesses of the man who held the Western Empire together.
evt-mp-rhine-crossing: The Rhine gorge near the Loreley rock — the natural barrier that a frozen river briefly erased on the last night of 406, letting the Vandals, Suebi, and Alans pour into Roman Gaul.
evt-mp-burgundians: A map of the first Burgundian kingdom on the Rhine, showing the territory the Burgundians occupied as Roman federates in the early 5th century.
evt-mp-visigoths-aquitaine: A medieval manuscript illustration of the Frankish-Visigothic conflict, depicting the Visigoths whose earlier settlement in Aquitaine in 418 made them the first barbarian group to carve out a formal kingdom on Roman soil.
evt-mp-alans-dispersed: Map showing the short-lived Kingdom of the Alans in central Hispania (409–426 AD), where the Alans settled alongside the Vandals and Suebi before being crushed by the Visigoths.
evt-mp-suebi-gallaecia: A medieval Galician manuscript illumination depicting figures from the Suebi kingdom era, the Germanic people who carved out a durable kingdom in the northwestern Iberian peninsula.
evt-mp-geiseric-africa: A 16th-century illustration of an ancient Vandal warrior, labeled "Vandal Antique" — the martial people Geiseric led out of Hispania and across the strait into Roman Africa in 429.
evt-mp-vandal-hippo: Philippe de Champaigne's portrait of Augustine of Hippo, the bishop and theologian who died in 430 while the Vandals besieged his city — the last great act of a civilization on the edge.
evt-mp-sack-455: Karl Briullov's sweeping 19th-century painting of Genseric's Vandals sacking Rome in 455, capturing the chaos of looting, the menorah from the Temple among the spoils, and Pope Leo I's futile appeal.
evt-mp-annona-collapse: A museum model of a Roman grain ship of the type that once shuttled North African wheat to feed Rome — the annona fleet that collapsed when the Vandals seized Carthage and its hinterland.
evt-mp-attila-rises: Attila the Hun depicted in his coronation regalia in the 14th-century Hungarian Képes Krónika, one of the oldest surviving portraits of the feared king.
evt-mp-eastern-tribute: Georges-Antoine Rochegrosse's 1880 painting captures the terror of a Hunnic raid — the kind of ruthless pressure Attila brought to bear on Constantinople to extract annual tribute.
evt-mp-priscus-embassy: Priscus of Panium, the Byzantine diplomat whose eyewitness account of Attila's court in 449 CE remains the most vivid surviving description of Hunnic life.
evt-mp-attila-gaul: A museum reconstruction of Attila the Hun in warrior dress, evoking the fearsome leader who swept into Gaul in 451 CE with an army large enough to alarm both Rome and the Visigoths.
evt-mp-catalaunian: The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains as depicted in the 15th-century Thuróczy Chronicle, with the Latin inscription noting that the great Gothic king Theodoric fell in this engagement.
evt-mp-theodoric-i-dies: Félix Castello's 1635 portrait of Theodoric I, king of the Visigoths, who fell fighting the Huns at the Catalaunian Plains — one of the defining moments of the Migration Period.
evt-mp-pope-leo-attila: Pope Leo I the Great in a Byzantine mosaic portrait — it was Leo who rode out in 452 CE to meet Attila on the Mincio River and, by persuasion or divine awe, turned the Huns back from Rome.
evt-mp-nedao: An illuminated initial from the 14th-century Képes Krónika showing Attila enthroned — the same manuscript tradition that recorded the collapse of Hunnic power after his death and the Battle of Nedao in 454 CE.
evt-mp-valentinian-murdered: Marble portrait bust of Valentinian III from the Louvre, the emperor whose murder in 455 touched off a decade of chaos on the throne.
evt-mp-shadow-emperors: Ivory consular diptych of Probus (406 AD) depicting Emperor Honorius in full military regalia — the kind of ceremonial display that masked how little power the Western court still wielded.
evt-mp-ricimer: Ricimer's personal seal, the tangible mark of the generalissimo who put four emperors on the Western throne and removed them just as casually.
evt-mp-majorian: Gold solidus of Majorian struck at Arles, the last Western emperor capable enough to terrify the Vandals — before Ricimer had him killed.
evt-mp-soissons: Map of Gaul in 476 AD, showing the Kingdom of Soissons as a small Roman holdout in a landscape already divided among Franks, Goths, Burgundians, and Alans.
evt-mp-romulus-augustulus: Gold solidus of Romulus Augustulus, the teenager whose deposition in 476 AD closed the final chapter of the Western Roman Empire.
evt-mp-odoacer: Silver coin of Odoacer from the British Museum — the Germanic warlord who ended the Western Empire not with a dramatic conquest but a polite letter to Constantinople saying the West no longer needed its own emperor.
evt-mp-nepos-exile: Gold tremissis of Julius Nepos, the last man the Eastern Empire recognized as legitimate ruler of the West, who governed a shrinking coastal enclave in Dalmatia until his own men murdered him in 480.
evt-mp-soissons-battle: A 19th-century engraving showing the Roman commander Syagrius brought before Clovis after the Battle of Soissons in 486, ending the last remnant of Roman rule in Gaul.
evt-mp-clovis-baptism: A medieval illumination depicting the baptism of Clovis by Bishop Remigius of Reims around 496, with the Holy Spirit descending as a dove — the moment that allied the Franks with the Catholic Church.
evt-mp-clovis-church-alliance: A carved ivory detail showing Remigius of Reims baptizing Clovis, the ritual act that forged the enduring alliance between the Frankish crown and the Roman Catholic hierarchy.
evt-mp-vouille: A medieval illumination depicting Clovis striking down the Visigothic king Alaric II at the Battle of Vouillé in 507, effectively ending Visigothic power in Gaul.
evt-mp-lex-salica: A Frankish royal legal document from the early 8th century, representative of the written law tradition that the Lex Salica established for the Frankish kingdoms.
evt-mp-breviary-alaric: The illuminated frontispiece of a 9th-century manuscript of the Breviary of Alaric, the Visigothic legal code issued in 506 that adapted Roman law for the Frankish-ruled population.
evt-mp-gundobad-law: A 1957 sculptural portrait of Gundobad, King of the Burgundians (c. 480–516), who issued the Lex Burgundionum to govern both his Burgundian and Roman subjects.
evt-mp-theodoric-ostrogoths: A gold solidus of Theodoric the Great, King of the Ostrogoths and Italy (493–526), struck in imitation of Roman imperial coinage to signal legitimacy to his Roman subjects.
evt-mp-boethius: A 12th-century manuscript illustration of Boethius labeled 'BOETIVS,' depicting him with a monochord — the philosopher and statesman who wrote the Consolation of Philosophy while awaiting execution under Theodoric.
evt-mp-arian-controversy: A fresco portrait of Arius, the Alexandrian theologian whose teaching that Christ was subordinate to God the Father divided the successor kingdoms — where Gothic rulers stayed Arian while their Roman subjects were Catholic.
evt-mp-visigothic-conversion: A 19th-century painting of the Third Council of Toledo in 589, showing King Reccared I (labeled 'FLAVIUS RECAREDUS REX') formally renouncing Arianism and converting the Visigoths to Catholicism.
evt-mp-justinian-ambition: Emperor Justinian I in the famous 6th-century mosaic at the Basilica of San Vitale, Ravenna — made during his own lifetime as he declared his intention to reunite the Roman world.
evt-mp-vandal-war-533: Campaign map of Belisarius's 533–534 Vandalic War, showing the Byzantine fleet's crossing from Sicily to North Africa and the rapid advance on Carthage.
evt-mp-belisarius-north-africa: Belisarius as depicted in the 6th-century mosaic at San Vitale, Ravenna, made shortly after his North African triumph — the closest thing to a contemporary portrait of Justinian's greatest general.
evt-mp-vandal-kingdom-end: Roman soldiers carry the Temple menorah in triumph — a relief on the Arch of Titus in Rome, the same treasures Belisarius recovered from the Vandals and paraded through Constantinople in 534.
evt-mp-gothic-war-italy: A campaign map of the Gothic War in Italy (535–554) charts Belisarius's advance from Sicily northward and the grinding back-and-forth over Rome and Ravenna that left the peninsula devastated long before Narses delivered the final blow.
evt-mp-belisarius-rome: A period illustration of a Gothic warrior, representative of the Ostrogothic forces Belisarius held at bay during the year-long siege of Rome from 537 to 538.
evt-mp-narses-gothic-war: A Byzantine mosaic portrait of Narses, the eunuch general who finished what Belisarius started, finally driving the last Ostrogothic resistance out of Italy by 554 and ending two decades of devastating war.
evt-mp-nika-riots: The surviving obelisks of the Hippodrome of Constantinople, the chariot-racing arena at the heart of the Nika Riots in 532, when factional violence nearly toppled Justinian's throne.
evt-mp-theodora: Empress Theodora in the 6th-century mosaic at San Vitale, Ravenna — the definitive contemporary image of the woman who co-ruled the Byzantine Empire and famously told Justinian not to flee during the Nika Riots.
evt-mp-hagia-sophia: The Hagia Sophia as it stands today in Istanbul, built by Justinian in just five years and consecrated in 537 — it remained the largest cathedral in the world for nearly a thousand years.
evt-mp-dust-veil-536: A sixth-century stone inscription from northern Italy records the year 536, when an eerie fog blotted out the sun and plunged the Mediterranean world into a years-long artificial winter.
evt-mp-536-dendro: Tree-ring and ice-core data plot the sharp temperature crash beginning in 536, the coldest decade in the Common Era, etched into wood grain across Europe and Central Asia.
evt-mp-plague-justinian: A late-medieval painting depicts the Plague of Justinian's horror — priests administering last rites as bodies pile in the streets, the same scene that devastated Constantinople and the Mediterranean world from 541 onward.
evt-mp-plague-spread: Advanced tissue necrosis in the fingers — the Black Death's signature symptom — illustrates the bacterium Yersinia pestis at work, the same pathogen that swept westward from Egypt through the ports of the Mediterranean in the 540s.
evt-mp-lombards-italy: A nineteenth-century historical map traces the Lombards' migration routes from their Scandinavian origins down through central Europe and Pannonia to the plains of northern Italy, the long road that ended with their 568 invasion.
evt-mp-alboin: Alboin leads his warriors through the gates of Pavia in 572 after a three-year siege, a nineteenth-century engraving capturing the moment the Lombard king made the city his new capital.
evt-mp-lombard-pavia: A map of the Lombard Kingdom in Italy shows Pavia at its heart in Langobardia Major, surrounded by the patchwork of Byzantine-held corridors and the rival Duchy of Benevento to the south.
evt-mp-lombard-pannonia: Lombard grave goods from Lesencetomaj in Hungary — the heart of ancient Pannonia — preserve the material culture of the people who spent two generations here before crossing into Italy in 568.
evt-mp-post-roman-west: Europe at 476 AD, the moment the Western Roman Empire formally ended, shows a fragmented landscape of successor kingdoms — Visigoths in Hispania, Burgundians on the Rhône, and Odoacer's Italy standing between the Franks and Constantinople.
evt-mp-federate-system: The Missorium of Theodosius I (388 CE), a silver ceremonial dish showing the emperor handing a document to a kneeling official flanked by soldiers — likely commemorating the foedus of 382 that made barbarian foederati a permanent fixture of Roman military power.
evt-fall-romulus-augustulus: A gold solidus bearing the face of Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire, deposed by Odoacer in 476.
evt-odoacer-italy: A silver coin struck under Odoacer, the Germanic warlord who deposed Romulus Augustulus and ruled Italy as king from 476 to 493.
evt-clovis-rule: Ary Scheffer's 19th-century painting of Clovis at the Battle of Tolbiac (496), the victory after which he reportedly pledged to convert to Christianity and unite the Franks.
evt-clovis-baptism: A medieval illuminated miniature depicting the baptism of Clovis by Bishop Remigius, with the Holy Spirit descending as a dove — the moment that allied the Frankish kingdom with Rome's church.
evt-theodoric-italy: A gold solidus of Theodoric the Great, the Ostrogothic king who ruled Italy from 493 to 526 and styled himself a Roman emperor while keeping Gothic warriors in command.
evt-boethius-consolation: A 1385 illuminated manuscript page showing Boethius presiding over a lecture (top) and imprisoned awaiting execution (bottom), the circumstances under which he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy.
evt-cassiodorus-vivarium: A medieval manuscript portrait of Cassiodorus Senator, the Roman statesman who withdrew from Ostrogothic court life to found the Vivarium monastery and scriptorium in Calabria around 540.
evt-vandal-kingdom-africa: A 16th-century illustration of an ancient Vandal warrior (labeled "Vuandal Antique"), representing the Germanic people who seized Roman North Africa in 429 and held it as an independent kingdom for over a century.
evt-visigothic-spain: A gold tremissis of Leovigild, the Visigothic king who unified most of the Iberian Peninsula under Gothic rule in the late sixth century.
evt-merovingian-decline: The Merovingian kingdoms at their greatest extent, divided into Neustria, Austrasia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine — a fragmentation that left real power in the hands of the mayors of the palace while the dynasty decayed.
evt-anglo-saxon-heptarchy: A 19th-century map of Anglo-Saxon Britain showing the seven kingdoms of the Heptarchy — Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Sussex, and Wessex — that emerged after the Germanic migrations.
evt-lombard-kingdom: A map showing the extent of the Lombard Kingdom of Italy at its height, with Langobardia Major in the north and the Duchy of Benevento in the south, surrounded by surviving Roman and Frankish territories.
evt-justinian-reign: The famous 6th-century mosaic portrait of Emperor Justinian I at the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna, one of the most recognizable images of any Byzantine ruler.
evt-corpus-juris-civilis: The ornate title page of a 1583 printed edition of the Corpus Iuris Civilis, the sweeping codification of Roman law commissioned by Justinian in the 6th century.
evt-hagia-sophia-completed: The Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, completed in 537 CE under Justinian — its vast dome remained the largest in the world for nearly a thousand years.
evt-plague-justinian: A medieval painting depicting plague victims in the streets as clergy minister to the dying, capturing the devastation of the Plague of Justinian that swept the empire from the 540s.
evt-lombard-invasion: Lombard burial goods from the 6th–7th century — helmet, swords, spearheads, and ornamental fittings — on display at the Museo Archeologico di Milano, artifacts of the warriors who seized Italy in 568.
evt-benedict-of-nursia: Hans Memling's portrait of Saint Benedict, founder of Western monasticism, holding his rule and pastoral staff — labeled 'Sanctus Benedictus' in the original panel.
evt-monte-cassino: Monte Cassino abbey, Benedict's mother house perched above the Liri valley in central Italy, rebuilt after its near-total destruction in World War II.
evt-rule-of-benedict: An 8th-century Old English manuscript of the Rule of Saint Benedict — an early copy of the text that structured monastic life across medieval Europe.
evt-gregory-the-great: Gregory the Great receiving divine inspiration, depicted in a 9th-century manuscript illumination showing the dove of the Holy Spirit whispering into his ear as he writes.
evt-iona-monastery: Iona Abbey on the Inner Hebrides island where Columba established his monastery in 563 AD, the beachhead of Irish Christianity's spread across northern Britain.
